title: Specify limit(0), nested limits, spawn_isolated under limit, and nested echo attribution
description:
## Why

fx-sz7 settled how a limited `spawn` meets cancellation (03 §6.1). Its reviews (rounds 80–86)
found four older gaps in `Tasks::limit` and the echo rule that predate it and that a checker
implementer would have to guess:

1. `limit(0)`: unspecified. Under §6.1 every spawn would wait until its scope is cancelled.
2. `limit` on an already limited `Tasks`: whether the inner count also counts against the outer.
   Attenuation suggests it must; 03 §6.1's shared count does not say.
3. `spawn_isolated` on a limited `Tasks`: whether the isolated task takes a slot.
4. TASK-2's echo bit across nesting: how a cancellation cause inside a nested scope relates to an
   outer child's echo bit, including a child that fails through a grandchild's `join` after an
   echo, and which cause wins when several cancel one scope.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §6.1 (limited spawn), TASK-2 (echo bit), §1.1 Tasks row.
- `design/reference.md` 7.1 (`limit`, `spawn_isolated`).
- `reviews/round81-consistency.md`, `round82-consistency.md`, `round83-consistency.md`, and
  `round84-codex.md` (out-of-scope sections).

## Scope

In scope: decide items 1–4 and state them in 03, and in the core only if it stays under D14's
budget. Out of scope: changing fx-sz7's decision.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each item with reasoning; nothing in `design/` contradicts it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge. The core is at 24,995 of 25,000 tokens. Item 4 may split
into its own bead if it grows.
close_reason: Decided in 03 §6.1 (limit(0), clones, chained counts, spawn_isolated) and TASK-2 (one cause per cancellation, nested and isolated attribution, failed joins). Reviews: rounds 87-90, 92 (Opus), 91, 93 (Codex, approve).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decision (03 §6.1 closing paragraph; TASK-2 echo paragraph; core unchanged, budget):
1. limit(0) panics, like chunks(0)/step_by(0). Every limited spawn from it would only wait until cancelled; denying spawn is done by not passing a Tasks. Rejected: NonZeroUsize parameter (port friction), silent no-op/unlimited (breaks attenuation).
2. limit on a limited Tasks adds a count and keeps the old one; a spawn through it takes a slot in each count at once (as LOCK-3 takes cells), so the outer bound holds and no spawn holds one count while waiting for another. Rejected: an independent fresh count (escapes the outer attenuation); sequential acquisition (hold-and-wait across counts).
3. spawn_isolated takes no slot: its caller waits for it, so running tasks do not grow, and a limited child calling it cannot deadlock on its own slot.
4. Echo attribution: a scope's cancellation has one cause, the first event that cancelled it. A checkpoint in a nested scope sets the outer child's bit only for a cancellation that reached the nested scope from the outer one; a cause inside the nested scope is reported by it and reaches the outer scope as the child's result. A child whose join of a sibling returns Err is also marked (the scope reports the sibling itself), fixing round 82's case of a child failing through a sibling's join and outranking the real cause.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after round 87 (B1, N1-N5): (1) limit(0) no longer panics: it returns a usable Tasks (checkpoint, shield, handle constructors), so limit(n.min(len)) on empty input works; a spawn under a zero count panics, like chunks(0). (2) Clones of a limited Tasks share its counts (capabilities are Clone with the same authority; otherwise cloning escapes the limit). (3) Sibling-join rule narrowed and widened: a join of one of this scope's children that returns Err WHILE THIS SCOPE IS CANCELLED sets the bit of the child it runs in, directly or in a nested scope. An unstarted echo in an uncancelled scope (fx-sz7) therefore marks nothing, and a joiner that propagates it fails normally. (4) Cause list adds the body's panic; an enclosing deadline at the same instant as the scope's own comes first. (5) Deadlock text covers shared counts; LOCK-3 analogy dropped; fairness between chained waiters left unspecified.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after round 88 (B1, N1-N3): a join that returns Err sets the bit exactly where a checkpoint at the same point, outside shield, would (cause and reach conditions included), replacing 'while this scope is cancelled'. So round 82's case is still an echo; a join in a scope cancelled by its own deadline, cancel(), an ancestor, or a nested scope's own cause marks nothing, and the joiner's error counts as TASK-4 already accepts for checkpoints. Checkpoints in a task the child waits for with spawn_isolated also set its bit. A spawn under a zero count always panics, even in a cancelled scope or under shield.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after round 89 (B1, N1-N3): the join rule's examples (which contradicted it in nested and uncancelled cases) are replaced by one unnested example: a child failing through x.join()? after a sibling's failure cancelled this scope is an echo. 'outside shield' became 'as if no shield were in force', so a join inside a user's shield still marks where an unshielded checkpoint would. The bit also covers scopes nested in an isolated task. 'has observed no such cancellation' became 'whose bit is clear' (TASK-2, §6.4).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after Codex round 91 (B1, N1): the failed-join rule now reads 'exactly where a checkpoint at the same point and moment would if no shield were in force there. Ignoring shield only lets that checkpoint see the enclosing scopes' cancellations; every scope keeps its actual first cause, so a nested scope that its own cause cancelled first still marks nothing.' This rules out replaying history without shields (Codex's case: H shields, S fails, nested s's child K fails independently, H joins K: s's actual cause is K, so H stays independent and bg reports K). Isolation is transitive ('directly or through further isolated calls'). TASK-2's echo paragraph rewrapped.

title: Decide how v1 imported Rust crate types are classified for Pure (RUST-2, RUST-4)
description:
## Why

Nothing states how the `Pure` check classifies types from v1 imported Rust
crates, and either default is wrong for common code. RUST-4 carries `Send`
and `Sync` over and RUST-2 makes `authority = []` wrappers
`#[trusted_pure]`, but neither says whether the deep rule walks a crate
type's private fields, or how real std's `Mutex`, `OnceLock`, or atomics
inside a crate count. If the rule walks fields, a `par_map` closure
capturing `&Regex` (the chapter's own example; its cache pool is `Sync`
through an `unsafe impl` over atomics and a mutex) is rejected. If it does
not, a `dashmap` or `once_cell::sync::Lazy` value is `Pure + Sync` and
parallel branches race on it. Found by round 34 (N6) while reviewing
fx-u18; fx-u18 removed `OnceLock` from Tide's admitted set, which makes the
question sharper for crates that use real std's.

## Evidence

- `reviews/round34-consistency.md` N6.
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §11, RUST-2 (wrappers
  `#[trusted_pure]` with `authority = []`) and RUST-4 (`Send`/`Sync` carry
  over; non-`Send` types import as `ThreadBound`).
- `design/02-memory.md` §9: the deep rule and the obligation that no
  operation on a `Pure` type returns a result depending on other tasks.
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §3.3: the determinism argument covers
  std and `unsafe impl Sync` in Tide crates, not imported crates.

## Scope

In scope:
- A v1 rule, under RUST-2 and RUST-4, for an imported type's `Pure` status:
  for example a per-crate or per-type declaration in `[rust-dependencies]`,
  a structural walk using real std's sync types as not `Pure`, or a
  conservative default with opt-in `#[trusted_pure]`-style overrides,
  each with how `&Regex` in `par_map` and `dashmap` come out.
- State the chosen rule in 03 §11 and 02 §9's v1 note, and say how the
  trust diff reports an override.

Out of scope:
- v0 text other than a pointer; implementation.

## Acceptance

- 03 §11 states how an imported type's `Pure` status is decided, with
  `regex::Regex` and `dashmap::DashMap` as worked verdicts, and the
  rejected alternatives with reasons.
- 03 §3.3's argument names imported crates as covered or as a listed trust
  hole.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction with D7, D18, RUST-2,
  or RUST-4.

## Implementation Notes

1. Read 03 §11 and RUST-2's FFI-3 claims first; prefer a manifest
   declaration over new syntax (D18).
2. Recommend a rule to the owner before writing; it changes which v1
   programs check.
3. Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.

## Verification

- A fresh reviewer finds no imported-crate type that is `Pure + Sync` under
  the rule yet lets parallel branches observe each other, other than ones
  the text lists as trust holes.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask before changing 01 D7 or D18.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: From round 36 N1 (fx-cze): io::Error is Rust's own type re-exported by Tide's std, and the Pure bound on io::Error::new/other is a checker obligation on admitted methods. Imported v1 crates and Rust callers (RUST-6) can build an io::Error with an unbounded, non-Pure payload and hand it to Tide code, where io::Error counts as Pure. The rule this bead decides must cover that, e.g. by treating an io::Error that crosses from an imported crate as a trust hole or by bounding at the wrapper.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Deferred 2026-10-21 by the owner-approved tier rule (GOVERNANCE.md, Merge Rule): v1 design work waits until v1 is scheduled; v0 work (fx-gcs, fx-kw8) comes first.

title: T074 Parse a small Ferox subset and emit structured diagnostics
description: Validate the syntax model and error-reporting shape before deeper semantic work begins.
design:
Primary question: What smallest Ferox syntax slice is sufficient to prove the parsing and structured-diagnostics direction?

Define and implement:

2. Error-tolerant parsing behavior for that subset.

The emphasis is proving parser and diagnostics shape, not maximizing grammar coverage.

title: Design sealed delegation boundaries for agent fleets
description:
## Why

Operators running many agents report review and merge as their main bottleneck and agents that delete or weaken the checks that judge them (research/13-agent-fleets.md, findings X1, X2, X6). Today a delegation boundary ("this interface is fixed, implement behind it") lives only in prompts, and agents cross it. Tide protects tests (`#[protected]`, design/01-design.md D14) but not signatures, contracts, or authority grants.

## Evidence

- design/01-design.md D14: `#[protected]` tests are part of the trust surface; agents cannot change them without approval.
- design/01-design.md D11: the trust surface diffs public signatures, authority, contracts, and trust holes between revisions.
- design/01-design.md D12: interface artifacts; a body edit never rechecks dependents.
- research/13-agent-fleets.md: "Needs, ranked" rows 2 and 3, and Implications item 3.

## Scope

In scope:
- A design for sealed delegation boundaries: an orchestrator seals a set of items (signatures, their contracts, their authority grants, and chosen tests); a delegate may change only bodies behind them; the checker rejects any change to a sealed item, and the trust diff reports attempts and any weakened `ensures`.
- Record the decision in design/01-design.md (D14 or a new decision), the rules in the owning chapter with rule IDs, and the agent-facing text in design/reference.md.

Out of scope:
- Implementation (no checker exists yet).
- Merge tooling and semantic merge (research/13 open question 2).

## Acceptance

- 01 states the feature, its tier, and rejected alternatives with reasons.
- The chapter rules say what is sealed, who may unseal (the approval path of D11), what the checker reports, and how the trust diff shows it.
- One worked example: an orchestrator seals an interface with a contract and a `Net` grant; a delegate's attempt to widen the grant or weaken the contract is rejected with a stable diagnostic code. The example may live in reference-companion.md with a core pointer: design/reference.md is at 24,989 of D14's 25,000 tokens (companion record; recount first), so new core text must be paid for: trim elsewhere, or put the detail in reference-companion.md with a one-line core pointer, and recount with scripts/count-tokens.sh. fx-jv9's reference fixes draw on the same headroom.

## Implementation Notes

1. Read research/13 and D18 first. fx-enq chose the Rust dialect, so the feature must be expressible as attributes or a toolchain lock file, not new syntax, and the admission driver (D18, architecture A), which gates every crate before rustc runs, is where a sealed-item check would sit.
2. Prefer a toolchain artifact (a lock of item hashes from D14's content hashing) over syntax, so it works on either path (research/13 open question 1).
3. Run one adversarial review of the design text (reviews/).

## Verification

- A fresh reviewer finds no blocking contradiction between 01, the chapter, and the reference.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the design needs a change to D11's approval model that the owner has not chosen.
close_reason: done

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Agent decision (2026-10-20), draft in working tree: sealed delegation boundaries are v0 core, recorded in D11 with rejected alternatives; rules SEAL-1..6 in 04 §11.1 with the worked example; core pointer in reference §11, agent text in companion §18; README v0 list. Mechanism: tide.seal lock (stable IDs + hashes), written only by tide seal. Entries: interface (path, signature, declared authority, contract use, spec-closure hash), whole (full definition; tests also cover test-only callees and attributes), manifest (grants, dependency grants, policies, uses). Admission driver rejects mismatches before rustc (FX0920, no override); tide review and the CI gate use the base's seal, and removing/changing an entry is FX0921 unless a D11 approval record (class unseal) covers it. No new key or approver class, so D11's approval model is unchanged (stop condition not hit). v0 review labels a removed ensures or added requires 'weakened' (04 §11). Core reference held at 24,996 tokens by trimming 13's tool-output detail. Next: review rounds (reviews/round43+), then Codex pass.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Done. Reviewed by Opus rounds 43-46, 48-50, 52 and Codex (gpt-6.1-sol, xhigh) rounds 47, 51, 53 (approve). Changes from review: per-configuration and per-target hashes (sealed targets listed; unlisted target is FX0920); SEAL-2 owns its hash, records what calls resolve to, and computes the spec-closure hash for every sealed fn; a whole type fixes every impl that applies to it except method bodies, with 'applies to' defined (self type names the type with any generic args, or the impl may hold for it, &/&mut/Box of it, or a crate-written type containing it; ambiguity counts as applying); test entries stop at interface entries; manifest entry covers the whole [contracts] table; SEAL-6 admits unsealed callers' resolution. Core reference 24,987 tokens.

title: T072 Create the Rust workspace skeleton and initial bootstrap crate boundaries
description: Start the narrow Rust bootstrap with the initial workspace and crate boundaries from the current implementation strategy.
design:
Primary question: What bootstrap workspace structure gives Ferox clean crate boundaries without locking in accidental architecture too early?

Define and implement:
1. Workspace layout and crate boundaries for syntax, diagnostics, formatter, CLI, and shared utilities.
2. Naming, dependency direction, and rules that prevent core logic from collapsing into the binary crate.
3. Hooks for the shared validation/observability harness so later tasks can add tests, fixtures, and tracing without reshuffling the workspace.
4. Basic contributor ergonomics for building, testing, and running the bootstrap path.
notes: Implemented the initial Rust workspace skeleton at the repo root with crates ferox_cli, ferox_driver, ferox_diag, ferox_syntax, ferox_ast, ferox_sem, and ferox_fmt. Added top-level tests/ corpus and e2e directories plus a workspace smoke script. Verified the bootstrap path with cargo test --workspace and scripts/test/e2e_workspace_smoke.sh.

title: T073 Implement source handling, spans, tokens, diagnostics core, and syntax scaffolding
description: Build the foundational frontend layer needed by both the parser and formatter.
design:
Primary question: What foundational frontend layer should Ferox build first so parser, formatter, and diagnostics work can proceed without rework?

Define and implement:
1. Source file representation, spans, and stable low-level location types.
2. Token model and syntax scaffolding suitable for error-tolerant parsing.
3. Diagnostics core aligned with the machine-facing tooling contract.
4. Integration points for the shared validation/observability harness.

This task should optimize for durable foundations, not clever abstractions.
notes: Implemented the foundational frontend substrate in the Rust bootstrap: source-file representation with line indexing, byte spans and location mapping, token kinds and bootstrap tokenization, structured diagnostics with primary/related labels and machine-contract-oriented fields, and a minimal syntax tree scaffold. Added unit coverage in ferox_diag and ferox_syntax, an integration test for the frontend foundation, and verified the path with cargo test --workspace plus the workspace smoke script.

title: Decide: a session runner that chains handoffs
description:
## Decision

Should Tide get a script that runs fresh headless sessions back to back from
`br` state, so a handoff no longer waits for the owner to start the next
session?

Recommendation: adopt, after the autonomous-run rules bead is decided. The
runner relies on agents leaving dead-ended beads blocked. Tide's "Decisions"
rule makes this an agent decision. Record it here, then do the work below or
close this as rejected.

Options considered:
- A Tide script. Recommended: Tide is the only caller.
- A generic runner in Starcompass. Not yet, because there is no second caller
  (AP-MINIMAL-001).
- One long session through compaction, as pstack does. Rejected: it goes
  against AP-SESSION-001.

## Why

AP-SESSION-001 ends a session with a handoff and the line "prime, then
continue <issue> from its handoff". Someone has to start that next session.
Owner direction, 2026-10-21: Tide runs autonomously, so a script should start
it. pstack avoids the step by keeping one chat alive through compaction, which
AP-SESSION-001 rejects.

## Evidence

- `scripts/count-tokens.sh` is the only existing script, and there is no
  runner yet.
- `git log origin/main..main` showed 69 unpushed commits on 2026-10-21. The
  owner pushes, so the runner must not.
- On 2026-10-21 a Claude session and Codex were both running in this
  checkout, and `.beads/` showed `br` lock files. Overlapping sessions are
  real, so the runner must not start one while another works here.
- `claude --help` lists `-p/--print` and `--max-budget-usd`. `codex exec` runs
  Codex non-interactively. `GOVERNANCE.md`'s review loop needs Codex.

## Scope

In scope:
- One script under `scripts/`, for example `scripts/autorun.sh`.
- A run log that `.gitignore` excludes.
- A few lines on the runner in `README.md`.

Out of scope:
- `GOVERNANCE.md`, the review loop, and any push or remote write.
- Changing how sessions prime, hand off, or close beads. Those belong to the
  imported protocols and the sibling rules bead.

## Acceptance

- Each iteration of one command does the following:
  - Takes a lock, or exits if another runner holds it.
  - Picks the work. That is an `in_progress` bead whose latest comment is a
    handoff, else the top `br ready` task that is not an epic, not deferred,
    and not labeled `owner`.
  - Starts a fresh headless session with "prime, then continue <id> from its
    handoff", or "prime, then work <id>".
  - Waits for it under a per-session timeout and budget.
  - Appends one log line: time, bead, outcome (closed, handed off, blocked,
    failed, timed out), and the new commit range.
- The runner stops and says why when any of these holds:
  - no work remains;
  - the same bead is handed off 3 times in a row without a new commit;
  - 2 sessions in a row fail or time out;
  - a total session or budget cap is reached.
- A dry-run mode with a stand-in agent command proves the selection and stop
  rules without spending tokens.

## Implementation Notes

1. Read `br --help`, and find how to get a bead's status, labels, and latest
   comment in a machine-readable form, with `--json` where available. Do not
   parse `.beads/` files.
2. Read `claude --help` for unattended permission and output flags. Choose
   the narrowest setting that lets a session commit and run `br`, `cargo`, and
   `codex`. Record the choice in the script's header comment.
3. Judge outcomes from `br` state and `git log` before and after the session,
   not from the session's own report.
4. Make the agent command overridable (for example `AUTORUN_AGENT`), so the
   dry run can use a stub.

## Verification

- A dry run with a stub agent that closes, hands off, or fails as told should
  pick the expected bead each time and stop on each condition above.
- `shellcheck scripts/autorun.sh` should pass, if shellcheck is installed.
- One real iteration on a small ready bead should leave one log line, and no
  push.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if `br` offers no machine-readable way to read status and comments.
  Record what is missing on this bead.
- Stop if unattended operation needs a permission setting broader than the
  repository work requires. Record the gap rather than widening it.
close_reason: Adopted: scripts/autorun.sh with offline test scripts/autorun-test.sh (22/22); reviewed fx-3md-r1 to r9, Codex approve at r9. One real-session iteration still to observe on the first run (see comment).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: From fx-9ag review (fx-9ag-r1-opus N4): br ready leaves out status=blocked, so a bead that dead-ends without the owner label is parked with no path back. The runner's selection and stop rules should say who revisits such beads and when. Find them with br list --status blocked; br blocked lists dependency-blocked beads only.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decision, 2026-10-21 (agent, per Decisions): adopt, as a Tide script (scripts/autorun.sh) with an offline test (scripts/autorun-test.sh). Permission choice: sessions run claude -p --permission-mode auto, the owner's default classifier-gated mode with hooks; bypassPermissions rejected as broader than the work needs. Remote writes are denied to sessions with --disallowedTools (git push, gh), and the runner stops if the upstream ref moves. Session exclusion: the lock keeps out runners; the runner refuses to start while any in_progress bead lacks a handoff as its latest comment, or, before new work, while the tree is dirty; sessions in other worktrees are invisible, so do not run it beside one. Blocked beads: listed when the run stops for the owner to review; never retried. Beyond the Acceptance: a session that ends without closing, blocking, or handing off counts as failed (fx-3md-r1-codex B5).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Review record: r1 Opus (read-only) revise 3 blocking + Codex request_changes 6 blocking, answered by a rewrite; Opus converge r2-r5 each changed something (blocked list on every stop; priority-order, .beads-only-commit, lock and prompt/bead-column tests; fail-closed lock kept against r5's release); r6 scoped Opus round strengthened tests; r7 Codex found one blocker (a hand-started continuation), fixed with a live claude/codex process check; r8 Opus confirmation found a vacuous scenario, fixed and mutation-checked; r9 Codex approve. Converge reached its 5-round cap before r6; the scoped r6 and the Codex re-checks closed it. Check: scripts/autorun-test.sh 22/22, three consecutive runs. Not yet run: the Verification's one real iteration. On 2026-10-21 the runner, run in Tide with a stub agent, stopped before any session because another agent's codex exec was working in the checkout (correct fail-closed behavior); the first owner-started run is that check.

title: T075 Build the first formatter on top of parsed syntax and source mapping
description: Prove that the syntax tree is usable for real tooling and that Ferox formatting rules are implementable.
design:
Primary question: What first formatter slice proves that Ferox can have canonical formatting on top of real parsed syntax?

Define and implement:
1. The initial formatting scope and style rules for the supported subset.
2. Formatting behavior over parsed syntax and source mapping rather than ad hoc text rewriting.
3. Snapshot/golden strategy for canonical output.
4. Observability that makes formatter decisions and mismatches debuggable.

This task should prove formatter viability and style stability, not cover the full language.
notes: Additional revision after syntax/tooling audit: formatter layout around imports, file-level docs, and declaration doc comments should follow an explicit comment-surface decision rather than informal assumptions from rustfmt or other tools.
close_reason: Superseded: the owner discarded the first Ferox design (archived in archive/v0-design/) for the first-principles redesign in fx-agent-first-redesign-tf4; this work no longer applies.

title: Define the regularized Ferox checked IR boundary and first lowering contract
description: The implementation strategy relies heavily on a regularized checked IR, but the queue still lacks an explicit task for defining its boundary and first lowering contract. This task should define what semantic information enters the first checked IR, what remains in CST/AST form, how ownership, error, and concurrency-relevant operations become explicit, and how the IR stays small enough for diagnostics, tooling, and later optimization.
design: Primary question: what should the first regularized Ferox checked IR contain, and where is the boundary between parsed syntax, lowered syntax, semantic analysis, and checked IR? Define: 1. the minimum IR shapes needed after parsing and initial semantic analysis; 2. how expressions, control flow, ownership-relevant operations, and Result/Option flows normalize; 3. source mapping and stable identity expectations; 4. what semantic passes operate before versus after IR creation; 5. explicit non-goals for the first IR.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what the first checked IR contains; what invariants it guarantees; how it preserves source mapping and stable IDs; and what stays out of scope. Include before/after examples from Ferox source to IR shape, rejected overgrown alternatives, validation expectations for lowering and identity preservation, and tracing requirements for CST/AST-to-IR transitions.
close_reason: Superseded: the owner discarded the first Ferox design (archived in archive/v0-design/) for the first-principles redesign in fx-agent-first-redesign-tf4; this work no longer applies.

title: Evaluate whether Ferox should adopt a small built-in ability model to reduce trait and marker complexity
description: Ferox now treats built-in semantic abilities as a serious design exploration, but the model is not yet resolved. This task is to evaluate whether a small built-in ability system for properties such as copy, drop, send, or share would make the language materially simpler and more analyzable than a broader trait or marker-based approach, and to define the boundary where abilities help versus where they would only create a second abstraction system.
design:
Primary question: Should Ferox adopt a small built-in ability model, and if so, what exactly belongs in it?

Evaluate this by comparing three options:
1. Built-in abilities for a very small set of semantic properties.
2. Traits/markers only.
3. A hybrid model with strict boundaries.

The analysis should define candidate abilities such as copy, drop, send, or share; explain how they interact with ownership, generics, and tooling; and identify the point where abilities simplify the language versus creating a second abstraction system.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- Does Ferox adopt built-in abilities at all?
- If yes, which abilities exist and what operations do they gate?
- Why is that better than traits/markers for Ferox specifically?
- What complexity costs or edge cases would the chosen model introduce?

Include:
- at least one worked example for the recommended model and one rejected alternative;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for ability checking and generic interaction, pass/fail corpus tests for gated operations, and end-to-end scripts that exercise representative language features using the chosen model;
- detailed logging/tracing requirements for ability resolution, gated-operation failures, and related diagnostics.
notes: Decision: Ferox does not adopt a general built-in ability system in v1. Keep built-in copy semantics as a special ownership property. Do not add user-facing drop, send, or share abilities in the current direction. Revisit only if later concurrency or linear-resource pressure proves one additional built-in property is simpler than explicit ownership, task-capture, and shared-wrapper rules.

title: Process inputs, output sinks, and exit codes
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) needs this surface to execute on the checked toolchain:
`trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §10.1 lists it as E1-P7, and no existing bead owns it.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P7, §10.2)`
- `design/reference.md §6.1, §6.2, §6.5, §6.8`

## Scope

Env (args, var, vars, current_dir, attenuations), Stdin (read_line, lines, read_to_string, read_to_end), stdout()/stderr() handles and the log sinks with root.log defaults, main returning (), Result<(), E: Debug>, or ExitCode with the stated exit codes, and sim.world.args/env_var/stdin and sim.records. Production std under crates/, built and admitted through tide-admit; no new
language semantics.

## Acceptance

A built binary reads its real arguments, environment, and standard input, writes standard output and error, and exits 0, 1 on Err, the ExitCode given, or 101 on panic; the same calls work against a SimRoot and appear in sim.records. Toolchain tests prove each item executes, not only type-checks.
Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

title: Define authoritative byte-offset spans with derived human and editor position views
description: Ferox needs one authoritative source-location unit across parser, diagnostics, formatter, and machine-readable outputs. This task should decide whether authoritative spans are byte offsets, how line/column data is derived from them, and how future editor-encoding conversions layer on top without introducing multiple competing position systems.
design: Primary question: should Ferox make byte offsets the sole authoritative internal span unit, with human-facing line/column data and future editor-specific encodings derived from that base? Compare byte-authoritative and character-authoritative models, decide indexing conventions, and define how diagnostics JSON, parser traces, and formatter/source reproduction consume the result.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task explicitly chooses the authoritative span unit, defines the derivation model for line/column data and later editor encodings, explains compatibility implications for diagnostics and tooling APIs, provides multibyte examples, and rejects competing multi-authority models.
notes: Decision: keep this idea. Ferox should use UTF-8 byte offsets as the sole authoritative internal span unit, with half-open ranges over source text. Human-facing line/column data should be derived views rather than competing primary coordinates, and future editor/LSP encodings should be layered on top as conversions, not as additional authoritative span systems. Rationale: this matches the most robust tooling practice from rust-analyzer and tree-sitter, composes cleanly with full-fidelity source preservation, and minimizes semantic drift in parser, diagnostics, formatter, and machine-readable outputs. Apply in v1 immediately as a bootstrap contract, before T074/T075/T076 harden more source-facing behavior. This is not a later enhancement; it is a foundational source-model decision. Follow-on tasks still need to settle invalid offsets, line-span variants, and preservation-versus-normalization details.

title: Run the D18 feasibility spike for the checked Rust dialect
description:
Owner decision (2026-10-19, fx-enq): Tide's v0 direction is a checked dialect of Rust (design/01-design.md D18), gated by this bounded feasibility spike. Until it passes, the other decisions keep their current text; if it fails, the new-language design stands.

Context: research/15-rust-dialect.md (experiments F1, F2; per-feature classification; Recommendation) and reviews/dialect-codex.md. Mechanism shown so far on stock rustc 1.96: user crates compiled with --extern std=<facade rlib> load the facade through normal std injection, and std::fs::read and extern crate std both resolve to the facade. Not confined by that alone (F2): safe core::arch::x86_64::__cpuid and ptr.addr() vary per run, core atomics need no Tasks, and std's inherent f64 methods (sin) beat a facade trait method.

Scope: a throwaway prototype outside design/, small enough for one session; not the v0 checker. Rust code here is agent-written (GOVERNANCE); it is a spike, so converge and the supervisor apply only if it is kept as production code.

Acceptance (each item can fail):
1. Facade std providing the v0 capability, task, Shared, and channel surface, injected by --extern std=.
2. An admission-allowlist prototype (resolving paths, methods, and impls) that rejects F2's four leaks, core::include_str!/core::env!, and any driver flag outside its fixed set.
3. #[requires]/#[ensures] toolchain macros, and a function-level loop-invariant lowering that fails on `for _ in 0..0 { invariant!(false) }` and on an invariant false at loop exit.
4. The Pure companion-supertrait spelling compiles, and the prototype rejects an impure implementor.
5. Facade float functions return canonical NaN bits and Tide's libm results.
6. Eon's orbit-protocol (~/pjs/eon/eon, read-only; copy it) builds as a Tide crate and Orbit builds against it unchanged.
7. A size count of each prototype part, replacing research/15's unmeasured cost comparison.

Outcome: record pass/fail per criterion in research/15 (or a short follow-up note) and on this bead; on pass, the owner approves applying D18's listed decision changes to 01 and the chapters (a separate bead).
close_reason: Gate passed (owner, 2026-10-19): all 7 criteria met at prototype scale; checker architecture A then B; recorded in D18 and research/15 Spike results. Follow-up bead applies D18's decision changes.

comments.text: Started (2026-10-19): spike code in spikes/d18/ (throwaway; facade/, macros/, examples/, eon/, scripts/ for criteria 1,3,5,6; admit/ for the nightly rustc_private allowlist and Pure checker, criteria 2,4). Results will be rerun by the main session before recording.

comments.text: Results (2026-10-19), recorded in research/15 'Spike results': all 7 criteria met at prototype scale; main session reran scripts/all.sh (exit 0) and admit/scripts/run-tests --facade (0 failures), plus C6/A5 from a clean copy that fetches Eon at 2332d4b. Gaps: CLAUSE-7 panic-as-violation, sampled budgets, ..= next-index (C3); orbit-protocol builds unchanged but needs ~21 edits for admission (f32 to_bits/from_bits x20, debug_assert_eq! x1). New findings: admission on rustc resolution needs a pinned nightly rustc_private driver (architecture A gate+oracle vs B own front end); more leaks (Path I/O methods, last_os_error, recv_timeout, __rt::root, raw pointer impls); allowlist keys churn per pin; cargo can inject the facade via std = { package = tide_std }. Awaiting owner: declare the gate passed, choose checker architecture, then a separate bead applies D18's decision changes.

title: Decide: autonomous-run rules in the local overlay
description:
## Decision

Should Tide's local overlay add rules for unattended runs: a done condition
that is never weakened, "a plateau is not a stop", and leaving a dead-ended
bead blocked so work moves on?

Recommendation: adopt. Tide's "Decisions" rule makes this an agent decision.
Decide, record the reasons here, then do the work below or close this as
rejected.

Owner direction, 2026-10-21: Tide should run autonomously, without the owner
making calls or starting sessions.

Rejected, 2026-10-21: switching Tide from Starcompass to pstack
(`cursor/plugins/pstack`) to move faster. pstack keeps one long chat going
through compaction. Its resume note goes to `/tmp`, its session pickup reads
Cursor transcript paths, and its pause playbook does not run under "keep
going". It is also unversioned and changes almost daily, so an unattended
agent's rules would move under it. The ideas worth taking from it are in this
bead and the session-runner bead.

## Why

An unattended agent needs three rules Tide does not yet state. (1) What done
means, as a check it cannot quietly weaken. (2) What to do on a plateau. (3)
How to leave a bead it cannot finish, so the session runner (sibling bead) can
move to the next one instead of retrying the same bead forever.

The imported protocols cover most of the rest. AP-PLAN-001 asks for acceptance
that names outcomes and cheapest falsifiers. AP-SESSION-001 owns handoffs and
token budgets. AP-SCOPE-001 stops on a missing scope choice. This bead adds
only the missing rules, adapted from pstack's autonomous-run playbook
(`cursor/plugins`, `pstack/skills/poteto-mode/playbooks/autonomous-run.md`).

## Evidence

- `.agent-protocols.local.md`, "Decisions": technical decisions are the
  agent's, and the owner sets scope, priorities, and direction.
- `AGENTS.md`, AP-SESSION-001: the handoff is an issue comment, and the next
  session primes from it.
- `AGENTS.md`, AP-PLAN-001: append only needed contracts, decisions, and
  failures to an issue. So per-iteration notes do not belong on beads, and the
  runner's run log holds them instead.

## Scope

In scope:
- A short "Autonomous runs" section in `.agent-protocols.local.md`.
- The regenerated `AGENTS.md` and `.agent-protocols.json`.

Out of scope:
- Canonical protocol text, and any exception in
  `.agent-protocols.exceptions.json`. The new rules must add to the imports,
  not narrow them.
- `GOVERNANCE.md`, and the runner script.

## Acceptance

- The overlay states the following, in a few lines:
  - Before work, take the bead's done condition from its Acceptance as a
    runnable check or observation. Never weaken it to close the bead.
  - A plateau is not a stop. Change approach.
  - A dead end ends the bead's attempt: the same check still fails after
    distinct approaches, or the bead needs an owner scope call. Then comment
    on the bead with what was tried and why it failed, set
    `br update <id> --status blocked`, label it `owner` when only the owner
    can unblock it, and end the session. Never wait for an answer.
- `AGENTS.md` and `.agent-protocols.json` are rendered, not hand-edited, and
  the drift checks pass.

## Implementation Notes

1. Read the overlay and the imported AP-SCOPE-001, AP-PLAN-001, and
   AP-SESSION-001 text in `AGENTS.md`. Word the section so it adds to them and
   does not conflict.
2. Render from a clean Starcompass checkout at the commit the manifest
   records (`source.commit` in `.agent-protocols.json`), with the flags
   Starcompass's README "Commands" section gives. Pass `--profile regular` and
   the four Tide paths.
3. Review per `GOVERNANCE.md`, Merge Rule, as a docs-only change.

## Verification

- `starcompass check-consumer --overlay .agent-protocols.local.md --exceptions .agent-protocols.exceptions.json --manifest .agent-protocols.json --agents AGENTS.md`
  should exit 0.
- `starcompass check` with the same flags, run from the pinned checkout,
  should exit 0.
- `git diff --stat` should show only the overlay, `AGENTS.md`, and
  `.agent-protocols.json`, plus Beads state.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if a rule can only be stated by narrowing an imported protocol. That
  would need an exception, and exceptions need owner approval.
- Stop if the pinned Starcompass checkout cannot render cleanly.

## Maintenance Notes

- Rejected, 2026-10-21: a per-iteration comment on the bead, as pstack's
  `show-me-your-work` does. It conflicts with AP-PLAN-001's "append only
  needed" rule, so the runner's log holds that record instead.
- If a second repository wants these rules, propose them for Starcompass
  rather than copying the overlay.
close_reason: Adopted: 'Autonomous runs' section in .agent-protocols.local.md, rendered from the pinned Starcompass e7c3a25 (check and check-consumer pass). Reviewed fx-9ag-r1 (Opus revise, Codex approve, plus a fresh-agent behavior probe that followed the rules), r2 Opus approve, r3 Codex approve.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decision, 2026-10-21 (agent, per Decisions): adopt. The overlay gains an 'Autonomous runs' section with the three rules as the bead states them, plus one clarification: an owner scope call excludes technical questions, which Decisions makes the agent's, so a dead end never parks a technical question on the owner. Reasons: the owner asked for unattended runs; the imported protocols say what done means (AP-PLAN-001) and how to hand off (AP-SESSION-001) but not that the done check cannot be weakened, that a plateau is not a stop, or how to leave a dead-ended bead so a runner can move on. The section only adds to the imports, so no exception is needed. Rendered from a clean clone at the pinned e7c3a25; the manifest changes only its overlay hash.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after fx-9ag-r1 (Opus B1): the clause now forbids weakening what done means, not changing it; a technical correction that keeps or strengthens the check is the agent's. Also added: close only when the check passes; the trigger is a run the owner does not attend; distinct approaches means at least two that differ in mechanism; budgets still apply; a scope-call comment names the choice and a recommended answer. 'End the run' replaces the Acceptance's 'end the session' to match AP-PLAN-001's run, which returns control at a block.

title: Define constructor and visibility discipline so public types do not imply public construction
description: Evaluate a stricter constructor and visibility model for Ferox where module boundaries help preserve invariants. The goal is to make public types, public fields, exported constructors, and private construction rights cohere cleanly without drifting into a complex visibility lattice.
close_reason: completed

title: Separate full-fidelity source preservation from formatter output normalization
description: Ferox should preserve original source text and line endings in its full-fidelity source model while allowing the formatter to produce canonical output as a separate layer. This task should make that separation explicit so parser, formatter, diagnostics, and source reproduction do not blur preservation and normalization semantics.
design: Primary question: how should Ferox separate source preservation from formatter normalization? Define the contract between full-fidelity source storage, CST/source reproduction, formatter output canonicalization, and line-ending handling so preservation and normalization never compete for authority.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task states exactly what source fidelity must be preserved, what the formatter may normalize, how recovered/uncertain regions behave, and how machine-readable tooling distinguishes preserved source from formatted output.
notes: Decision: keep this idea. Ferox should treat full-fidelity source preservation and formatter normalization as separate layers with different authority. The preserved source model remains the ground truth for byte spans, comment/doc attachment, reproduction, recovery, and tooling that needs exact original text. Formatter output is a derived canonical rendering that may normalize layout and line endings according to formatter policy, but it must not redefine what the original source was. Recovered or uncertain regions should preserve original text rather than pretending formatting succeeded there. Machine-readable tooling should distinguish original-source spans/text from formatted output explicitly instead of conflating them. Rationale: this matches the needs of full-fidelity CST tooling and avoids the common mistake of letting formatter behavior become the accidental source model. Apply in v1 immediately as part of the bootstrap source and formatter contract, before T075 hardens formatting behavior. This is a foundational contract decision, not a later polishing step.

title: Redesign Ferox from first principles as an agent-first safe, fast, verifiable language
description:
Redesign Ferox from first principles as a language for agent-written software: as safe and fast as Rust, lighter and much faster to compile, strongly typed, with optional machine-checked proofs, and ideal for AI coding agents (Opus-class models) to write, check, and maintain. The owner loves Rust and Bend; the design may inherit from Bend, interoperate with it, or ignore it.

Owner decision (2026-10-19): the previous Ferox design and architecture may be discarded entirely. Reason from first principles, research the web and papers, delegate research to subagents, and update the repository as the design develops.

Acceptance:
- research/ holds cited evidence reports covering memory models, compile speed, verification, LLM coding empirics, agent-native tooling, effects and capabilities, type system core, Bend/HVM, concurrency, adoption and interop.
- design/ holds a coherent language design with stated principles, core semantics, and explicit rejected alternatives with reasons.
- Independent adversarial reviews (including a second model) find no remaining blocking objection, and each objection is recorded as resolved or deliberately accepted.
- A fresh agent given only the design can write correct small programs in the language (in-context learnability trial).
- README and the repository guide describe the new direction; superseded documents are archived, not silently deleted.
close_reason: Acceptance met; round-7 second-model review approves

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision (2026-10-19): do not compete with Bend. At most a few similarities. Preferred: a language that works in tandem with Bend (Bend 2), or simply a Rust replacement. Research subagents that hit the web-search limit may be relaunched where the gap matters.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Design decision (round 2, prompted by reviews/round2-simplicity.md): split into a v0 core and later tiers. v0 core cuts Frozen (Pure+Sync), the lock keyword (Shared::with/with2 with Pure closures), par blocks (library join/par_map), field-borrow declarations, Shape, FFI, Rust import, exercised authority, evented runtime, Bend boundary; contracts are executable only (prove, final, views, laws later); child panics propagate to the scope as in std::thread::scope; Encode/Decode JSON only; from-syntax provisional pending an E1 arm against Rust lifetime syntax. Proofs remain the designed later tier.

comments.text:
Handoff (2026-10-19, end of first redesign session).

State:

- design/01-design.md draft 3 owns decisions D0-D17 with a Tiers table (v0 core / v1 / later). Thesis: no ambient authority + whole-program deterministic simulation + trust surface on a Rust-familiar surface with fast builds; contracts support it; Bend 2 tandem, not competition.
- design/reference.md teaches only v0 (about 19k tokens). Chapters 02-memory, 03-authority-concurrency, 04-contracts are normative but were written before draft 3; a sync pass to draft 3 was running at handoff (check git log for "Sync chapters").

Next step: if trials/e1-round2 exists, grade it like trials/e1/grading.md against draft 3 and the reference; then run a round-3 review (consistency + Codex) on draft 3 and the synced chapters.

title: State and test the guarantee that unreviewed branches are safe to check and test without a VM
description:
## Why

Fleet operators wrap each agent in a VM or microVM because building and testing an unreviewed branch runs arbitrary code: build scripts, proc macros, and tests with ambient I/O (research/13-agent-fleets.md, findings X3 and X8). Tide's design implies that running `tide check`, `tide test`, and `tide sim` on an unreviewed branch can reach only the holes its trust surface lists, but no document states that as a guarantee, names its exceptions, or says how it is tested.

## Evidence

- design/01-design.md D7 (no ambient authority), D13 (Tide packages run no build scripts or install hooks; an imported Rust crate's build script runs sandboxed), D11 (trust holes: `unsafe`, FFI), D15 (simulation).
- design/01-design.md D18 (decided by fx-enq): the admission driver owns every rustc invocation and gates each crate before rustc runs; no build scripts or proc macros run for Tide crates except the toolchain's; the facade std and the admission allowlist close ambient access. spikes/d18/examples/leaks.rs lists what the facade alone does not confine.
- research/12-newcomer-sweep.md: kernel enforcement (capability analysis compiled into a kernel sandbox) was adopted as an idea.
- research/13-agent-fleets.md: "Needs, ranked" row 4 and Implications item 4.

## Scope

In scope:
- A stated guarantee, with a rule ID, of what `tide check`, `tide test`, and `tide sim` may do on an unreviewed branch: which capabilities the test harness grants, what the simulator grants, and the complete list of holes (`unsafe` grants, `ffi` grants, the Bend boundary, foreign effects without simulator models).
- How the holes are surfaced before running (the trust diff) and how kernel enforcement backs the guarantee.
- Conformance tests the guarantee implies, listed by rule ID for the future checker.

Out of scope:
- Implementing a sandbox or the checker.

## Acceptance

- 01 (D13 or D11) states the guarantee and its holes; the owning chapter carries it as a numbered rule with its conformance tests listed.
- 01 also states the complement (owner's scope clarification, comment of 2026-10-19): a microVM or OS sandbox per agent session, no VM per test run, kernel enforcement for the deployed process, and what a microVM does not give.
- The reference says, in agent-facing terms, when an unreviewed branch is safe to test without a VM. design/reference.md is at 24,989 of D14's 25,000 tokens (companion record; recount first), so new core text must be paid for: trim elsewhere, or put the detail in reference-companion.md with a one-line core pointer, and recount with scripts/count-tokens.sh. fx-jv9's reference fixes draw on the same headroom.

## Implementation Notes

2. Name every exception rather than claiming totality.
3. Run one adversarial review of the text (reviews/), asking the reviewer to construct an escape.

## Verification

- A fresh reviewer cannot construct an unreviewed-branch escape that the stated holes do not list, or each escape found is recorded and closed.

## Stop Conditions

Agents run arbitrary shell commands (git, package managers, curl), which only a microVM or OS confinement (Landlock, seccomp) can bound, so the design should state the complement explicitly: microVM or OS sandbox per agent session; no VM per test run, because Tide tests and seeded simulations run in-process with only granted capabilities and virtual time; and kernel enforcement (research/12) derives an OS sandbox for the deployed process from its declared authority. Also state what a microVM does not give: protection of credentials inside the VM, review evidence, or bounds in production (research/13, X8 and E6).

comments.text:
Decisions (agent, 2026-10-20), drafted in 03 §2.6 RUN-1..5, D13, companion 19:

Reason: rustc has open soundness bugs (rust-lang/rust#25860, cve-rs) that let safe code forge a capability, so a type-level-only claim would overclaim. Results report sandbox: full|partial|none.

- Surfacing: tide review <base> prints run: covered | not covered; covered = no added/widened grant, no new Rust crate/build script/Bend dep, no new hole, no change in a module holding a hole (unsafe soundness is module-scoped), no new version of a granted package.

title: Decide the Pure status of std types that erase a Send + Sync payload (io::Error, Waker; owner decision)
description:
## Why

Std types that erase a `Send + Sync` payload have no stated `Pure` status,
which opens a determinism hole in v0 parallel regions. If `io::Error::new`
or `io::Error::other` is admitted with Rust's signature
(`E: Into<Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>`) and `io::Error` is `Pure` (the
default reading, since 02 §9 does not list it), a user error type whose
`Display` runs `Shared::with` lets two `join` branches observe each other's
order: `join(|| e1.to_string(), || e2.to_string())` captures only
`&io::Error`, yet the shared log ends `[1, 2]` or `[2, 1]` by schedule, and
authority-free code runs a blocking lock. `core::task::Waker`, built safely
by `Waker::from(Arc<W>)` for `W: alloc::task::Wake` holding a `Sender`, is a
second route. Found by round 35 (N1) while reviewing fx-u18; it predates
fx-u18.

## Evidence

- `reviews/round35-consistency.md` N1: the full construction and both
  routes.
- `design/02-memory.md` §9: the deep rule "looks through every field,
  private ones included"; applied to std's own fields it would make `Vec`
  not `Pure` through its raw pointer, so std's types must take their status
  from the table, which names neither `io::Error` nor `Waker`.
- `design/02-memory.md` §9 "What std must provide in return": "No operation
  on a `Pure` type may return a result that depends on other tasks"
  implies `io::Error` cannot be `Pure` with an unbounded payload, but no
  text states the decision.
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` ADMIT-1: the "at least" list names
  neither `core::task` nor `alloc::task::Wake`; D8 and reference 7 exclude
  only `async`, `Future`, `Pin`, and executors.
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §3.3: "`Pure` arguments reach no
  capability or handle" fails here if `io::Error` is `Pure`.
- `design/reference.md` 92–94: std error types are `Send + Sync`.

## Decision needed (owner)

How is `io::Error`'s erased payload handled? Options: (a) bound the payload
of `io::Error::new` and `io::Error::other` by `Pure` (a Tide std signature
divergence; cheap, since `io::Error` appears in most `Result`s and stays
`Pure`); (b) classify `io::Error` as not `Pure` (breaks authority-free code
that returns `io::Result`); (c) another shape. Round 35 recommends (a).
Recommend before writing; this changes which programs check.

## Scope

In scope:
- the decision above, stated in 02 §9 and in the std signature text that
  owns `io::Error`;
- add `core::task` and `alloc::task::Wake` to ADMIT-1's "at least" list
  (`FX0520`), under D8, and to reference 6.9 if core tokens allow;
- one sentence in 02 §9: std's types take their `Pure` status from the
  table and their type arguments, not from a walk of std's private fields;
- an audit of std's other payload-erasing types (`Box<dyn Error + Send +
  Sync>` conversions, `Any` payloads such as panic payloads, and any `dyn`
  field in a std type) against the 02 §9 obligation, listing each verdict.

Out of scope:
- v1 imported crates (separate bead).
- Changing 01 D7 or D8 without asking.

## Acceptance

- 02 §9, 03 ADMIT-1 and §3.3, and the reference agree on `io::Error`'s and
  `Waker`'s status, and the round-35 construction no longer type-checks
  under the stated rules.
- The audit's list is recorded in the review or in 02.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction and no new
  construction of the same shape.

## Implementation Notes

1. Ask the owner the decision first.
2. Find where Tide std's `io::Error` constructors are specified
   (`grep -rn "io::Error" design/`).
3. Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.

## Verification

- A fresh reviewer asked to rebuild round 35's N1 construction, or another
  through an erasing std type, cannot.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask before changing 01 D7 or D8.
- The core reference is at 24,969 of D14's 25,000 tokens (companion "Core
  count" line); recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh design/reference.md`
  and pay for any core addition with a cut, or put it in the companion.
close_reason: io::Error::new/other admit only alloc's four From impls (Pure error, String, &str, Cow<str>); std types walked with raw-pointer and erased-payload exceptions; fmt::Arguments/Formatter not Pure; core::task/alloc::task outside ADMIT-1. Opus rounds 36-38, 40-41; Codex rounds 39 (request_changes) and 42 (approve). Core 24,996 tokens.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decision (agent, under AGENTS.md 'Decisions', 2026-10-20): (a) Tide std's io::Error::new and io::Error::other take E: Into<Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> + Pure, so io::Error stays Pure and io::Result, NetError, TaskError are unaffected. Rejected (b) io::Error not Pure: it would strip Pure from every error enum wrapping it and from authority-free code returning io::Result. core::task and alloc::task (Waker, Context, Wake) go outside ADMIT-1: they exist only for async (D8). Audit of std types that erase a payload: io::Error (bounded by Pure); Box/Rc/Arc<dyn Trait>, dyn Any, Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> (not Pure by the dyn rule unless a Pure companion trait); fmt::Arguments (neither Send nor Sync, so no branch shares one); Waker/Context (not admitted); Panicked carries a String; TaskError, LockError, NetError, UrlError, Cancelled, json::Error hold data or io::Error. 02 §9 states std's types take their Pure status from the table and their type arguments, not a walk of std's private fields.

title: Define invalid-offset behavior for Ferox source locations and line index conversions
description: Ferox should define what happens when a requested offset falls in the middle of a multibyte codepoint, beyond file bounds, or on otherwise invalid boundaries. This task should settle whether invalid offsets are rejected, rounded, clamped, or reported structurally, and it should align parser, diagnostics, and tooling behavior on that choice.
design: Primary question: what should Ferox do when an offset is out of bounds or lands in the middle of a multibyte codepoint? Define invalid offset behavior for parser utilities, diagnostics rendering, line-index conversions, and future tooling APIs, including whether failures are structural errors, option-like absence, or explicit diagnostics-only behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task defines invalid offset behavior for in-bounds non-boundary offsets, out-of-bounds offsets, empty files, and line-ending edge cases; aligns parser and diagnostics expectations; and includes examples showing why Ferox rejects silent rounding/clamping by default if that is the chosen model.
notes: Decision: keep this idea. Ferox should reject invalid offsets by default instead of silently rounding or clamping them. Offsets that are out of bounds or that land in the middle of a UTF-8 codepoint should be treated as invalid for source-location conversions and structured utility APIs. Safe conversion APIs should return explicit absence or structured failure; internal assertion-style helpers may panic in debug-only or clearly internal contexts, but machine-readable outputs and parser-facing helpers must not silently coerce to a nearby boundary. Rationale: this matches rust-analyzer's try_line_col/offset discipline and Rust's own char-boundary model, and it avoids hidden drift in diagnostics, formatting, and future tooling. Apply in v1 immediately as part of the bootstrap source-location contract, before T074/T075/T076 stabilize more offset conversions. This is a foundational behavior choice, not a later ergonomics feature. Follow-on work still needs to specify line-span variants and preservation-versus-normalization semantics before fx-e1i closes.

title: Later-tier review findings (v1 and Later)
description:
## Why

Owner decision, 2026-10-21: later-tier review findings no longer block or
restart a review loop. They are recorded here instead, so they are neither
lost nor fixed early. The rule lives in `GOVERNANCE.md`, "Merge Rule".

The test (GOVERNANCE.md): a finding blocks when its fix would change a tier
the change edits or an earlier one. It comes here only when its fix would
change later-tier text alone that the change does not edit. A v0 rule that
overreaches into a later-tier feature is a v0 defect and blocks: for example
`reviews/round96-consistency.md` B1, where TASK-3's abandonment rule caught
an in-process Bend kernel and the fix went into TASK-3.

Evidence for the change: since the Codex rule, beads took about 6 review
rounds each (fx-arx 14, fx-sz7 about 10).

## How to use

- A reviewer or author who meets a later-tier finding adds a comment here:
  the review round, the file and line, the tier, and the finding in a few
  lines. One comment per finding.
- This bead stays deferred. When v1 design work is scheduled, triage its
  comments into beads, then close it.

## Acceptance

- Every later-tier finding from a review round after 2026-10-21 appears here
  as a comment, or in a bead filed from one.

title: Define the Ferox source-text, span, and line-ending contract for diagnostics, parser, and tooling
description: The bootstrap code now uses UTF-8 Rust strings, byte spans, line-column mapping, and newline-sensitive source handling, but the spec does not yet define that contract explicitly. This task should define the Ferox source-text model for parser, diagnostics, formatter, and machine-readable outputs so later tooling does not accidentally diverge on encoding, span meaning, or line-ending treatment.
design: Primary question: what is the exact source-text and location contract Ferox uses across parser, diagnostics, and tooling? Define: 1. source file encoding assumptions; 2. whether primary spans are byte-based, character-based, or both; 3. how line and column data is derived; 4. what newline normalization or preservation rules apply; 5. how diagnostics JSON and formatter/source reproduction interact with this contract.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: Ferox source encoding assumptions; the authoritative span model; line and column derivation rules; newline handling; and validation/logging expectations. Include concrete examples for multibyte text and line endings, rejected alternative models, compatibility implications for diagnostics JSON, and corpus/e2e expectations for source mapping behavior.
notes: Synthesis decision: keep the overall source-text contract and apply it in v1 immediately. Ferox should use UTF-8 source text with byte offsets as the sole authoritative internal span unit, represented as half-open ranges over preserved original source text. Human-facing line/column data is derived from byte offsets rather than stored as competing primary coordinates. Invalid offsets, including offsets inside a multibyte codepoint or outside file bounds, should be rejected by safe conversion APIs rather than silently rounded or clamped. Ferox should explicitly model both line spans excluding trailing line breaks and line spans including them; the excluding-break form is the default logical line-content view, while the including-break form is used explicitly for physical-layout and formatter-sensitive operations. Full-fidelity source preservation and formatter normalization are separate layers: preserved source remains the ground truth for spans, recovery, and reproduction, while formatted output is a derived canonical rendering that may normalize layout and line endings without redefining the original source. This is a foundational v1 bootstrap contract that should be locked before T074/T075/T076 stabilize parser, formatter, diagnostics, or machine-readable source locations.

title: Close cancellation gaps: output/status orphan child, exists, owned-buffer errors, write counts
description:
## Why

The fx-ms8 reviews (rounds 95–97) found cancellation gaps that predate it:

1. A cancelled `Command::output()` or `status()` can orphan its child. Both are checkpoints that
   start a `Child` internally; cancelled after the spawn, the call drops the running `Child`, and
   the caller cannot `kill` or `wait` it. The Receivers note uses exactly this outcome to justify
   `wait_with_output`'s `&mut self`.
2. `Fs::exists` returns `bool` but is a checkpoint, so it has no error to carry a cancellation.
3. The error type of `read_owned` and `write_owned` is never named, so nothing says how the `Vec`
   comes back inside it (TASK-3).
4. A cancelled socket or pipe write may have reached the peer, but its error carries no byte count.
5. Core 7.2 says joins, scope exit, and `File::close` "are never interrupted" without saying that
   this makes cleanup deadlines soft (TASK-5); agents may treat them as hard.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 (Proc row, Receivers note, Owned buffers), TASK-3,
  TASK-5.
- `design/reference.md` 6.x (`Fs`), 7.2.
- `reviews/round95-consistency.md`, `round96-consistency.md`, `round97-consistency.md`
  (out-of-scope sections).

## Scope

In scope: decide each item in 03 (for example, `output`/`status` kill and reap the child before
returning a cancellation; `exists` under cancellation; name the owned-buffer error type; whether a
cancelled write reports a count), and state in the core only what fits D14's budget. Out of scope:
TASK-3's rules settled by fx-ms8.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each item with reasoning; nothing in `design/` contradicts it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge. The core is at 24,996 of 25,000 tokens.
close_reason: Five cancellation gaps decided in 03; reviews r1-r5, Codex approve at r5

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Baseline, 2026-10-21: claimed by session tide-96; work on branch fx-e3t in worktree ../tide-fx-e3t from main 76dfe06 (main checkout dirty with fx-3md's uncommitted runner work, untouched). Docs-only: review rounds per GOVERNANCE.md; first check is the core recount with scripts/count-tokens.sh.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decisions, 2026-10-21 (agent, per Decisions), in 03 §1.1, TASK-3, TASK-5, TASK-6:
1. A cancelled output()/status() whose child has started tries to kill it, closes its own ends of the child's pipes, waits for it to exit (shielded) even if the kill failed, and returns Cancelled; a failed kill (e.g. EPERM for a setuid child) is logged as warn!. Leaving the child running orphans it; returning the kill error drops the only handle; keeping pipe readers open can deadlock a surviving child (r2 B1).
2. Fs::exists -> io::Result<bool>, as std::fs::exists; Ok(false) only for NotFound.
3. read_owned/write_owned return Result<Vec<u8>, io::BufError>, after IntoInnerError's shape (error, into_error, into_inner, into_parts, From for io::Error) plus kind, is_cancelled, written; read_owned appends one read into spare capacity, write_owned writes all.
4. A cancellation error from a single write means no byte was accepted; accepted bytes return Ok(n). write_owned reports partial progress via BufError::written(); write_all keeps io::Result<()>, as in Rust.
5. Joins, scope exit, and uncancellable system calls make every deadline soft (TASK-5, TASK-6, core 7.2).
Also: conformance stub std's Fs::exists now returns io::Result<bool>. Core: 24,996 of 25,000 tokens (scripts/count-tokens.sh). Deferred for budget: naming BufError in core 2.2. Out of scope, not done: simulated short writes (r1 N2). For fx-djp: std-emitted warn! under SINK-9 (commented there).
Proof: conformance/run.sh exit 0 (3 PASS, 2 AWAITS CHECKER) at ac29d69; reviews r1 Opus clean + Codex request_changes, r2 Opus changes needed, r3 Opus clean, r4 narrow Opus clean, r5 narrow Codex approve. Commit on branch fx-e3t.

description: Turn the early frontend libraries into a usable thin CLI path without collapsing core logic into the binary crate.

Primary question: What thinnest CLI layer turns the bootstrap frontend into a usable developer workflow without smearing logic across the binary crate?

Define and implement:

title: Decide: trim the review loop after e32775f
description:
## Decision

Is `GOVERNANCE.md`'s review loop still worth its cost after `e32775f`, or
should named steps be trimmed?

Recommendation: measure first, then decide, once at least 5 beads have closed
under `e32775f`'s rules. Expected answer: keep the parallel first review and
the second-model rule, and trim the later confirmation and re-check rounds only
where the data shows they rarely change a result. This is the biggest lever on
how fast Tide moves autonomously. Record the decision here.

## Why

The review loop in `GOVERNANCE.md` is the main limit on how fast Tide lands
changes. `fx-djp` records about 6 review rounds per bead since the Codex rule,
with fx-arx at 14 and fx-sz7 at about 10. `reviews/` reached round 101 on
2026-10-21. Commit `e32775f` changed the loop to parallel first reviews and
tier-scoped blocking. Whether that is enough has not been measured.

## Evidence

- `GOVERNANCE.md`, "Merge Rule": the round sequence and the tier test.
- `fx-djp`: the per-bead round counts before `e32775f`.
- `reviews/round<N>-*.md`: one file per round, with its model, verdict, and
  blocking findings.

## Scope

In scope:
- A measurement over `reviews/` and `git log`: rounds per landed bead, and
  which rounds produced blocking findings that changed the result, before and
  after `e32775f`.
- A decision, recorded on this bead. Then either no change, or an amendment to
  `GOVERNANCE.md` and the overlay's "Governance" summary, rendered.

Out of scope:
- Removing the independent second-model review, or the rule that no change
  lands without a supervisor verdict. Both stay.
- Design documents.

## Acceptance

- This bead records the before and after numbers, with how they were counted.
- It records a decision, with its reasons: keep the loop, or change named
  steps. The decision cites the rounds whose findings justify each kept step.
- Any governance change keeps the two rules out of scope above, and is
  rendered with a clean drift check.

## Implementation Notes

1. Start only once at least 5 beads have closed under `e32775f`'s rules.
   Before that, comment with the current count and stop.
2. Count with a small script, not by hand, so the numbers can be rerun. Keep
   it in the bead comment, or in `scripts/` if it is reused.
3. Tide's "Decisions" rule makes this a technical decision for the agent.
   Report it to the owner, without asking first.

## Verification

- Rerunning the counting script should reproduce the recorded numbers.
- If governance changed, `starcompass check-consumer` should pass with the
  four Tide paths.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if fewer than 5 beads have closed under the `e32775f` rules.
- Stop if the data cannot separate rounds that changed a result from rounds
  that did not.

## Maintenance Notes

- The candidate trims are the later confirmation and re-check rounds. The
  parallel first review is the part to keep.
close_reason: Measured (comment has numbers and script): design changes fell from 7.0 to 4.2 reviews each after e32775f. Decision: keep the loop unchanged; the docs-only Codex re-check (clean 4/4) is the trim candidate, to recount after about 10 more docs-only changes.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Note, 2026-10-21: review files are now named per bead (GOVERNANCE.md, Merge Rule): <bead>-r<N>-opus.md and <bead>-r<N>-codex.md, with the first-round pair sharing N. Count review files under both schemes (round<N>-*.md mapped to beads through git log; <bead>-r<N>-*.md by name), and count Opus and Codex reviews separately rather than round numbers.
