comments.text:
Measurement and decision, 2026-10-21 (agent, per Decisions). Head 6f23e82.

Counted with the script at the end (run from the repo root). Each review file maps to a bead: reviews/round<N>-*.md through the subject of the commit that added it, reviews/<bead>-r<N>-<reviewer>.md by name. Only reviews added after 4a05cc7 (the Codex rule) count; "before" and "after" split at e32775f's commit time. A review blocks when its verdict asks for changes, or, for a converge round without a verdict, when it lists fixes it made. Sequences: o = Opus, c = Codex, ! = blocking.

Before e32775f (9 beads, all design): 7.0 reviews per bead, 59% blocking.
  fx-0ai o! o! o! o c! o c | fx-1am o! o! o! o c! o! o! o! c! o c | fx-arx o! o! o! o! o! o! o o c! o c! o! o c | fx-cze o! o! o c! o! o! c | fx-kdj o! o o c | fx-ms8 o! o! o! o c | fx-nyy o! o c | fx-obr o! o c! o c | fx-sz7 o! o! o! o c! o c
After (5 beads plus 2 bead-less governance changes): 6.3 reviews per change, 50% blocking.
  design: fx-9ag c o! o c | fx-e3t c! o o! o o c | fx-t99 c o o | governance (e32775f) o! c! o c | review-names c! o o c  -> 4.2 reviews per change
  code: fx-3md c! o! o! o o! o! o c! o! c | fx-gcs.1 c! o! o! o! o! o! o c! o! c o! o c  -> 11.5 reviews per change, mostly converge rounds that fixed something

Decision: keep the loop as GOVERNANCE.md states it; change no step now. The parallel first review cut design changes from 7.0 to 4.2 reviews. Each kept step has findings behind it:
- Parallel first Codex pass: blocked in round 1 on 5 of 7 changes (fx-3md, fx-e3t, fx-gcs.1, review-names r1, round100). Before, Codex blocked after Opus came clean on 6 of 9 beads (fx-0ai, fx-1am, fx-arx, fx-cze, fx-obr, fx-sz7), restarting the loop.
- Opus confirmation after fixes: fx-e3t r2 found a gap in the round-1 fix; fx-9ag r1 Opus found the Decisions conflict Codex approved past.
- Narrow Codex re-check: on code it blocked twice on real defects (fx-3md r7: a hand-started continuation could be launched twice; fx-gcs.1 r7). On design it came clean 4 of 4 (fx-9ag r3, fx-e3t r5, round102, review-names r3). That is the one trim candidate: skipping the re-check for docs-only changes. Four observations are too few to remove a second-model check, so it stays; recount when about 10 more docs-only changes have landed.
- Code converge rounds are the remaining cost (fx-gcs.1 13 reviews, fx-3md 10), but their late rounds kept finding real defects (fx-3md r4: commits touching only .beads/ reset the handoff stop; r5's lock finding; r6's untested prompt and log rules), so no trim there either.

Script:
"""Review cost per landed bead, before and after e32775f (fx-eit).

Run from the Tide repository root: python3 review_stats.py
Old files (reviews/round<N>-<kind>.md) map to the bead named in the subject of
the commit that added them; new files (reviews/<bead>-r<N>-<reviewer>.md) map
by name. Only beads whose reviews all postdate 4a05cc7 (the Codex rule) count.
A review is blocking when its verdict line asks for changes, or, for a
converge round (no verdict), when it lists fixes it made.
"""
import glob, os, re, subprocess, collections

def git(*a):
    return subprocess.run(['git', *a], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()

codex_rule = int(git('log', '-1', '--format=%ct', '4a05cc7'))
cutover = int(git('log', '-1', '--format=%ct', 'e32775f'))

def verdict(path):
    lines = open(path).read().splitlines()
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        if re.match(r'^#+\s*verdict', l, re.I) or l.lower().startswith('**verdict'):
            rest = [x for x in lines[i:i + 4] if x.strip()][:2]
            v = ' '.join(rest).lower()
            return 'block' if re.search(r'request.?changes|changes needed|changes requested|revise|reject|with fixes', v) else 'clean'
    # A converge round has no verdict: it changed the result if it lists fixes.
    for i, l in enumerate(lines):
        if re.match(r'^##\s*(fixed|blocking fixes)', l, re.I):
            nxt = [x for x in lines[i + 1:] if x.strip()][:1]
            if nxt and re.match(r'^\s*([-*]|\d+\.|###)', nxt[0]):
                return 'block'
    return 'clean'

rows = collections.defaultdict(list)  # (era, bead) -> [(n, reviewer, verdict)]
for f in glob.glob('reviews/*.md'):
    name = os.path.basename(f)[:-3]
    added = git('log', '--diff-filter=A', '--format=%ct %s', '--', f).splitlines()
    if not added:
        continue
    t, subject = added[-1].split(' ', 1)
    t = int(t)
    if t < codex_rule:
        continue
    m = re.match(r'(.+)-r(\d+)-(opus|codex)$', name)
    if m:
        bead, n, who = m.group(1), int(m.group(2)), m.group(3)
    else:
        m = re.match(r'round(\d+)-(\w+)$', name)
        if not m:
            continue
        n, who = int(m.group(1)), ('codex' if m.group(2) == 'codex' else 'opus')
        b = re.findall(r'fx-[a-z0-9.]+', subject)
        bead = b[0] if b else 'governance'
    rows[('after' if t >= cutover else 'before', bead)].append((n, who, verdict(f)))

for era in ('before', 'after'):
    tot = collections.Counter()
    print(f'== {era} e32775f')
    print(f'{"bead":<18}{"reviews":>8}{"opus":>6}{"codex":>6}{"block":>6}  sequence')
    for (e, bead), rs in sorted(rows.items()):
        if e != era:
            continue
        rs.sort()
        c = collections.Counter(w for _, w, _ in rs)
        nb = sum(v == 'block' for *_, v in rs)
        seq = ' '.join(f'{w[0]}{"!" if v == "block" else ""}' for _, w, v in rs)
        print(f'{bead:<18}{len(rs):>8}{c["opus"]:>6}{c["codex"]:>6}{nb:>6}  {seq}')
        tot.update(beads=1, reviews=len(rs), opus=c['opus'], codex=c['codex'], block=nb)
    if tot['beads']:
        print(f'beads {tot["beads"]}, reviews/bead {tot["reviews"] / tot["beads"]:.1f}, '
              f'blocking share {tot["block"] / tot["reviews"]:.0%}')

title: Decide v0 contract details left open by the E1 dialect round: generated tests, private fields, while-loop invariants
description:
## Why

The held-out E1 round under D18 (trials/e1-dialect/, bead fx-jv9) used attribute contracts
correctly, which D18's reversal condition watches, but three contract-semantics questions are
undecided for v0, and ring's tests rested on two of them (grading.md C5, C6).

## Evidence

trials/e1-dialect/grading.md §5:
- G10: do generated tests over a type with private fields build it only from call sequences that
  respect each call's `requires` (discarding a violating call), and how are sizes such as
  `with_capacity(n)` drawn (04 §2.4 rule 1)? And fix the violation message prefix that
  `#[should_panic(expected = ..)]` matches (04 CLAUSE-7; reference 10.1 marks it provisional).
- G11: may a `pub` method's v0 clause read a private field (04 §1.4 is about v1 spec fns;
  reference 10.1's visibility rule is provisional)? The answer decides whether
  `self.len == old(self.len) + 1` is checked or must go through `len()` and be sampled
  (04 CLAUSE-5).
- G12: where `invariant!` runs in `while` and `while let` loops (01 D10 says only entry and exit;
  04 §2.4 fixes the next-index rule for `a..b` alone; the D18 spike checks before each evaluation
  of the condition).

## Scope

In scope: decide G10, G11, G12 in 04 (and 01 D10 if a decision changes it), then update
reference 10.1/10.2.

Out of scope: std and simulator details (the sibling bead for G3-G6, G9); v1 proof forms (fx-qzp).

## Acceptance

- 04 decides each item with its reasoning; reference 10.1/10.2 state the decisions and drop the
  matching "provisional" markers; the core stays under D14's budget (24,989 of 25,000 tokens;
  recount with scripts/count-tokens.sh).
- A review round in reviews/ finds no contradiction among 01, 04, and the reference pair.

## Implementation Notes

1. Check each decision against the D18 spike's contract lowering (spikes/d18/macros/) and say
   where it would change.
2. Docs-only design work: review rounds, not converge (GOVERNANCE.md).

## Verification

- The review file's verdict is approve or approve with notes.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask the owner if a decision changes D10's v0 contract model.
close_reason: G10-G12 decided by the owner and written to 01 D10, 04, 02, and the reference; rounds 23-24 (approve with notes)

comments.text: Owner decisions (2026-10-20). G11: a v0 clause may name whatever the function body can name (private fields and functions included); v1's prove-time visibility (04 §1.4) applies only under prove. G10: generated call sequences evaluate each call's requires first and skip a call that fails it (the generator is the caller); scalars are full-range, biased to small and boundary values, so limits belong in requires; violation panics start 'requires violated: ', 'ensures violated: ', 'invariant violated: ' plus the clause text. G12: invariant! in while/while let is checked each time control reaches the condition, before evaluating it; the check before the failing evaluation is the exit check; a side effect of the failing condition is not checked (matches the D18 spike, for's next-index rule, Dafny). title: Decide whether Tide is a new language or a checked dialect of Rust
description:
Decide whether Tide ships as a new language (the current design) or as a checked dialect of Rust: every Tide program is valid Rust and compiles with rustc, and Tide adds a capability std, the simulator, and the trust diff.

Context:
- Draft 3.4 (af8a99c) adopted Rust's lifetime syntax, so the translation to Rust (design/02-memory.md §11) is the identity on lifetimes.
- research/12-newcomer-sweep.md (24cd216) records lust (https://github.com/t3dotgg/lust-lang): a checked subset of valid Rust whose warm daemon reports one-line body edits checked 60-250x faster than cargo check (cold about 2.5x; self-reported). Fast builds therefore no longer distinguish Tide. Its open question 7 states this question.
- The thesis in design/01-design.md says tools layered on Rust cannot give D7 (no ambient authority), D15 (deterministic simulation), and D11 (trust diff). That is shown for Rust as a whole, not for a checked subset with its own std.
- Owner decision (2026-10-19): settle this before planning v0 implementation. The handoff's plan to build the origin/borrow checker first depends on the answer: under a dialect, rustc checks borrows.

Method:
1. Write a design study, research/13-rust-dialect.md. For every v0-core item in 01's Tiers table, classify it under the dialect as: valid Rust as is; an attribute, library, or std replacement; a checker-only analysis; or impossible without changing rustc. Known hard cases: requires/ensures syntax, Pure, main(root: Root), overflow traps in release, Shared::with closures, scopes, simulator interception of std and blocking calls, deterministic HashMap, impl placement and module rules, FX diagnostics, the Bend boundary, and v1's evented runtime and field-borrow declarations.
2. For each path, estimate what must be built for the first demo (an agent-written concurrent service whose bug is found by seed and replayed exactly, and a PR that widens network authority flagged by the trust diff), plus ecosystem reach, the expected effect on E1 learnability, and what the thesis loses.
3. Cite prior art for the dialect path: lust, cap-std, capsec, cargo-cackle, Capslock, Prusti and Creusot attribute contracts, and loom, shuttle, turmoil, and madsim for deterministic simulation of Rust.
4. Run one adversarial review of the study (a second model preferred), written to reviews/.
5. Present a recommendation to the owner and record the decision in design/01-design.md (Thesis, Positioning, and D12/D13 as affected) and on this bead.
acceptance_criteria: research/13-rust-dialect.md exists with cited prior art and the per-feature classification of every v0-core item; an adversarial review of it is in reviews/ with each objection resolved or recorded; the owner's decision is recorded in design/01-design.md and on this bead. Cheapest falsifier: if D7, D15, or D11 cannot hold for safe code under the dialect without changing rustc, the dialect cannot carry the thesis and the new-language design stands.
close_reason: Owner adopted the checked Rust dialect as the v0 direction (D18, draft 3.6), gated by the feasibility spike fx-7qu; study research/15, review reviews/dialect-codex.md resolved.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decision criteria from research/13-agent-fleets.md (2026-10-19): (1) per-spawn context tax: every fresh subagent pays the reference (about 19k tokens now), while Rust knowledge comes with the model, so measure the delta each path needs; (2) the check loop must hit D12's tens-of-milliseconds edit target, since fleets leave Rust over compile time (X7); (3) both paths must support sealed delegation boundaries and running an unreviewed branch's tests without a VM (beads filed alongside); (4) deterministic simulation with virtual time, so suites do not flake under parallel agents.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Concrete test case (owner, 2026-10-19): Eon (~/pjs/eon/eon, github.com/Yazelix/eon), a ~64k-line Rust workspace for long-running agent work: Orbit (terminal process server: PTYs, sessions, attach/detach), Venus (wgpu/Vulkan renderer), runtime and protocol crates, eon-manifest. Dependencies include wgpu, winit (Wayland), glyphon, accesskit, libghostty-vt (C), libc, serde/serde_json/toml (serde derive is a proc macro), arboard, wl-clipboard-rs; unsafe in about 10 files; almost no async. The study must answer for both paths: can Eon adopt Tide crate by crate, in what order (likely orbit-protocol and eon-workspace-protocol, then eon-manifest, then Orbit's core with a capability std), what blocks each crate (PTY/libc FFI, serde derives, C libraries), and what Orbit gains from deterministic simulation of attach, detach, and crash interleavings. Venus and windowing are expected to stay Rust. Also note the product fit: Eon could surface Tide's trust diff, replay seeds, and sealed boundaries per agent tab (research/13).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Two more fleet needs from research/13 (P5, P7, P8), for both paths: every tide command bounded in time and output, with failures attributable to a change and seed ('Claude can't tell time'; agents disown broken builds); and a build cache safe for many concurrent agents across worktrees. The dialect path inherits Cargo's shared target/ lock, which blocks agents in separate worktrees (P15), so the study must say how a dialect avoids it.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Path correction (2026-10-19): the study goes in research/15-rust-dialect.md; research/13 is taken by 13-agent-fleets.md (and 14 by autoresearch). Read research/13 references in this bead as research/13-agent-fleets.md.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Progress (2026-10-19): research/15-rust-dialect.md drafted (uncommitted). Key finding F1: stock rustc 1.96 with --extern std=<facade rlib> compiles user code against a capability std via normal std injection; std::fs::read and extern crate std both resolve to the facade, so the ambient std is unreachable without a rustc change. core::include_str!/env! and unsafe intrinsics still leak; the fixed ! set and unsafe grants close them. Draft recommendation: adopt the dialect for v0 (rustc+LLVM replace the C and Cranelift backends). Next: second-model review to reviews/dialect-codex.md, resolve findings, then owner decision; 01-design.md is untouched until the owner decides.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Review done (2026-10-19): reviews/dialect-codex.md, request_changes, B1-B7 and N1-N3, all accepted and answered in research/15 (Review resolution table). B1/B2 reproduced locally: safe core::arch __cpuid and ptr.addr() vary per run, core atomics need no Tasks, std's inherent f64::sin beats a facade trait. Recommendation revised: adopt the dialect as v0 direction, gated by a bounded feasibility spike (7 acceptance criteria in research/15) before v0 planning commits; new-language path stays the fallback. Awaiting owner decision; 01-design.md untouched.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision (2026-10-19): adopt the checked Rust dialect as the v0 direction, gated by a bounded feasibility spike (fx-7qu). Recorded as D18 in design/01-design.md (draft 3.6), with pointers in Thesis, Positioning, D12, D13, and open question 7; the other decisions keep their text until the spike passes. Study research/15-rust-dialect.md; review reviews/dialect-codex.md, all findings answered.

title: Define the staged Ferox symbol-record and symbol-graph rollout plan for the machine contract
description: The tooling specs now promise stable symbol identity, symbol records, and later symbol-graph data, but the queue does not yet track how those surfaces should be staged without overpromising during bootstrap. This task should define what symbol outputs appear first, what stability tier each belongs to, and what compiler prerequisites must exist before Ferox exposes richer symbol relationships.
design: Primary question: how should Ferox stage symbol-record and symbol-graph outputs so the machine contract is useful early without freezing unreliable semantics? Define: 1. the first symbol facts to expose; 2. the boundary between declaration records and richer graph edges; 3. stability tiers and versioning expectations; 4. dependencies on parsing, name resolution, package loading, and stable IDs; 5. non-goals for the bootstrap phase.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what symbol data Ferox exposes first; what stays provisional; what graph edges are deferred; and what validation/diagnostic/logging expectations apply. Include staged output examples, rejected early overreach, and explicit prerequisites in the compiler pipeline.
notes: Additional revision after source-model audit: symbol-record and symbol-graph rollout should not stabilize source locations until the source-text/span contract is explicit, because byte spans, line/column data, and newline behavior are part of the public machine surface.
close_reason: Superseded: the owner discarded the first Ferox design (archived in archive/v0-design/) for the first-principles redesign in fx-agent-first-redesign-tf4; this work no longer applies.

title: Define the exact initial T074 Ferox grammar slice and parser recovery boundary
description: T074 currently names a small Ferox subset in broad terms, but the spec still exposes more syntax forms than the first parser should absorb. This task should define the exact initial grammar slice and recovery boundary for T074 so implementation proves parser shape without overcommitting grammar coverage too early.
design: Primary question: what exact syntax forms should the first real Ferox parser accept, reject, and recover around? Define the precise T074 grammar slice for declarations, statements, expressions, patterns, type syntax, comments/docs, and recovery boundaries. The goal is a deliberately small but coherent subset that matches the current source personality and formatter roadmap without pulling in deferred language systems.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task enumerates the exact T074 grammar surface, explicit exclusions, representative recovery scenarios, and the subset boundaries needed for parser tests, formatter work, and diagnostics snapshots. It should include examples of accepted files, rejected files, and partially recovered files, plus rationale for why omitted syntax stays out of the first slice.
notes: Decision: keep this planning bead and apply its outcome to T074 in v1 immediately. The exact initial parser slice should be: 1. file-level `////` docs, declaration `///` docs, and ordinary `//` comments preserved as trivia; 2. zero or more top-level `fn` declarations only, each with a name, explicit typed parameters, explicit `->` return type, and a block body; 3. statement forms limited to `let` / `let mut` with required initializer, optional local type annotation, simple assignment statements, `return`, and expression statements; 4. expression forms limited to name references, integer/string/bool literals, grouped expressions, block expressions, function calls, field access, a small binary operator set needed for basic examples, `if`/`else`, `match`, and postfix `?`; 5. type syntax limited to simple names and bracketed generic application such as `Option[T]` and `Result[T, E]`; 6. pattern syntax limited to `_`, name binding, simple literal patterns, unit-like names, tuple/variant patterns such as `some(value)` and `ok(value)`, plus tuple patterns. Explicit exclusions from T074: `async fn`, `await`, `pub`, `unsafe`, structs/enums/traits/use/module declarations, named-field struct/variant patterns, broad collection literals, float literal support, guards/or-patterns/alias patterns, destructuring `let`, and advanced type syntax. Recovery boundary: top-level recovery should sync on the next plausible `fn`; block recovery should sync on `;` or `}`; parameter and argument recovery should sync on `,` or closing delimiters; match-arm recovery should sync on `,` or `}`. Rationale: this is the smallest coherent slice that still exercises the Ferox source personality, `Option`/`Result` handling, formatter path, and structured diagnostics without pulling in deferred language systems. Apply in T074 now; later syntax growth should come from separate beads rather than expanding this bootstrap slice ad hoc.

title: Define the Ferox FP profile so it strengthens regularity and safety without increasing semantic entropy
description: Evaluate how far Ferox should lean into FP ideas such as ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression-oriented code, immutability-by-default, pipelines, and pure helper functions. The goal is to identify which FP influences strengthen Ferox's core thesis around safe change, low entropy, and agent-friendly tooling, and which FP directions would harm compile times, local reasoning, or systems-language coherence.
design: Current working hypothesis: restrained FP helps Ferox when it improves source-code regularity and local reasoning, but harms Ferox when it introduces major new semantic machinery. Likely good fits include ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression orientation, immutable-by-default style, and a narrow pipe operator. Likely bad fits include effect-heavy purity systems, monadic abstraction culture, operator proliferation, higher-kinded types, lazy defaults, and multiple equivalent composition idioms.
acceptance_criteria:
Produce a clear Ferox FP doctrine that explains:
1. Which FP ideas are core to the language identity.
2. Which are useful but secondary.
3. Which are out of scope because they would widen the core too much.
4. How the recommended FP profile interacts with ownership, async, tooling, compile times, and future verification.
5. Which canonical source examples demonstrate the doctrine in practice.

Also include a downstream implementation validation plan that covers:
- unit tests for parsing, lowering, formatting, and diagnostics of the accepted FP forms;
- golden/corpus tests for canonical examples and rejected anti-patterns;
- end-to-end scripts that exercise idiomatic transformation-heavy workflows;
- detailed logging/tracing expectations so failures in FP-related syntax, lowering, or formatting can be diagnosed quickly.

title: Multi-file conformance cases for SEAL-2 and SEAL-3
description:
## Why

SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 (`design/04-contracts.md:1265-1330`) are v0 driver rules with no
conformance cases, because a case is one file and a seal needs a crate plus its
`tide.seal` (`conformance/rules.md:135-139`). fx-gcs cannot close until they have
cases (fx-gcs comment, 2026-10-21). The corpus is design work and needs no checker:
cases wait for the driver as other checker cases did.

## Evidence

- `conformance/rules.md:135-139`: SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 rows and the one-file limit.
- `conformance/README.md`: the case format and the runner's "awaiting the checker"
  listing.
- `design/04-contracts.md:1265-1318`: SEAL-2's interface, whole, test, and manifest
  entries; `:1319-1330`: SEAL-3's configurations, targets, and diagnostic parts;
  `:1369-1453`: the worked example.

## Scope

In scope: a multi-file case form in `conformance/` (a base package tree, the seal
taken from it with the writer fx-zr3 names, and one candidate edit with an
expected verdict: admitted, or FX0920 with its changed parts), the runner support to
list these cases, and cases for each SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 clause:
- interface entry: body edit admitted; signature, contract-use, or clause change and
  a changed body of a function a clause calls rejected; renaming a referenced helper
  admitted; a new impl or import that changes which item a sealed call selects
  rejected;
- whole function, whole type (an added `impl PartialEq`; a blanket impl that applies
  through `&T`; a changed associated type), and whole trait (a new impl admitted
  unless it applies to a type sealed whole);
- test entry: an edit to an unsealed function the test reaches rejected; an edit to a
  body behind an interface entry admitted; fewer seeds rejected;
- manifest entry: an added grant rejected;
- configurations and targets: a sealed `#[cfg(test)]` test not checked in the debug
  build; a build for a target the seal does not list rejected.

Out of scope: driver code; SEAL-4/5 (FX0921, `tide review`); rule changes.

## Acceptance

- Every SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 clause listed above has an admitted and a rejected case
  where both exist, with expected verdicts and parts.
- `conformance/run.sh` (or its Rust port, fx-upy) exits 0 and lists these cases as
  awaiting the checker; `conformance/rules.md` points SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 at them.

## Implementation Notes

1. Seal the base in the runner rather than committing hashes, so cases never hold
   stale hash bytes; the expected verdict names parts, not hashes.
2. Build on the runner fx-upy produces, so the multi-file form is written once.

## Verification

- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0 and its listing includes every new case.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if a SEAL-2 clause cannot be expressed as base plus edit; record it on fx-gcs.

title: Evaluate a functional-source, in-place-backend optimization direction for Ferox
description: Evaluate whether Ferox should deliberately target a backend strategy where transformation-friendly source code can compile to storage reuse or in-place updates when ownership and uniqueness prove that reuse is safe. The goal is to improve performance without polluting the surface language with mutation-heavy optimization idioms.
notes: Decision: Keep the idea only as a long-term backend optimization direction. Do not make functional-source/in-place-backend behavior part of the v1 or core v2 language promise. Revisit after the checked IR, ownership tracking, and first native backend are credible. Treat it as V3-or-later optimization and observability work, not as a surface-language feature.

title: v0 conformance corpus: executable verdicts per rule ID
description:
## Why

Owner decision, 2026-10-21: keep working in design space, but move from prose review to

  accepting and one rejecting case, with an expected verdict (accept, a rustc error, or an `FX`
  code).

  the rest as awaiting the checker.

title: Conformance corpus format, runner, and rule inventory
description:
## Why

The corpus children and the v0 checker's first slice share one case format and one runner. Pick
them once, before cases exist. Parent epic has the context.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md:143-147`: D0's conformance oracle, IDs traced to tests.
- `trials/e1-dialect/rustc/run.sh` and `trials/e1-dialect/rustc/std/`: a rustc oracle that type-
  and borrow-checks Rust 2024 crates against a stub Tide std injected as `std`. The runner should
  reuse this mechanism, not invent another.
- `spikes/d18/admit/tests/{pos,neg,pure,gate}`: the spike's admission cases, a shape to compare.
- About 83 rule IDs exist today, nearly all in 03 (SINK, LOCK, FFI, TASK, SEAL, RUST, RUN,
  GLOBAL, ROOT, PAR, ...); 02 has almost none.

## Scope

In scope:
- `conformance/`: the case format (one `.rs` file per case, with its rule IDs and expected
  verdict in a header comment, or a better shape if you find one), `conformance/run.sh`, and a
  trace table from rule ID to cases.
- Moving or copying the stub std into `conformance/` if the trial's copy must stay frozen as a
  record.
- A rule inventory: every v0-core normative rule in `design/02-memory.md`,
  `design/03-authority-concurrency.md`, and `design/04-contracts.md` that the checker or rustc
  decides, with its ID or `none yet`. An ID scheme for the rules that lack one, written into the
  chapter that owns them only if the scheme is decided here; assigning the IDs themselves is the
  sibling beads' work.
- About five seed cases that exercise every verdict kind.

Out of scope:
- Cases beyond the seeds (sibling beads).
- Runtime and sandbox tests.
- Any checker code.

## Acceptance

- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0 on the seed cases and reports, per case, PASS, FAIL, or AWAITS
  CHECKER (expected verdict is an `FX` code rustc cannot produce).
- A seed case whose expected verdict is wrong makes the runner exit nonzero.
- The format and the ID scheme are written down in `conformance/README.md`, and
  `design/01-design.md` D0 points to it.

## Verification

- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0; flipping one seed's expected verdict makes it exit nonzero.
- The runner and seeds finish through converge, then the review loop in `GOVERNANCE.md`.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the stub-std mechanism cannot express a needed verdict; record why on the bead.

design gives Tide's std its own fixed-key `HashMap::new()` (03 GLOBAL-5) and its own
`DirEntry` and `Metadata` (03 §1.1). fx-kw8.1's driver is right to reject Rust's versions
(FX0520), so it also rejects code the design admits: `HashMap::new()`, `entry.path()`,
`metadata.is_file()`, as in E1's `canon`, `dedupe`, `deps`, `rules` and `backup`
(`reviews/fx-kw8.1-r2-opus.md`, "Stub artifacts"). No case hits this yet. The first one that
uses them fails the driver pass.

fx-kw8.1's round-1 review (N7) also found missing cases: timed waits (`recv_timeout`) and
hardware queries.

## Scope

In scope: stub definitions of `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `DirEntry` and `Metadata` that follow
the design's API (mark guesses `GUESS`). Accepting cases that use them, plus cases for timed
waits and hardware queries, each verdict cited to the design text that settles it.
Out of scope: driver policy changes, unless a design-admitted program still fails under the
driver.

## Acceptance

- Accepting cases built on `HashMap::new()`, `DirEntry::path` and `Metadata::is_file` pass
  both runner passes.
- Timed-wait and hardware-query rules have cases with design-cited verdicts.
- `conformance/run.sh` exits 0.
close_reason: done

title: Freeze the checked-toolchain E1 protocol
description:
## Why

D0 requires a paired learnability experiment on the checked toolchain; prior stub metadata builds do not establish its executable gate.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md (D0, D11, D14, D15, D18)`
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md (ROOT, TASK, LOCK, authority and replay rules)`
- `conformance/README.md (stub oracle limitations)`

## Scope

Ready independently. Scope: 30 held-out tasks and paired Tide/Rust writer protocol, no expected solutions leaked; fixed sample/iteration/error/time/token accounting and exact D0 thresholds. Distinguish a metadata-only admission pilot from the actual executable first-check/final-pass gate. Determine the exact supported APIs and execution prerequisites before freezing tasks, and link any real missing prerequisites to fx-ic2; do not rewrite task difficulty to manufacture a pass. A protocol can finish with unavailable-toolchain limitations named; it cannot declare E1 passed. No new language semantics.

## Acceptance

Freeze 30 held-out tasks and the paired protocol with the unchanged D0 thresholds. Record exact executable prerequisites and add their blocker edges to fx-ic2 before closing. A metadata-only pilot cannot declare E1 passed.
close_reason: Protocol and 30 tasks frozen in trials/e1-checked; prerequisites block fx-ic2; review loop converged

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Closed by the freeze of `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` and `trials/e1-checked/tasks.md` (2026-10-31).

Acceptance check (named observation):
- 30 held-out tasks frozen in tasks.md (A1-A10 core language, B1-B10 authority and I/O, C1-C10 concurrency, parallelism, contracts), none reused from earlier trials or docs; close models disclosed in protocol §2.
- Paired Tide/Rust protocol with D0's thresholds unchanged (protocol §8: F(Tide) >= 0.8 F(Rust), P(Tide) >= P(Rust), I(Tide) <= 1.5 I(Rust)).
- Exact executable prerequisites in protocol §10.1, each owned by a bead that blocks fx-ic2: fx-kw8.9, fx-nkv.1-6, and the fourteen new e1-prereq beads fx-zc1, fx-o8j, fx-ugm, fx-o4h, fx-iob, fx-byk, fx-5vj, fx-hxw, fx-3iu, fx-08m, fx-mhd, fx-m72, fx-yg5, fx-u65 (`br dep tree fx-ic2`).
- A metadata-only pilot (protocol §9) cannot report E1 as passed or failed; neither can a gate run missing any readiness item (§1, §10.2).

Technical decisions (AGENTS.md Decisions), with reasons:
1. Sample: two independent fresh writers per task per arm (60 trials per arm). One per task leaves the P(Tide) >= P(Rust) comparison at the mercy of a single trial; more costs writer sessions without changing the gate's point-estimate form.
2. One fresh session per task, not one writer doing all tasks: no carry-over learning or order effects between tasks.
3. Rust arm may use serde, serde_json, thiserror (pinned 1.0.229 / 1.0.154 / 2.0.21): exactly the crates whose behavior Tide builds in (derive(Error), Encode/Decode), so paired tasks ask the same work of both arms.
4. Rand, Net::get/HTTP, Proc, simulated crashes left out (protocol §11): Rust's std cannot express a paired task without handing that arm extra code.
5. Checked cases are visible to writers and the grader's suites implement exactly them: grading stays mechanical and identical in both arms; held-out means held out from the reference and earlier trials, not hidden from the writer.
6. First check also compiles the acceptance suite for libraries, so a skeleton first run cannot pass.
7. Iterations: mean runs over trials that pass final (D0's "iterations to green"); counting failures as the cap diluted the 1.5x ratio (r1 Opus finding 1). The censored mean is reported as information.
8. Concurrency that no checked case can witness (C1-C6, C9) is checked by a recorded, line-cited grader review; text-search structure checks alone do not prove it (r1 Codex 5, r2 Opus 1).
9. fx-u65 (every FX code the reference names) is a prerequisite: without it a Tide writer can pass with code the reference forbids, which flatters Tide (r1 Codex 2).
10. Writer code runs only in a harness OS sandbox with a read allowlist (protocol §10.3): fx-kw8.9's build mode is for reviewed code, and the sandbox must keep suites and reference solutions unreadable.

Reviews (reviews/fx-gfq-r<N>-<reviewer>.md): r1 Opus and Codex on frozen candidate d1bd3f2c (both request_changes), r2 Opus (2 text fixes), r3 Opus approve, r4 Codex narrow re-check (lint severity), r5 Opus+Codex narrow (FX0510 is v1), r6 Opus+Codex narrow approve on final diff e37f7903 (taken before the review files were added).

Not taken (non-blocking, recorded for fx-ic2): an unblocked bead that builds the harness, suites, and reference solutions early to surface prerequisite gaps sooner; narrowing fx-u65 to the FX codes a single-file package can reach (that would loosen readiness item 3 and is the owner's call).

title: Define the Ferox ownership model so it preserves Rust-grade safe-code guarantees through a smaller and more restrictive mechanism
description: Synthesize the Ferox ownership model from the now-separated subproblems: guarantee boundary/invariants and concrete ownership/borrowing rules. This bead should consolidate those decisions into one coherent ownership proposal that the rest of the language can depend on.
design:
Primary question: Given the guarantee boundary and the concrete ownership/borrowing rules, what is the final integrated Ferox ownership model?

This synthesis task should:
1. Reconcile the invariant-level commitments with the rule-level design.
2. Surface any tension between simplicity, usability, and soundness.
3. Produce the final ownership model that downstream concurrency, source-language, and verification beads can treat as canonical.
4. Carry forward implementation obligations, open risks, and validation requirements in one place.
close_reason: Integrated the ownership guarantee boundary, invariants, concrete rules, deliberate exclusions, examples, and validation implications into the canonical language and implementation docs.

title: Define the exact Ferox safe-code guarantee boundary and core ownership invariants
description: Before the ownership model can be finalized, Ferox needs a precise statement of what safe code guarantees and invariants it commits to. This task defines the guarantee boundary for memory safety and data-race safety, the core semantic invariants that must always hold, and the high-level safety model that later ownership and borrowing rules must preserve.
design:
Primary question: What exact guarantees and semantic invariants must Ferox safe code preserve, independent of specific borrow-checking rules?

Define:
1. The precise boundary of Ferox's safe-code commitment for memory safety and data-race safety.
2. The core semantic invariants that must hold for ownership, aliasing, mutation, and sharing.
3. The assumptions about unsafe or privileged escape hatches, if any.
4. The classes of bugs that Ferox explicitly does and does not claim to prevent.

This task should establish the target that the ownership rule set must satisfy.
close_reason: Defined the safe-code guarantee boundary, core ownership invariants, explicit non-goals, boundary examples, and validation implications in spec/LANGUAGE.md and spec/IMPLEMENTATION.md.

title: Define the concrete Ferox ownership and borrowing rules, including deliberate exclusions
description: Once the guarantee boundary is clear, Ferox needs a concrete rule set that preserves it. This task defines the actual ownership and borrowing rules, the intentionally forbidden patterns relative to Rust, and the checker-facing shape of the model from a language-design perspective.
design:
Primary question: What ownership and borrowing rules should Ferox actually adopt to preserve the guarantee boundary while staying smaller and more restrictive than Rust?

Define:
1. Core ownership transfer, borrowing, mutation, and aliasing rules.
2. The role of lexicality, lifetime scope, and any simplified borrow restrictions.
3. Deliberately rejected Rust patterns and why forbidding them improves Ferox.
4. The shape of checker obligations from the language-rule perspective.

This task should turn invariants into a concrete rule system with accepted and rejected examples.
close_reason: Defined the concrete v1 ownership and borrowing rules, deliberate exclusions, accepted/rejected examples, and validation implications in spec/LANGUAGE.md and spec/IMPLEMENTATION.md.

title: Decide: stop attended sessions from handing off early
description:
## Why

In attended sessions, agents stop after one or two beads, or offer "continue or handoff?", when they have used 10–30% of a 1M window. The owner has had to correct this in at least seven sessions. Each early handoff costs another prime and another round of owner attention. The agent's own context estimate is also unreliable: one session said it was at "about 230k tokens", and the owner answered "we have context enough.. continue".

## Evidence

Owner corrections (session prefix, UTC date, quote):
- 3748816d, 2026-10-19: "the limit of context is 600k. we have room"
- 119d07a5, 2026-10-19: "we have tons of context, you do more stuff now", then "we only used 10%"
- 73454788, 2026-10-19: "we have a lot of context continue fx-origin-syntax-trial-u49"
- 0c465b0b, 2026-10-19: "we have context enough.. continue"
- e1f15d82, 2026-10-19: "we are at 20% ctx used, so we can maybe continue"
- f54f050d, 2026-10-20: "we only used 20% of ctx. what is next?"
- 319fa31b, 2026-10-21: "contineu", answering a stop at about 230k
- c697036a, 2026-10-21: the owner agreed with an audit finding that sessions hand off at 230–300k, though the rule allows up to 400k

Current owners and why they failed:
- AP-SESSION-001 (canonical) sets when to stop adding scope (400k) and when to hand off (600k). It sets no floor, so stopping early never breaks it. Ambiguous.
- The agent cannot see its real context use, so it guesses, and it guesses high. Missing.
- The user memory `session-length-400k` (2026-10-21) is wording only and is not loaded outside this owner's machine. No session since it was written has been attended, so it is unproven.
- `scripts/autorun.sh` (fx-3md) chains sessions only in unattended runs. It does not apply to attended sessions.

## Scope

In scope:
- the project's Claude Code hooks (`.claude/settings.json` or a hook script under `scripts/`)
- if needed, one line in `.agent-protocols.local.md` with a re-render of `AGENTS.md`

Out of scope:
- AP-SESSION-001's text. A floor belongs in the Starcompass source repository; propose it there only if the owner asks.
- `scripts/autorun.sh`

## Acceptance

- In an attended session that closes a bead below 350k context with a ready, non-epic bead that is not labelled `owner`, the agent picks the next bead without asking. Observed in one behavior trial with a fresh agent.
- The agent's stated context use is within 10% of the transcript's real `usage` count.

## Implementation Notes

Recommended enforcement, highest that works:
1. Structure: add a hook (UserPromptSubmit and Stop) that reads the transcript's last assistant `usage` (input + cache read + cache creation tokens) and prints `context: <N>k of 1000k`, so the agent stops guessing.
2. Mechanical check: add a Stop hook that blocks the stop once, with a reason, when context is under 350k, `br ready` lists a pickable bead, no bead is in progress for this session, and the last assistant message proposes a handoff or a fresh session. Allow the second stop, so the owner is never trapped.

Rejected:
- More wording in AGENTS.md: the memory already says this, and wording is what failed.
- Using `scripts/autorun.sh` for attended work: it gives up the owner's interjections, which they use.

## Verification

- A hook unit test feeds a recorded transcript tail at 250k and 450k, and checks that the hook reports the count and blocks only in the first case.
- Behavior trial: a fresh attended-style session closes a small bead and goes on to the next one.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if Claude Code hooks cannot read transcript usage. Fall back to the reporting hook only.
- Stop if the owner rejects a Stop hook that can block in attended sessions.

## Maintenance Notes

- A Stop hook can misfire on conversational answers, so it must match only handoff proposals and block at most once per stop.
- Related: fx-hbs (parallel agent fronts) changes how many sessions run at once, not how long each runs.

title: Decide: parallel agent fronts in Tide
description:
## Decision

Should Tide run several agent sessions at once as standing "fronts", each owning
one area of work, and if so, which fronts and what rules keep them from
colliding?

Owner call (scope and direction, AP-SCOPE-001): the owner said on 2026-10-21
that they will review the first parallel run and decide whether separate fronts
are worth it. Recommendation: adopt two fronts at most until the review loop is
trimmed (fx-eit), with the shared-resource rules below written into the
overlay.

## Why

On 2026-10-21 three Tide sessions ran at once: an older session holding fx-3md
(dirty in the main checkout) and fx-gcs.1 (its own worktree), plus tide-96
(fx-e3t) and tide-8b (fx-t99), each in its own worktree and branch. This was
the first parallel run. Whether it pays for itself has not been judged.

## Evidence

What the run showed:
- Claiming with `br` before starting, plus one worktree and branch per bead,
  kept the sessions apart. Two short cross-session messages split the ready
  beads.
- `design/reference.md` is a shared budget, at 24,996 of D14's 25,000 tokens.
  Two sessions that both change the core reference compete for it. The
  sessions agreed to ask each other before spending any core tokens.
- The main checkout is the merge bottleneck. fx-gcs.1 was approved through r9
  but could not fast-forward `main`, because another session had uncommitted
  README.md edits in the main tree.
- The review loop (`GOVERNANCE.md`, Merge Rule) costs more than drafting, so
  more fronts add review load in proportion. fx-eit measures that loop.

## Scope

In scope:
- Whether to run fronts, how many, and how work is split: by bead, by design
  chapter, or by kind (design, conformance corpus, tooling).
- Rules for shared resources: the core token budget, the main checkout, the
  merge order onto `main`, and `.beads/issues.jsonl` written by several
  sessions.
- Whether the session runner (fx-3md) should start fronts or stay serial.

Out of scope:
- The review loop itself (fx-eit).
- Any change to the supervisor merge rule.

## Acceptance

- The owner records the decision on this bead: no fronts, or named fronts with
  their areas.
- If fronts are adopted, `.agent-protocols.local.md` states the shared-resource
  rules above, rendered into AGENTS.md with a clean drift check.

## Notes

- Inputs: the fx-e3t, fx-t99, fx-3md, and fx-gcs.1 histories (comments,
  reviews, commits), and how long each waited on another session.
- A front-per-chapter split would clash with beads that cross chapters, such as
  fx-e3t (03 and the core reference).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Evidence from tide-8b's fx-t99 run, 2026-10-21 (input only, no decision):
- fx-t99 drafted in a worktree, ran the full loop (r1 Opus+Codex parallel, r2 Opus, r3 Codex narrow) with every review delegated to subagents/Codex, and landed as a3b0177. Drafting took a few tool calls; reviews took most of the wall time.
- Merging onto main is the bottleneck twice over: (1) `git merge --ff-only` aborts whenever the main checkout has an uncommitted .beads/issues.jsonl, which br rewrites on every claim/comment/close from any session; I had to back up the file, stash it, fast-forward, and restore it byte-identical. (2) Each landing moves main, so a branch approved against the old main (fx-gcs.1 at ad837c0, based on 76dfe06) can no longer fast-forward and needs a rebase plus, by AP-PROOF-001, a check that its approval still holds.
- The commit's ledger change was made by copying only the bead's own line from the main checkout's export into the worktree's issues.jsonl, so other sessions' uncommitted ledger state was neither committed nor lost.
- The dcg hook blocks `git checkout -- <path>` and `git branch -d`, so a front cannot clean up its merged branch (fx-t99 is left) without the owner.
Suggested rule if fronts are adopted: one session (or the runner) owns merges to main and the ledger commit; fronts end at an approved branch.

title: Turn the query-oriented compiler direction into an explicit Ferox architecture commitment
description: Ferox now points toward query-oriented compiler services, incremental checking, and reusable tool-facing compiler data, but the commitment is still too architectural and fuzzy. This task is to define the intended compiler service model more concretely: what should be query-based, what stable identities and caches are needed, what outputs should be exposed to tools, and how the compiler architecture should support fast feedback, refactors, and future verification work.
design:
Primary question: What compiler architecture best delivers Ferox's safe-change tooling contract and fast feedback goals?

Define the intended architecture in terms of:
1. Core queries/services: parse, lower, resolve, type/ownership check, diagnostics, symbol graph, checked IR, formatting support.
2. Stable identities and cache boundaries: files, packages, modules, items, symbols.
3. Incrementality model: what invalidates what, and how single-file edits stay cheap.
4. Service reuse: how CLI, IDEs, refactors, and future verification tooling share the same engine.

The outcome should be an explicit architectural commitment, not just an implementation preference.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- Which compiler functions are explicit reusable queries/services?
- What stable IDs and cache boundaries does the system require?
- How does the architecture support fast incremental check and machine-safe rewrites?
- What architectural choices are deliberately out of scope for V1?

Include:
- a small service graph and rationale for why this architecture best fits Ferox;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for invalidation and cache behavior, corpus tests for incremental correctness, and end-to-end scripts for repeated edit/check/refactor flows;
- detailed logging and trace requirements for query execution, invalidation, cache hits/misses, and service reuse paths.
close_reason: Defined the query-oriented compiler architecture in spec/IMPLEMENTATION.md, including service graph, identities, cache boundaries, invalidation, reuse, validation, and tracing expectations.

title: TCP through Net: bind, connect, and simulated loopback
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) needs this surface to execute on the checked toolchain:
`trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §10.1 lists it as E1-P8, and no existing bead owns it.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P8, §10.2)`
- `design/reference.md §6.1, §6.7`

## Scope

Net::bind, Net::connect, TcpListener, TcpStream (io::Read/io::Write, also for &TcpStream), and Net attenuations only/no_bind, real and simulated, with network operations as checkpoints. Net::get and HTTP are outside this bead. Production std under crates/, built and admitted through tide-admit; no new
language semantics.

## Acceptance

Two tasks in one simulation connect over a simulated loopback address and exchange bytes deterministically per seed; a no_bind Net cannot bind; real loopback works in the harness sandbox. Toolchain tests prove each item executes, not only type-checks.
Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

title: Evaluate opaque public types and smart constructors as an invariant-preserving Ferox feature
description: Evaluate whether Ferox should support opaque public types with private constructors and explicit smart-constructor APIs. The goal is to strengthen invalid-state prevention and API invariants without introducing heavyweight proof machinery or widening the semantic core too much.
close_reason: completed

title: Decide channel, filesystem, network, and simulator-setup details left open by the E1 dialect round
description:
## Why

The held-out E1 round under D18 (trials/e1-dialect/, bead fx-jv9) passed 11/11, but five
std and simulator details that no normative chapter decides left three programs' first check and
two tests resting on guesses (grading.md C1-C4, C8). Agents writing against the reference will
keep guessing until these are decided.

## Evidence

trials/e1-dialect/grading.md §5 (each gap names its reference section and normative source):
- G3: channel errors. Rust's unit `RecvError` and reason-less `SendError(T)` cannot say that a
  checkpoint failed because of cancellation; reference 7.2 implies `is_cancelled()` on channel
  errors, 03 §1.1 promises it only for capability errors. Also state that a disconnect is not an
  echo (03 TASK-2 already implies it).
- G4: whether a crash before `sync_dir` leaves a renamed target old-or-new or can lose the entry
  (03 §9.5, D15); then the atomic-replace pattern in reference 6.3.
- G5: `NetError::is_transient`'s cases and the simulated cost of one `Net::get` (03 §9.3).
- G6: `Fs::read_dir`'s item type, which `DirEntry` methods ADMIT-1 admits, and whether
  `OsStr`/`OsString` keep their Rust API (03 §1.1, ADMIT-1).
- G9: whether `Stdin` reads are inherent; parameter types of `world.args` and `world.stdin`;
  whether a `world.http` peer closure must be `Send` (03 §1.1, §9.2).

## Scope

In scope: decide each of G3, G4, G5, G6, G9 in its owning chapter (03, with 01 D7/D15 where a
decision changes), then update the reference (6.1, 6.3, 6.7, 6.8, 7.1-7.3) or companion 17.

Out of scope: contract semantics (the sibling bead for G10-G12); implementing std.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each item, with the reasoning, and drops the matching "provisional" markers.
- The reference or companion states each decision; the core stays under D14's budget
  (24,989 of 25,000 tokens; recount with scripts/count-tokens.sh; detail goes to the companion).
- A review round in reviews/ finds no contradiction among 01, 03, and the reference pair.

## Implementation Notes

1. Prefer Rust's API wherever it can carry the meaning (D18: a Tide program is valid Rust); a
   departure needs a stated reason, as `Shared::new(v, tasks)` has.
2. For G4, POSIX rename atomicity is the reading every atomic-replace protocol needs; check what
   the simulator's crash model (03 §9.5) must then guarantee.
3. Docs-only design work: review rounds, not converge (GOVERNANCE.md).

## Verification

- `grep -n provisional design/reference.md` no longer marks the decided items.
- The review file's verdict is approve or approve with notes.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask the owner if a decision changes a D-level rule in 01 (D7, D15, D18).
close_reason: Decided G3, G4, G5, G6, G9 in 03 and D15; reference pair updated (core 24,995 tokens); rounds 25-28, round 28 approves with notes.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Owner decisions, 2026-10-20 (all recommended options):
- G3: RecvError {Disconnected, Cancelled}; RecvTimeoutError {Timeout, Disconnected, Cancelled}; SendError<T> {Disconnected(T), Cancelled(T)} with into_inner() and is_cancelled(); try_* keep Rust's types (not checkpoints); iteration ends at the first error of either kind; a disconnect is never an echo.
- G4: each unsynced entry change (create, rename, remove, new dir) survives whole or is lost; a rename leaves the target old or new and the source gone exactly when the target is new; only file contents tear; which unsynced changes survive is otherwise unspecified. title: Define the Ferox full-fidelity syntax trivia and comment-preservation model for CST, formatter, and docs
description: The specs now assume full-fidelity syntax, conservative formatter recovery, doc-comment attachment, and comment/trivia preservation, but the queue does not yet track the exact model that parser and formatter work should implement. This task should define how Ferox represents trivia, comments, and doc comments in the concrete syntax tree so later formatter, docs, and safe rewrite tooling can rely on one durable source-preserving model.
design: Primary question: what full-fidelity syntax model should Ferox use so parsing, formatting, documentation, and later refactors preserve source meaning and source-adjacent structure without inventing ad hoc side channels? Define: 1. whether trivia is token-attached, node-attached, or stored in a separate full-fidelity layer; 2. how line comments, block comments if any, and doc comments are tokenized and attached; 3. what syntax tree invariants the formatter and parser recovery logic may rely on; 4. what stays intentionally out of scope for the first parser slice.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: how comments and trivia are represented; how doc comments attach to declarations; what parser/formatter invariants the CST guarantees; and what validation/logging expectations apply. Include worked examples for preserved comments and doc comments, rejected alternative models, unit/corpus/e2e validation expectations, and tracing requirements for trivia-preserving parsing and formatting decisions.
notes: Decision: Ferox should use one full-fidelity CST model that preserves comments, doc comments, whitespace, and other trivia in source order rather than discarding them into side tables. AST/lowered views may omit trivia, but formatter, documentation generation, and later structural rewrites should all derive from this same source-preserving CST. Conservative recovery must preserve original text for uncertain regions.

title: Order sink output against an inherited child's stdout/stderr; spell stdout-to-stderr redirection
description:
## Why

`Stdio::inherit()` (the default for `status()` and `spawn()`) hands a child file descriptors 1 and
2 directly, while Tide's `out` and `err` sinks go through a process-wide buffer that a writer
thread drains (SINK-5). So `println!("building"); cmd.status()?;` can print the child's output
before "building", which Rust never does. Separately, Rust's `.stdout(io::stderr())` idiom lost its
spelling when fx-obr dropped `From<io::Stdout>`/`From<io::Stderr>` for `Stdio`, and nothing names a
replacement. Found by round 68 (N5) while reviewing fx-obr; the ordering gap predates that change.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 `Stdio` note; §2.4 SINK-1, SINK-4, SINK-5.
- `design/reference.md` 6.5; `design/reference-companion.md` 20.
- `reviews/round68-consistency.md` N5.

## Scope

In scope: decide how sink output and an inherited child's output are ordered (for example, spawn
flushes the task's `out` and `err` buffers and waits for the writer first), including inside
`join`/`par_*` branch buffers (SINK-4) and under simulation; decide whether a child's stdout can be
redirected to the parent's stderr and how to spell it. State both in 03 and the reference pair.

Out of scope: other process semantics under simulation.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides both points with reasoning; companion 20 (or the core, within D14's budget) states them.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction among 03, the reference pair, and the SINK rules.

## Notes

Prefer Rust's observable behavior (D18). Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.
close_reason: SINK-4 orders sink output before a child on the process's descriptors; SINK-5 discards unwritable records; Stdio regains From<io::Stdout/Stderr>; rounds 76-79 clean (Codex approve, round 79)

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decisions (03 SINK-4, SINK-5, §1.1 Stdio note; companion 20):
- Order: when Command's spawn/status/output starts a child whose stdout or stderr is the process's own (inherit, the spawn/status default, or io::stdout()/io::stderr()), it first waits until the writer has written every earlier sink record (or dropped it where SINK-5 allows); branch records count once their join appends them. Backpressure, not suspension; the simulator needs none (SINK-6). SINK-5 adds: a record that cannot be written to stderr is discarded, so the wait always ends. Rejected: piping the child through the writer thread (round 68 N5's alternative): extra copies and changes the child's isatty view; unconditional wait (blocks output() needlessly).
- Redirection: restore Rust's From<io::Stdout>/From<io::Stderr> for Stdio (reverses fx-obr's drop): they name fds 1 and 2, exactly as inherit() does, so they grant nothing new, and SINK-4 removes the ordering hazard that motivated the drop. .stdout(io::stderr()) ports unchanged (D18). Cost: under root.log.to_file, io::stderr() as a sink writes to the file, but as a Stdio it is fd 2.
- Simulation: sim.world.proc model output placement stays out of scope (bead).
Core unchanged (24,999).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Wording update after rounds 77-78: SINK-5 says out/err are never dropped under load, and any record (other than the closed-stdout exit-141 case) that cannot be written to its destination is discarded, so SINK-4's wait always ends; SINK-4 counts a branch's records as emitted when the outermost join appends them to its task's output.

title: #![no_std] hides Tide's std from tide-admit, switching off Pure
description:
## Why

`Crates::new` (`crates/tide-admit/src/crates.rs`, `injected_std`) takes Tide's std to be the crate
behind the `extern crate std` that rustc's std injection adds. A candidate's `#![no_std]` changes
that injection to `core`, and an explicit `extern crate std;` still links the operator's Tide std.
`Crates::tide_std()` is then `None`, so (a) the walk builds no `Pure` decision (`Walk::new`), which
switches off every rule that needs one (GLOBAL-1 statics, AFREE-1/2, LOCK-1/4, PAR-4..7, PURE-1),
and (b) Tide's std's items get `Role::Other`, so each use is FX0520 and none of its re-exports
count as exported. Found by Codex in fx-kw8.8 round 1 (`reviews/fx-kw8.8-r1-codex.md`, B1);
fx-kw8.8 moved only FX0512's switch to the operator's `--tide-std`.

Evidence: `conformance/cases/authority/root_main_no_std.rs` shows (b): `fn main() {}` under
`#![no_std]` + `extern crate std;` gets FX0520 for `impl Termination for ()`. Whether (a) admits a
crate that the injected-std build rejects (for example a core-only non-`Pure` `static`, or a
`#[pure]` fn over a core type with interior mutability) is not yet shown.

## Scope

Decide and enforce how a candidate's `#![no_std]` (and `#![no_core]`, already unstable) is treated:
either reject it (it is not part of the Tide surface; check `design/reference.md` and D18's
allowlist before choosing, and pick the FX code the design gives or record the choice) or identify
Tide's std from the operator's `--tide-std` artifact rather than from the candidate's std injection.
Record the decision and its reason on this bead.

## Acceptance

A conformance case with `#![no_std]` + `extern crate std;` that defines something the injected-std
build rejects for `Pure` (or the attribute itself, if rejected) gets the same verdict as without
`#![no_std]`; `conformance/run.sh` exits 0 and `cargo test --workspace` passes.

title: Enforce FX0506: no code calls main (ROOT-5)
description:
## Why

ROOT-5 (`design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §2.1): no code calls `main` or uses it as a value
(`FX0506`), so a test cannot mint a real `Root` through it. tide-admit does not decide FX0506 yet
(`conformance/cases/authority/root_main_called.rs` is AWAITS CHECKER). Once fx-kw8.9 builds and
runs test executables, a `#[test]` that calls the crate-root `main` that `#[tide::main]` generates
mints a real `Root` inside a test, which breaks RUN-1's sandbox guarantee. Found by the fx-nkv.1
worker (2026-11-01).

## Scope

Enforce ROOT-5 in `crates/tide-admit` under `FX0506`: any call of, or reference to, the binary's
`main` (including through a path, a re-export, or a function pointer) outside the toolchain's own
entry wiring. Keep the generated entry point and the test harness admitted.

## Acceptance

`conformance/cases/authority/root_main_called.rs` PASSes (no longer AWAITS CHECKER for FX0506),
with a case that takes `main` as a value; `conformance/run.sh` exits 0 and
`cargo test --workspace` passes.

title: Stable item identity and definition hashes in tide-admit
description:
## Why

Every seal hash (SEAL-2, `design/04-contracts.md:1265-1280`) and §11's spec-closure
hash (`04:1200-1213`) identify items by stable ID and abstract the names hashed text
references, so a rename changes nothing while an edit to a referenced definition does.
fx-kw8.10 gives public items an identity for the authority artifact; seals also need
private items, impl methods by qualified path (`<Entry as PartialEq>::eq`), and tests,
per configuration. This slice builds the one identity and definition-hash owner.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md:894` (D14): definitions are content-hashed; symbols have stable IDs.
- `design/04-contracts.md:1247-1280`: SEAL-1 entries by stable ID; SEAL-2's resolution
  and dependency rules (std by toolchain version, dependencies by locked content hash).
- The stable-ID and cycle decisions recorded by fx-zr3.
- fx-kw8.10's public-item identity in `crates/tide-admit/`.

## Scope

In scope: `crates/tide-admit/`: stable IDs for every item the seal can name; a
definition hash per item and configuration that records what each path, method call,
operator, and associated-type projection resolves to, by stable ID and content hash,
not by name; cycles hashed as fx-zr3 decides; std hashed by toolchain
version, dependencies by locked content hash. Extend fx-kw8.10's identity rather than
adding a second one.

Out of scope: clause normalization (fx-kw8.16); seal files and FX0920.

## Acceptance

- Tests in `crates/tide-admit/tests/` show: renaming a referenced item leaves the
  referencing item's hash unchanged; editing it changes the hash; a new impl or import
  that changes which item a call selects changes it; a doc-comment or formatting edit
  changes nothing; mutually recursive functions hash deterministically.
- fx-kw8.10's artifact uses the same identity.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` exits 0.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if fx-zr3's decisions do not cover a case this slice meets; record it there rather than deciding a second owner here.
- Stop if verification fails twice for the same reason after a reasonable fix attempt.

title: Clause normalization and spec-closure hashes in tide-admit
description:
## Why

An interface seal entry fixes a function's contract through §11's spec-closure hash
(`design/04-contracts.md:1200-1213`, SEAL-2 `:1275-1284`): normalized clauses plus,
transitively, the bodies of functions clauses call (operator impls included), types,
constants, and traits they name. No code normalizes clauses or computes this hash;
fx-mhd's macros lower clauses to runtime checks, which is a different job.

## Evidence

- `design/04-contracts.md:1200-1213`: what the spec-closure hash covers and excludes.
- `design/04-contracts.md:383-514` (§1.8): v0 clause forms.
- fx-mhd: the production contract macros (`#[requires]`, `#[ensures]`, `invariant!`,
  `old`, `result`, bounded quantifiers).
- fx-zr3's decision on what an erased (release) configuration hashes.

## Scope

In scope: `crates/tide-admit/`: one clause normalizer and the spec-closure hash for
every function, public or not, with or without a contract, per configuration, built
on the stable-identity owner (fx-kw8.15). Contract use (§2.1) is part of the interface hash, not
of this one.

Out of scope: runtime lowering (fx-mhd owns it); solver refinement classes (v1);
`spec fn`, views, and laws beyond what v0 parses.

## Acceptance

- Tests show: reformatting a clause or renaming a function it calls leaves the hash
  unchanged; changing a clause, or the body of a function or `PartialEq` impl a clause
  calls, changes it; editing only the specified function's body changes nothing.
- A changed hash reports which clauses differ, with §11's `weakened` label for a
  removed `ensures` or added `requires`.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` exits 0.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if fx-zr3's decisions do not cover a case this slice meets; record it there rather than deciding a second owner here.
- Stop if verification fails twice for the same reason after a reasonable fix attempt.

title: Seal whole types and traits with the impls that apply
description:
## Why

Types, traits, and constants are always sealed whole (SEAL-2,
`design/04-contracts.md:1285-1310`): a whole type fixes its fields, variants,
generics, bounds, attributes, derives, and every impl in the crate that applies to
it; a whole trait fixes its items, default bodies, laws, and its impls at seal time.
This needs trait selection and is the hardest SEAL-2 part.

## Evidence

- `design/04-contracts.md:1285-1310`: whole entries, which impls apply (`&Feed`,
  `Vec<Feed>`, `impl<T: Copy> Bar for T` through `&Feed`), and which new impls are allowed.
- SEAL-6 (`04:1353-1368`): limits this slice must not exceed.

## Scope

In scope: `crates/tide-admit/`: whole entries for structs, enums, aliases,
constants, and traits; the applies-to relation, counting an impl as applying wherever
trait selection cannot rule it out; private inherent methods fixed; new trait impls
admitted unless they apply to a type sealed whole; FX0920 parts `definition`.

Out of scope: test entries; manifest; method bodies (free, except as hashed elsewhere).

title: Require the unsafe grant for safe fns in unsafe extern blocks
description:
## Why

Found by fx-kw8.10's round-1 Opus review (reviews/fx-kw8.10-r1-opus.md, out of scope): a foreign function declared `safe` in an `unsafe extern` block (`unsafe extern "C" { pub safe fn abs(x: i32) -> i32; }`) is admitted without the `unsafe` grant, and callers call it with no `unsafe` block. A foreign call is a trust hole (D11) and FFI is v1 (03 §5), so a package without the grant can reach foreign code.

## Evidence

- `crates/tide-admit/src/walk.rs` `fn_item` flags FX0901 only for `header.is_unsafe()`; `visit_foreign_item` records a foreign-item hole but flags nothing.
- design/03-authority-concurrency.md §5 (FFI, v1) and UNSAFE-1.

## Acceptance

Without the grant, any `extern` block item, `safe` ones included, is rejected (FX0901 or the code the design names); with it, it is admitted and listed as a hole. A driver test covers both.

title: tide-admit owns every rustc invocation
description:
## Why

D18: the driver owns every rustc invocation. It passes `-Zallow-features=`, adds no user-controlled
`--extern`, `-L`, `--sysroot`, `--cfg`, or semantic `-C` flags, runs no build scripts or proc macros
for Tide crates except the toolchain's, injects Tide's std with `--extern std=`, and keeps its own
content-addressed cache. The spike's `spikes/d18/admit/scripts/tide-rustc` is the prototype gate.
Parent epic has the context.

## Scope

In scope: the invocation layer in `crates/`, its tests, and the RUN-2 build-isolation cases that
need no sandbox (rejected `include_*!`, `env!`, `#[path]`, ignored `RUSTFLAGS`, `RUSTC_WRAPPER`,
`.cargo/config.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml`; `build.rs` is FX0915). Out of scope: the OS sandbox
and the test harness (RUN-3 onward).

## Acceptance

- A crate cannot change the flags rustc receives; each RUN-2 case in scope passes.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` and `conformance/run.sh` exit 0; converge, then the review loop.
