title: Mono-item backstop for denied impls in tide-admit
description:
## Why

fx-kw8.1's HIR walk closes admission routes one at a time: review rounds 2–5
(`reviews/fx-kw8.1-r2..r5-opus.md`) each found another route to a denied impl
through obligations, fn-item where-clauses, or `main`'s `Termination` bound. Every one of
them ends in a few denied impls (core's `impl<F: FnPtr> Debug/Hash/PartialOrd/Ord/Pointer
for F`, `impl Default for RandomState`, and the array `From` impls of `HashMap`/`HashSet`).
All of these are generic or `#[inline]`, so an instance that can run is among the local crate's
mono items however the code reached it. A check over mono items would catch the routes
the walk has not found yet.

## Design (from round 5, not built)

- In `after_analysis`, which runs only when rustc and the walk found no errors, call
  `tcx.collect_and_partition_mono_items(())`. For each `MonoItem::Fn` that is a method of a
  non-local trait impl, build the impl key as `admit_impl` does. Reject only on an explicit
  `Deny` or an ungranted `Unsafe` rule. Unlisted keys do not count, because std's internals
  instantiate unlisted impls.
- Report at the nearest local mono item: walk `mentioned_items` back from the instance, and
  only when something is rejected. Failing that, report at the crate root and name the
  instance.
- Record in D18/ADMIT-1 that this part of the gate runs after type checking.

## Open points

- Forcing mono collection in `--emit metadata` builds costs time, and post-mono const errors
  then appear in check builds.
- `-Zshare-generics` is on by default at opt-level 0. A downstream crate can link an upstream
  instance instead of making its own. `-Zshare-generics=no` would need an ADMIT-2 line.
- In a lib, the roots are only the reachable non-generic items.
- Testing: once the walk is right, no program reaches the backstop alone. Pick one: a test
  switch that disables the walk's obligation step, or a probe corpus kept as evidence.

## Acceptance

- With the walk's obligation step disabled, the backstop alone rejects each of fx-kw8.1's
  r2–r5 hole probes with FX0520 at a local span. With the walk enabled, the diagnostics are
  the same as before.
- D18/ADMIT-1 state when the backstop runs; `cargo test --workspace` and
  `conformance/run.sh` exit 0.
close_reason: Backstop in tide-admit (walk/mono.rs, after analysis): denied/ungranted impl instances FX0520 and Pure where-clauses at uses, over rustc's lazily collected mono items with build-equivalent roots (reachable_non_generics override) and -Zshare-generics=no. With --tide-test-backstop the backstop alone rejects every fx-kw8.1 r2-r5 route at a local span (tests/driver.rs) and the fx-kw8.2 Pure routes that have instances; with the walk on, diagnostics unchanged (conformance 181 PASS/28 AWAITS, exit 0; cargo test --workspace exit 0). ADMIT-1, ADMIT-2, D18 record when it runs. Reviews r1 (Opus+Codex), r2-r3 Opus (r3 clean), r4 Codex approve.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Scope extension from fx-kw8.2 (decision, 2026-10-21): fx-kw8.2's review rounds 4–7 kept finding routes where rustc discharges a local item's `X: Pure` clause through std's blanket impl without selecting a checked impl: Drop-impl bounds, impl-item where-clauses, opaque associated-type bounds, GAT where-clauses named in generic args, and constructors used as values. Each was closed in the HIR walk (reviews/fx-kw8.2-r4..r7-opus.md; r6 has a 29-row discharge-site table). The route-independent closure is this bead's backstop: for every local mono item, instantiate its predicates and its parents' (impl and trait) and decide their `Pure` part with pure.rs. That catches any remaining route in reachable code. Same open points as above: lib roots, share-generics, cost, and how to test something the walk already covers.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decisions, 2026-10-31 (agent; technical, per AGENTS.md Decisions):

- Mechanism: `crates/tide-admit/src/walk/mono.rs`, run from `after_analysis` (rustc's analysis raises fatal on any earlier error, so it runs only when rustc and the walk found none). rustc's collector (`collect_and_partition_mono_items`) runs eagerly (`-Clink-dead-code`): a metadata-only build exports no symbols, so lazy collection has no library roots (`rustc_codegen_ssa/src/back/symbol_export.rs:55`). Eager collection also instantiates provided methods, const values, and drop glue that never run (round 1, both reviewers), so the backstop keeps only items reachable from local non-generic fns, local statics, and the `start` instance through `items_of_instance(UsedItems)` and static-initializer pointers.
- `-Zshare-generics=no`: the crate instantiates upstream generics itself (except `#[inline(never)]` ones an upstream crate made), so their instances are among its mono items. Both flags are recorded in ADMIT-2.
- FX0520: a non-local trait impl method whose `impl_key` an explicit Deny rule or an ungranted Unsafe rule matches; unlisted keys do not count. Reported at the nearest local users (BFS back through non-local users; `start` stands for `main`), else the crate root.
- Pure (scope extension): for live items of the local crate, Tide's std, or other Tide crates, `use_generic` plus the trait method's own clauses at rebased args, in a fully monomorphized environment; decided once, reported only at uses. Roots' clauses are their callers' preconditions, so an uncalled root is not checked.
- Test switch: `--tide-test-backstop` skips the walk's `obligation` and `pure_obligation`. Kept as an operator-trusted flag (operators already choose grants; the cache key records it) rather than a debug-only build, so `cargo test` exercises the shipped binary.
- Not covered: generic-only code with no instance in the crate (the walk owns it; a downstream crate's backstop sees its instances); `std::path::absolute` from r2 was a missing path rule, not an impl route.
- Constraint: the backstop needs optimized MIR for every upstream generic it reaches. A dependency checked by tide-admit alone is a metadata-only rmeta without MIR, and collection would stop with rustc's NoOptimizedMir fatal; dependencies must be full rlibs (as the stub std is) until multi-crate builds are designed.
- Cost: conformance corpus 2m18s before the roots fix, 2m22s after (209 cases, 4 driver runs each); round 1 measured 1.6x wall time on a 600-line library before per-use deciding was removed.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Correction, 2026-10-31, after review round 2 (reviews/fx-kw8.4-r2-opus.md): the earlier decisions comment is stale on collection. Eager collection (`-Clink-dead-code`) is gone: rustc's collector raised post-monomorphization errors (a provided method's failing `const` assert) in code that never runs, which no root filter can stop. The driver now collects lazily and overrides the `reachable_non_generics` query with `rustc_codegen_ssa::back::symbol_export::reachable_non_generics_helper` (the helper rustc exposes for Miri), so a metadata check has a full build's roots: what a library exports (Rust-level threshold), statics, and the entry point; a bin or `--test` build checks what its entry reaches. Metadata output is unchanged (round 3 checked the encoder). Every collected item is live; ADMIT-2 records one added flag, `-Zshare-generics=no`. What a library's build does not export (generics, `#[inline]` functions, closures returned uncalled) is checked in the crates that instantiate them. Round 3 was clean; conformance takes 2m25s (2m18s at the first candidate).

title: FX0915 finds build.rs only beside src/ entries
description:
## Why

D13 and `design/reference.md` §12.4 ("No `build.rs`") make a package build script `FX0915`. tide-admit finds the package root by a heuristic: when the entry file's directory is named `src`, its parent is the package; otherwise the entry's own directory is (`crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, the `lexical_package` computation in `run()`, then `package.join("build.rs")`). An entry at `pkg/src/bin/tool.rs` or `pkg/tests/t.rs` therefore misses `pkg/build.rs`, so a package with a build script gets no FX0915. The driver never runs the script, so nothing executes; the gap is a missing verdict. Found in fx-kw8.3 review rounds 1 and 5 (`reviews/fx-kw8.3-r1-opus.md` N9, `reviews/fx-kw8.3-r5-opus.md`).

## Evidence

- `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, `run()`: `lexical_package` takes the parent only when the entry's directory is named `src`, and FX0915 checks `package.join("build.rs")`.
- `design/reference.md` §12.4: the manifest is `tide.toml` (provisional name and keys), with no `build` key.
- `README.md` (the tide-admit section) documents the current rule: "The source directory is the entry's parent; when it is named `src`, its parent is the package directory."

## Scope

In scope:
- Package-root detection in `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, its tests in `crates/tide-admit/tests/invocation.rs`, and the README sentence above.

Out of scope:
- Parsing `tide.toml` or `Cargo.toml` keys; a package manager.
- The snapshot root: the source directory stays the entry's parent, and only the FX0915 lookup and the out-of-package checks use the package root.
- Running anything.

## Acceptance

- A package with `build.rs` at its root gets FX0915 (exit 1) when the entry is `src/lib.rs`, `src/main.rs`, `src/bin/<x>.rs`, or `tests/<x>.rs`, and nothing reads or runs the script.
- Single-file roots (an entry whose directory has no package marker) behave as today.

## Implementation Notes

1. Pick the marker: the nearest ancestor of the entry, within a bounded walk, that holds `tide.toml` or `Cargo.toml`, falling back to today's `src` rule when none is found. Record the choice and why on this bead and in the README.
2. Keep the existing symlink and containment checks (the package path must not traverse a directory symlink; output must sit outside the package) working with the new root.
3. Add the four entry shapes to `build_scripts_are_rejected_without_running` in `crates/tide-admit/tests/invocation.rs`.

## Verification

- `timeout 1200 cargo test --workspace < /dev/null` exits 0.
- `timeout 1800 conformance/run.sh < /dev/null` exits 0 with 0 FAIL.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if choosing the marker needs an owner decision on the manifest's name. `design/reference.md` calls `tide.toml` provisional; ask only if the design changes it.
- Stop if the walk would need to read files outside the entry's ancestors.

## Maintenance Notes

- Finish through converge, then the GOVERNANCE.md review loop.

title: Candidate-controlled inputs give exit 2 instead of a verdict
description:
## Why

RUN-2 says a symbolic link or path that leaves the candidate tree "reads as missing", and exit 2 is tide-admit's setup-error class: `conformance/run.sh` treats a driver exit above 1 as "the driver crashed". fx-kw8.3 fixed this for unreferenced snapshot entries. These candidate-controlled inputs still turn a check into exit 2 instead of a verdict (exit 1), or into reading as missing:
- an unreadable subdirectory under the source directory (`fs::read_dir(dir)?` in `Sources::snapshot`'s `walk`);
- an entry file that is not valid UTF-8, or an entry symlink that resolves outside the source directory ("candidate source is not admitted");
- an `--out-dir` whose missing part contains `..` (`destination()`). This one is operator input, so it is lower priority.
Found in `reviews/fx-kw8.3-r3-opus.md`, `r5`, and `r6`.

## Evidence

- `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, `Sources::snapshot`: `fs::read_dir(dir)?` aborts the snapshot.
- `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, `run()`: `return Err("candidate source is not admitted".into())`, which exits 2.
- `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, `destination()`.
- `crates/tide-admit/tests/invocation.rs`, `candidate_content_gets_rustc_diagnostics_and_every_verdict`: the existing test for unreferenced dangling or non-UTF-8 entries.

## Scope

In scope:
- `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs` (snapshot walk, entry admission, `destination`) and its tests.

Out of scope:
- The loader's authorization rules: what the snapshot serves must not grow.
- The cache key layout, except as needed to record a skipped entry.

## Acceptance

- An unreadable subdirectory reads as missing: the crate is checked, and a module in it gets rustc's E0583 (exit 1).
- A non-UTF-8 entry, or an entry symlink leaving the source directory, gets a verdict (exit 1, a short-format error naming the entry) and never discloses the target's bytes.
- `--out-dir` with `..` in a missing component either works or fails with a clear setup error; record which on this bead.

## Implementation Notes

1. Write a failing test for each input first, in `crates/tide-admit/tests/invocation.rs`.
2. Skip unreadable directories the way fx-kw8.3 skips unreadable files.
3. Report entry failures as a rejection (exit 1). Do not let them reach rustc's parse fallback, which reopens paths directly after a loader error on this pin (`rustc_parse/src/lib.rs` around line 118).

## Verification

- `timeout 1200 cargo test --workspace < /dev/null` exits 0.
- `timeout 1800 conformance/run.sh < /dev/null` exits 0 with 0 FAIL.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if a fix would let the loader serve any path outside the snapshot.

## Maintenance Notes

- Finish through converge, then the GOVERNANCE.md review loop.

title: rustc ICE reports can be written into the candidate tree
description:
## Why

RUN-2 allows the toolchain to write only its artifact cache and the run's output directory. tide-admit runs rustc with an empty environment (fx-kw8.3). On this nightly, a compiler crash then writes `rustc-ice-<time>-<pid>.txt` to the process's current directory (`rustc_driver_impl/src/lib.rs:1404-1428`: `RUSTC_ICE` unset gives `-Zmetrics-dir`, else `current_dir()`), and that directory may be inside the candidate tree. fx-kw8.3 review round 3 found such a file in the repository, left by a seeded crash (`reviews/fx-kw8.3-r3-opus.md`). A candidate that can trigger an ICE can make the gate write into its own tree, and the report holds compiler internals.

## Evidence

- `/home/lucca/.rustup/toolchains/nightly-2026-08-09-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/rustlib/rustc-src/rust/compiler/rustc_driver_impl/src/lib.rs:1404-1428`: ICE path selection; `RUSTC_ICE=0` opts out.
- `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, `run()`: the top-level re-exec with `env_clear()` whenever the environment is non-empty, and the `--tide-compile` child, also spawned with `env_clear()`.

## Scope

In scope:
- Where the compile child's crash reports go, in `crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs`, plus one test.

Out of scope:
- The OS build sandbox (Landlock/seccomp), which is later work.
- Changing the cleared environment for anything other than this one variable or directory.

## Acceptance

- When rustc ICEs under tide-admit, no file appears outside the output directory's `.tide-cache`. The ICE either goes nowhere (`RUSTC_ICE=0`) or into the staging directory, which is removed on failure.
- The driver still exits non-zero with rustc's ICE message on stderr.

## Implementation Notes

1. Pitfall: `run()` re-execs with a cleared environment whenever any variable is set. Simply adding `RUSTC_ICE=0` to the child makes the child re-exec and drop it. Either let the worker mode keep exactly that variable, or pass `-Zmetrics-dir=<staging dir>` among the driver-built rustc arguments (no env change; check that it also accepts the ICE path on this pin).
2. Test: force an ICE with a seeded change if no stable trigger exists. Use `-Ztreat-err-as-bug` only if the fixed interface can reach it in a test-only path. Otherwise verify by reading the code path and record why.

## Verification

- `timeout 1200 cargo test --workspace < /dev/null` exits 0.
- `timeout 1800 conformance/run.sh < /dev/null` exits 0 with 0 FAIL.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the fix needs a user-controlled rustc flag: ADMIT-2 forbids them.

## Maintenance Notes

- Finish through converge, then the GOVERNANCE.md review loop.
close_reason: done

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Done. The clean process's whole environment is RUSTC_ICE=0: run() re-execs unless the environment is exactly that (an empty one too), both spawns set it, and rustc's ICE hook is installed only after that normalization (moved from main.rs), so a crash in the compiler or a panic before compilation writes no rustc-ice file; the crash message still goes to stderr and the exit code passes through. Test-only flag --tide-test-ice seeds a compiler panic (in the cache key). Test crashes_write_no_report_files: red before the fix (rustc-ice file in the package), green after; the /dev/full subtest fails by mutation with the hook back in main. Proof: cargo test --workspace exit 0 (2+9+14) on the final tree (diff SHA-256 8a927b1a); conformance/run.sh exit 0, 188 PASS on the same driver code (later rounds touched only the test and docs). Reviews r1 Opus clean + Codex request_changes (empty env, early hook), r2-r3 Opus test/doc fixes, r4 Opus clean, r5 Codex approve. Out of scope: core files from a crash by signal (RUN-2 OS sandbox).

title: Enforce FX0512 for unmarked main
description:
## Why

ROOT-1 already requires FX0512. Existing metadata conformance fixtures can check it independently of executable codegen.

## Evidence

root_main_plain.rs, root_main_unmarked.rs and admit_main_return.rs get their normative per-line verdicts under the conformance runner, including a marked valid entry; conformance/run.sh must exit 0 for the complete corpus, including every existing FX0512 mark such as pure_routes.rs. description:

comments.text: From fx-kw8.14 (0eb9845): FX0506 now covers any crate built with --test, so a library's or integration test's crate-root fn main (a plain helper, or a #[test] fn main) is rejected under --test though it mints nothing; rename it. A crate-root #[tide::main] main of a library is trusted under --test, and FX0506 keeps its tests from calling it.

title: Define the Ferox comment and doc-comment syntax surface, attachment rules, and bootstrap support boundary
description: The tooling specs already assume file-level doc comments, declaration doc comments, and preserved comments in formatter recovery, but the language surface still lacks an explicit comment syntax decision. This task should define the concrete Ferox syntax for ordinary comments and doc comments, how they attach to modules and declarations, and what comment forms the bootstrap parser/formatter must support first.
design: Primary question: what exact comment and doc-comment forms should Ferox support, and how should they attach to source structure? Define: 1. whether Ferox uses line comments only, line plus block comments, and what doc-comment markers exist; 2. what counts as a file-level doc comment versus a declaration-attached doc comment; 3. how comments participate in the full-fidelity CST and formatter behavior; 4. what comment forms are intentionally out of scope for the first bootstrap parser if any.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: the exact comment/doc-comment syntax forms; attachment and precedence rules; formatter and documentation implications; and bootstrap validation/logging expectations. Include concrete examples for file-level and declaration doc comments, rejected ambiguous alternatives, and explicit parser/formatter/doc-generation expectations.
notes: Decision: Ferox v1 uses a deliberately small comment surface: // for ordinary line comments, /// for declaration doc comments, and //// for file-level doc comments. Declaration docs attach to the next declaration; file-level docs attach to the file/module at the top of the file. Block comments and Rust-style inner-doc variants stay out of the v1 surface.

title: Run an autoresearch-style loop on checker speed once the checker exists
description:
Why: research/14-autoresearch.md finds Karpathy's autoresearch loop (frozen evaluator, one mutable file, keep-or-revert on one metric, a log of every attempt) does not fit Tide's design work but fits checker speed (D12 target: about 30 ms edit to diagnostics; D0 E4).

Start only after the v0 checker exists and has a test and conformance suite.

Scope:
- A frozen benchmark corpus and timing harness the loop cannot write to (the prepare.py role).
- One checker module or crate the agent may edit (the train.py role).
- Metric: median edit-to-diagnostics time on the corpus. Gate: the full test and conformance suite passes; a failing run is a discard.
- Keep-or-revert per attempt on one branch, an append-only results log (commit, time, status, description), and the simplicity rule: equal time with less code wins.
- An AP-EXCEPTION-001 exception the owner approves, bounded to that branch, since the loop runs without asking per step (AP-SCOPE-001, AP-PLAN-001, AP-GIT-001). Converge and the supervisor verdict still apply to the kept diff before it merges.

Out of scope: loops over design/reference.md or trial tasks (research/14 explains why), and the diagnostic-text loop, which gets its own bead if this one works.

Acceptance: the harness and corpus sit outside the agent's write set; one bounded run produces a results log and a kept diff whose speedup reproduces on a rerun of the harness; the kept diff passes the full suite.

Cheapest falsifier: if a bounded run keeps no change that reproduces, the loop is not worth its exception.

title: Define the new Ferox vision around safe change: low-entropy systems design, FP-shaped readability, fast feedback, and verification-ready tooling
description: Refine the Ferox vision into a sharper and more defensible thesis. The current direction under discussion is an ownership-based systems language for safe change: Rust-grade safe-code guarantees, lower semantic entropy than Rust, explicit performance behavior, FP-shaped readability, fast incremental feedback, and tooling designed for humans and agents to evolve large codebases without semantic drift.
design: Target shape: ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression-oriented code, immutable-by-default data flow, and a narrow pipe style inspired by the best parts of Gleam and Elixir, but without runtime magic or effect-heavy complexity. Keep ownership, mutation, async, and sharing explicit. Avoid syntax macros, trait/generic sprawl, and capability-heavy concurrency in the near term. Strengthen the tooling story around query-native incremental compilation, full-fidelity syntax trees, canonical formatting, structured diagnostics, normalized checked IR, and a first-party structural rule/autofix system. Treat verification as a later optional layer built around contracts, ghost/spec code, and proof-oriented tooling for critical modules rather than as a proof-first core language. Current version framing under discussion: v1 = Safe Core, v2 = Safe Change, v3 = Deep Assurance.
acceptance_criteria: A revised Ferox vision should clearly explain: 1. why Ferox exists if Rust already delivers strong safety; 2. what 'better for agents' means mechanically; 3. how FP influence improves readability without increasing entropy; 4. why fast feedback and incremental checking are core product requirements; 5. which high-leverage external ideas genuinely strengthen Ferox; 6. which ideas remain out of scope because they would widen the core too much; 7. how simple staged descriptions for v1, v2, and v3 follow from the thesis rather than feeling like unrelated feature buckets.
notes: The vision cleanup pass is now complete in principle: the accepted direction has been folded into the canonical docs, and the temporary draft vision files were removed to leave one primary vision set. .beads/.gitignore was also updated to ignore .br_history tracker artifacts produced by br.
close_reason: Vision rewrite completed in canonical docs; remaining work now lives in the narrower follow-on design beads.

title: Property tests and generated contract tests
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) needs this surface to execute on the checked toolchain:
`trials/e1-checked/protocol.md` §10.1 lists it as E1-P12, and no existing bead owns it.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P12, §10.2)`
- `design/reference.md §10.2; design/04-contracts.md §2.4`

## Scope

Test functions with parameters, generation and shrinking for the listed types, requires-guided generation, the vacuity floor, #[sim_test] parameters and seeds, and generated contract tests for every function with an ensures. Production std under crates/, built and admitted through tide-admit; no new
language semantics.

## Acceptance

A false property fails with a shrunk input and its seed; a vacuous one fails as vacuous; a function whose ensures is violated on some generated input fails its generated test. Toolchain tests prove each item executes, not only type-checks.
Std API changes must also satisfy fx-nkv acceptance on production/conformance equivalence; the production library owns runtime behavior.

title: Define the Ferox explicit duplication model for copy-safe values, deep duplication, and generic duplication boundaries
description: The ownership spec now makes copy-safe values explicit, but the exact explicit-duplication surface is still intentionally open. This task should define how Ferox handles deliberate deep duplication for non-copy values, what generic constraints or library hooks are allowed, and how duplication remains visible without letting copy/clone semantics become muddy or trait-heavy.
design: Primary question: how should Ferox express explicit duplication for non-copy values while keeping copy-safe behavior simple and ownership reasoning local? Define: 1. whether duplication is a built-in operation, library function, trait-backed convention, or staged combination; 2. how generic code states duplication requirements; 3. what types may never be duplicated or only duplicated through domain-specific APIs; 4. how diagnostics and tooling should explain copy-safe versus explicit-duplication boundaries.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what syntax or API shape Ferox uses for explicit duplication; how generic duplication boundaries work; how duplication differs from implicit copy; and what stays out of scope. Include at least one recommended example, one rejected alternative, validation expectations for copy-safe versus explicit-duplication cases, and logging expectations for duplication eligibility diagnostics.
close_reason: Superseded: the owner discarded the first Ferox design (archived in archive/v0-design/) for the first-principles redesign in fx-agent-first-redesign-tf4; this work no longer applies.

title: Decide: run /correct from the session runner
description:
## Decision

Should the session runner (fx-3md) also run Starcompass's `correct` skill on
a schedule, so repeated owner corrections turn into decision beads without the
owner asking?

Recommendation: adopt, once fx-3md exists. Run `/correct` in a fresh headless
session when the runner stops with no work left, and otherwise at most once
every 10 sessions. Tide's "Decisions" rule makes this an agent decision.
Record it here, then do the work below or close this as rejected.

Owner suggestion, 2026-10-21: the owner asked why agents do not run `correct`
on their own, and asked for this as a decision.

## Why

`correct` (Starcompass `skills/correct`, linked into `~/.claude/skills` by
`skills/install.sh`) reads the owner's typed and queued messages from this
project's Claude Code sessions. It groups corrections that repeat across
sessions and files one bead per class, proposing the strongest enforcement:
structure, then checks, then trials, then wording. Skills run only when invoked
or matched, and nothing invokes this one. So the owner's corrections stay
buried in transcripts unless the owner remembers to type `/correct`.

## Evidence

- Starcompass `ap-1bu` (closed 2026-10-21): the skill, its converge rounds,
  and an isolated trial that correctly found real corrections and filed
  nothing below the two-session threshold.
- `~/.claude/projects/-home-lucca-pjs-lab-tide/` held 23 sessions with 116
  owner messages on 2026-10-21. That is enough history for real classes.

## Scope

In scope:
- The fx-3md runner: one more trigger that starts `/correct` in its own
  session, plus a run-log line for it.

Out of scope:
- The `correct` skill itself, which Starcompass owns. Report changes it needs
  there.
- Acting on the beads it files. They are decisions for later sessions.

## Acceptance

- The runner starts a `/correct` session when it stops with no work left, and
  at most once every 10 sessions otherwise.
- Each `/correct` run leaves one log line: time, the beads it filed or
  "none", and its cost.
- Two runs in a row over unchanged history file no duplicate beads.

## Verification

- With the runner's stub agent, the trigger fires at the stated points and
  nowhere else.
- One real run in Tide files beads only for classes seen in at least two
  sessions. Check each bead's quoted evidence against the transcript.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if fx-3md was rejected or has no trigger point to extend. Record that
  here.
- Stop if a real run files beads without transcript evidence. Report it to
  Starcompass as a `correct` defect.
close_reason: Trigger landed; test 27/27; two real runs passed; r3 Codex approve

title: Scope TASK-3: by-value arguments, Bend call cancellation, uninterruptible file I/O
description:
## Why

TASK-3 makes two claims that real operations do not meet. First, "checkpoints that consume a value
return it inside the error": read literally, that covers arguments passed by value to a checkpoint,
such as `Fs::write(p, vec)` and `write_synced` (`impl AsRef<[u8]>`), path arguments,
`Net::connect(addr)`, and Bend kernel calls that consume `board` (03 §10). Their errors have no room
for the value, and `BendFault` has no cancellation variant although 03 §1.1 says every capability
error type has one. Second, "an in-flight kernel operation is cancelled before the error returns":
Linux regular-file I/O and `fsync` (on NFS, for example) sleep uninterruptibly, so `write` and
`sync` can overrun a deadline, even a shielded scope's, just as `File::close` can, while TASK-5
names only `close`. Found by rounds 73 and 74 while reviewing fx-nyy; both predate it.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 intro (cancellation variants), TASK-3, TASK-5, §10
  (Bend calls are checkpoints).
- `design/reference.md` 6.3 (`Fs` signatures), 7.2.
- `reviews/round73-consistency.md` (out-of-scope findings); `reviews/round74-consistency.md`
  (out-of-scope finding, with suggested TASK-3 and TASK-5 wording).

## Scope

In scope: say which by-value arguments TASK-3's return rule covers (for example, only values the
operation delivers or keeps, such as `send` and `write_owned`, not arguments it only reads); give
Bend calls a cancellation story consistent with §1.1; state in TASK-3 and TASK-5 which kernel
operations cannot be cancelled in flight and what that does to deadlines. State it in 03 and,
within D14's budget, the reference pair.

Out of scope: `File::close` (fx-nyy decided it).

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each point with reasoning; the reference pair does not contradict it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (it is at 24,999 of 25,000; recount with
  `scripts/count-tokens.sh`, trimming elsewhere if needed).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.
close_reason: Decided in 03 TASK-3, TASK-5, §1.1 Receivers note, §9.3, §10; core 7.2 and D8 wording. Reviews: rounds 94-97 (Opus), 98 (Codex, approve). Follow-ups: fx-e3t.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decision (03 TASK-3, TASK-5, §1.1 Receivers note, §10 Accel and Failures; core 7.2 and 01 D8 wording):
1. TASK-3's return rule covers values a checkpoint hands over: channel payloads and owned buffers (send, read_owned, write_owned). Arguments it only reads (impl AsRef data, paths, addresses, Bend arguments copied to the server) are dropped with the call; callers that need them pass a reference or a clone. Reason: returning every argument would need a generic error type per operation, and AsRef already lets callers keep ownership. Core 7.2 and D8 say 'hand a value over' instead of 'consume a value'.
2. BendFault gains Cancelled (is_cancelled() true), satisfying §1.1. Process mode abandons the request and restarts the server; in-process mode cannot stop a running kernel, which finishes first like a foreign call.
3. Kernel calls the kernel cannot cancel once running (regular-file reads, writes, fsync) run to the end and return their own result; the task observes cancellation at its next checkpoint, so a finished write reports success. Rejected: reporting Cancelled after the effect happened (hides a completed write). Multi-call operations (fs.write, remove_dir_all) check between calls and can stop partway. TASK-5 lists a running regular-file kernel call; with close, it can block on NFS inside a shielded scope with a deadline.
Core at 24,996 of 25,000.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after round 94 (B1, B2, N1-N4, N6): (1) TASK-3/TASK-5 name the class: file-system calls on regular files and directories (reads, writes, fsync, opens, renames, removals, metadata queries, directory reads) cannot be cancelled once running and return their own result; 'system call' replaces 'kernel call' (Bend's kernel calls differ). (2) A cancellable call that completes before the cancel takes effect returns its own result; a call with no effect (name lookup) may be abandoned. (3) Multi-call operations check before each call they start except a final close; a cancelled fs.write can leave its target truncated. (4) The simulator follows the same rules; simulated Bend cancellation follows the declared mode. (5) In-process Bend: a running kernel finishes and returns its own result, cancellation observed at the next checkpoint; a call still waiting for the serialized runtime returns BendFault::Cancelled. Not applied: N6's 'Unlike send' marker (nit).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after round 95 (B1, N1-N3, N5): a library call the kernel cannot cancel and that has no effect, such as a name lookup, is abandoned and returns the cancellation error (always, not 'may'); this is distinct from system calls, so file reads are never abandoned. The run-to-end rule covers any system call the kernel cannot cancel, file-system calls being the main case. Socket and pipe waits are cancellable; a cancelled socket or pipe write may have reached the peer. Multi-call operations check before each call except a close. §9.3: cancellation cuts a modeled latency short only where TASK-3 lets it; simulated stdin behaves as a pipe. Bend process mode returns Cancelled unless the reply already arrived; in-process Bend is a foreign call. Not applied: N4 (companion note on soft cleanup deadlines; pre-existing core 7.2 gap).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Revision after round 96 (B1, N1, N2, N4): the abandonment rule names its member: 'A name lookup, a library call that cannot be cancelled and has no effect, is abandoned instead and returns the cancellation error; it runs on, on its own copy of the name, and its result is discarded. A foreign call, such as an in-process Bend kernel, is not abandoned (TASK-5, §10).' TASK-5 lists 'a running system call the kernel cannot cancel (TASK-3)', matching TASK-3. TASK-3 split into three paragraphs; wording fixes. Not applied: N3 (is_terminal under the simulator; optional). Pre-existing finding to file: cancelled output()/status() can orphan a child.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Codex round 98 approved. Not applied: its N1 (FUSE can honor interrupts, so file-system run-to-end is Tide's policy rather than a kernel limit on every file system); the behavior stands as written, and it is a wording precision for a later pass. Follow-ups filed as fx-e3t.

title: Define the Ferox safe-change tooling contract as a concrete machine-facing product surface
description: Synthesize the Ferox tooling contract from the now-separated read-side and mutation-side machine interfaces. This bead should consolidate those decisions into one coherent official safe-change tooling contract that compiler architecture and later tooling work can rely on.
design:
Primary question: Given the read-side and mutation-side machine contracts, what is the final integrated Ferox safe-change tooling contract?

This synthesis task should:
1. Reconcile machine-readable outputs with machine-driven mutation surfaces.
2. Define the official contract boundary, stability story, and phase-by-phase rollout.
3. Produce the canonical tooling contract that architecture and bootstrap tasks can reference without ambiguity.
4. Carry forward compatibility, observability, and validation requirements in one place.
close_reason: Integrated the read-side and mutation-side safe-change tooling contract into the canonical tooling spec, including stability, rollout, and validation expectations.

title: Define the Ferox machine-readable read contract for diagnostics, symbols, metadata, and determinism
description: Ferox's safe-change tooling story depends first on stable machine-readable outputs that tools can consume reliably. This task defines the read-side contract: diagnostics, spans, symbol identity, symbol graphs, project/package metadata, formatter output expectations, and determinism guarantees.
design:
Primary question: What official machine-readable outputs should Ferox tools be able to consume reliably from day one and beyond?

Define:
1. Diagnostic structure, spans, codes, related information, and suggested-fix shape.
2. Stable symbol identity, symbol graph, and package/project metadata outputs.
3. Expectations for deterministic formatting/build-related outputs where they are part of the toolchain contract.
4. Stability and versioning expectations for these read-side outputs.

This task should define the read contract that later compiler services and automation can depend on.
close_reason: Defined the read-side machine contract in spec/TOOLING.md, including diagnostics shape, symbol and metadata outputs, determinism expectations, stability tiers, and validation obligations.

title: Define the Ferox machine-readable mutation contract for refactors, structural rules, and autofix
description: Ferox's tooling moat also depends on what automation is allowed to change safely, not just what it can read. This task defines the mutation-side contract: refactor APIs, structural-rule surfaces, autofix boundaries, safety checks around automated edits, and the point where tools must fall back to human review.
design:
Primary question: What kinds of machine-driven code changes should Ferox officially support, and where are the safety boundaries?

Define:
1. Refactor API surface and expected granularity.
2. Structural-rule and autofix capabilities, preconditions, and guarantees.
3. Boundaries between safe automated edits, suggested edits, and edits that require human confirmation.
4. Logging, traceability, and artifact capture expectations for machine-applied changes.

This task should define the mutation contract that makes safe automated change a real product surface rather than an aspiration.
close_reason: Defined the mutation-side machine contract in spec/TOOLING.md, including official mutation surfaces, safety tiers, structured edit packaging, automation boundaries, auditability, and validation obligations.

title: Decide Fs::remove_dir_all: listed in reference 6.3, absent from 03
description:
## Why

Reference 6.3 says `Fs` has `remove_dir_all` "as std::fs", but 03, which owns the capability
set, never lists it, and 03 §9.5's crash rules name only `create`, `rename`, `remove_file`, and
new subdirectories as directory-entry changes. Agents can call a method whose authority and crash
behavior no normative text defines. Found by round 26 (N6) while reviewing fx-i5p; it predates
that bead.

## Evidence

- `design/reference.md` 6.3, the `impl Fs` comment: "rename, remove_file, remove_dir_all: as
  std::fs".
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 `Fs` row (no `remove_dir_all`, no `remove_dir`),
  §1.1 durability note and §9.5 (entry changes listed without directory removal).
- `reviews/round26-consistency.md` N6.

## Scope

In scope: decide in 03 whether `Fs` has `remove_dir_all` (and `remove_dir`); if it does, add it
to §1.1, say which entry changes it makes durable with `sync_dir`, and say in §9.5 how an unsynced
recursive removal survives a crash (each entry removal whole? the whole tree as one change?).
Then align reference 6.3 (and companion 17 if crash detail is needed). If it does not, remove it
from reference 6.3.

Out of scope: other `Fs` methods.

## Acceptance

- 03 and reference 6.3 agree on whether `remove_dir_all` exists, and 03 states its crash
  behavior if it does.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction among 01 D15, 03, and the reference pair.

## Notes

Prefer Rust's API (D18). A crash rule that loosens fx-i5p's "each entry change survives whole"
model touches D15; ask the owner first. Core reference budget is tight; detail goes to 03 or
companion 17.
close_reason: remove_dir and remove_dir_all decided in 03 §1.1/§9.5, reference 6.3, companion 17; rounds 29-31, round 31 approves with notes.

title: Define the shared Ferox validation, corpus, and observability harness for bootstrap and later compiler work
description: Before implementation spreads across parser, formatter, checker, and CLI work, define a shared validation and observability foundation: unit-test conventions, corpus/golden-test layout, end-to-end script structure, fixture naming, snapshot/update workflow, detailed logging and tracing expectations, failure artifact capture, and CI/local execution strategy. The goal is to prevent each implementation task from inventing its own testing and debugging model.
design:
Primary question: What shared validation and observability system should all early Ferox implementation work plug into?

Define the harness in terms of:
1. Test layers: unit, corpus/golden, integration, and end-to-end.
2. Shared fixture and snapshot layout for parser, formatter, diagnostics, checker, and CLI outputs.
3. Logging and tracing strategy: levels, event categories, structured fields, failure artifacts, and how to enable verbose investigation locally and in CI.
4. Script and automation model: how developers and agents run focused checks versus full validation suites.
5. Forward compatibility: how the same harness can grow into later ownership, concurrency, and verification work without churn.

This task should produce one coherent validation/observability doctrine for the whole bootstrap path.
close_reason: Defined the shared validation, corpus, e2e, logging, artifact, and phased-adoption harness in spec/IMPLEMENTATION.md for bootstrap compiler and tooling work.

title: First running Tide demo: concurrent bug replay and authority widening
description:
## Why

Deliver the next bounded slice of the recorded first demonstration (fx-enq, research/15-rust-dialect.md:237), with the existing language decisions preserved.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md (D0, D11, D14, D15, D18)`
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md (ROOT, TASK, LOCK, authority and replay rules)`
- `conformance/README.md (stub oracle limitations)`

## Scope

A labelled partial-v0 demonstration; existing language decisions and D0 gates remain authoritative.

## Acceptance

the agent-written concurrent service uses supported production std/runtime code under crates/, built only by the admission driver and its trusted toolchain; one command finds a seed that exposes a logical concurrency bug, replays that seed twice with identical event/output traces, and runs a fixed revision over an explicit fixed seed set without the failure. A widened public interface carrying Net produces an access-path authority diff. Publish supported/unsupported surfaces, exact revision/toolchain/seed setup, and a human quickstart. Across EVERY slice that exposes std items (including Tasks, Scope, Task, Shared, SimRoot and Net), production is the runtime owner and the conformance std is a compile-time fixture: replace the corresponding stub item or verify signature/verdict equivalence for every exposed production item. No two unreconciled std surfaces. Each std-exposing child must carry this acceptance or refer to this parent acceptance explicitly. Disk crashes, network I/O, full contract/property tooling, E3 effectiveness, unreviewed-program execution safety and complete-v0 claims are outside this demo. Net can be a genuine unforgeable capability type with operations unavailable in this slice: the widening example need only demonstrate declared authority, not perform network I/O.

## Planning authorization and review

Owner, 2026-10-31: "check with claude before you prime the beads, only do it once you've converged"; later, "nevermind, lets focus on tide, you can use opus from claude". Planning only: six Claude Opus (claude-opus-5-5) passes ended with an approve on the unchanged final candidate. No implementation, v0 scope cut, gate weakening or governance change is part of this run.

Final candidate SHA-256: f83572bbc182fef83c64f95c7f64e0ca8b507e00975fe5e8e0dc935901d13080.

comments.author: codex-priority-planning
comments.text:
Planning-only convergence, 2026-10-31. Repository revision observed at application: 5472a9336661e2cbe9e16f436f8d842d2d76b868; implementation working tree already dirty in another session. Six read-only Claude Opus CLI passes (claude-opus-5-5; rounds 1-5 high effort, round 6 medium/narrow) preceded all tracker writes. Corrections preserved the recorded scheduling-bug demo and executable E1 gate; split entry/lifecycle/cancellation/runner/replay work; reconciled std surfaces; replaced unsized seal coding with a bounded prerequisite-planning task; made that task standalone to avoid parent/blocker ambiguity. The sixth pass approved without required changes. No implementation or language-doc edits and no code tests were part of this planning batch.

Created batch:
fx-nkv: First running Tide demo: concurrent bug replay and authority widening
fx-nkv.1: Production std bootstrap and trusted main entry
fx-kw8.8: Enforce FX0512 for unmarked main
fx-kw8.9: Build admitted binaries and executable tests through tide-admit
fx-nkv.2: Structured task lifecycle on the thread runtime
fx-nkv.3: Scope failure results and level-triggered cancellation

fx-gfq: Freeze the checked-toolchain E1 protocol
fx-ic2: Execute and grade paired E1 on the checked toolchain
fx-koo: Plan seal implementation and contract-hash prerequisites

Final Opus report:

**Verdict: approve.** This resolves the prior blocker and adds no new material error.

**The blocker:**
- SEAL-PLAN is now a standalone P3 task, not a child of fx-gcs (`candidate-v6.md:40`). The edge fx-gcs → SEAL-PLAN can no longer block its own child or form a parent-child cycle. The fx-gcs → fx-k0z edge no longer holds SEAL-PLAN back.
- The acceptance rules out the same trap for successors: "No successor that blocks fx-gcs may also be its child." Implementation beads go under fx-kw8 or another epic. Corpus fixture tasks stay standalone and are linked by labels and blocker edges (`:41`).
- fx-gcs still can't close early. SEAL-PLAN has to swap its temporary blocker for the real incomplete implementation outcomes before it closes (`:42`, `:46`).

**ENTRY:** It now requires `conformance/run.sh` to exit 0 on the whole corpus, including `pure_routes.rs`'s FX0512 mark (`:16`). That takes the earlier advice and weakens nothing.

**Regression check:** Nothing else in the batch weakens an outcome, scope, priority, threshold, or the fx-gcs/fx-kw8 acceptance.

**One wording nit, not blocking:** The risk that matters is a successor's parent epic waiting on that successor, not fx-gcs waiting on the epic. fx-kw8 doesn't wait on its children through blocker edges, so the current wording is safe.

You can apply it through `br`.

title: Production std bootstrap and trusted main entry
description:
## Why

Deliver the next bounded slice of the recorded first demonstration (fx-enq, research/15-rust-dialect.md:237), with the existing language decisions preserved.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md (D0, D11, D14, D15, D18)`
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md (ROOT, TASK, LOCK, authority and replay rules)`
- `conformance/README.md (stub oracle limitations)`

## Scope

Scope: a production facade under crates/ reusing reviewed concepts from spikes, not depending on the throwaway spike or frozen trial stubs; Root, minimal output sinks, Pure declaration, genuine capability identities needed by later slices, and #[tide::main] owned by the toolchain. Root only minted at the trusted entry/test machinery. Record which std surface policy.rs and conformance/run.sh target. Every exposed production item either replaces its conformance/rustc/std stub counterpart or has a compile-time signature/verdict equivalence test against that counterpart, using the same supported candidate fixtures; frozen trials stay frozen. Production runtime behavior has one owner and the conformance stub is only a compile-time fixture. No two unreconciled std surfaces.

The user-visible global-deadlock report (03 section 9.3) stays an obligation for the slice exposing channels or limit; do not add those APIs to satisfy this demonstration. title: Define the minimal Ferox v1 package manifest and workspace-loading contract for bootstrap check/fmt flows
description: The spec now defines ferox.toml, workspace manifests, package-loading facts, and deterministic machine-readable metadata, but the bootstrap queue does not yet track the minimal contract needed to make early ferox check and ferox fmt flows honest. This task should define the smallest package/workspace-loading surface the Rust bootstrap must implement, what can stay stubbed, and how CLI/output behavior should expose package-loading and manifest facts without overbuilding the package system.
design: Primary question: what minimal manifest and workspace-loading contract is required for the first real bootstrap CLI flows? Define: 1. the smallest ferox.toml and workspace manifest subset needed for single-package and workspace-local flows; 2. how package loading, workspace member discovery, and target selection should behave in v1 bootstrap; 3. what machine-readable metadata and failure facts must be exposed; 4. what registry, publishing, and advanced dependency features remain intentionally out of scope.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task clearly answers: what manifest fields and workspace rules are required for bootstrap; what package-loading behavior ferox check/fmt must support; what machine-readable package/workspace facts are emitted; and what package-system features remain deferred. Include one worked single-package example, one worked workspace example, validation expectations for pass/fail manifest fixtures, and logging expectations for manifest parsing, workspace discovery, and package-loading diagnostics.
notes: Decision: the first bootstrap package/workspace-loading layer should support local package roots, explicit workspace member lists, conventional or explicit lib/bin targets, local path dependencies, and deterministic machine-readable package-loading facts. Registry fetching, alternate sources, feature flags, and advanced dependency modes stay out of the first real check/fmt flows and must fail explicitly if encountered.

title: Decide: stop agents asking the owner technical questions
description:
## Why

Agents keep handing the owner technical choices: option menus, "yours to make", and "want me to file beads?". The owner answers with "do what you think is better", "i trust your judgment", or "you make the decisions". This continued at least twice after the Decisions rule landed in AGENTS.md (04302c9, 2026-10-20). Every such question stalls the run until the owner replies.

## Evidence

Owner corrections (session prefix, UTC date, quote):
- 3748816d, 2026-10-19: "2. do what you think is better"; "i will trust your research"
- 0c465b0b, 2026-10-19: a three-way menu on AI_SUPERVISOR.md, answered "do it"
- 9cc7dc47, 2026-10-20: "dont ask me tecnical questions", the answer to a question about io::Error's Pure bound (recorded in the `no-technical-questions` memory)
- 3536eb7f, 2026-10-20, after the rule: the agent called raising the 25k budget "a scope call and yours to make"; the owner said "you make the decisions, i just help here and there"
- c697036a, 2026-10-21, after the rule and the memory: "Should I add 3 to that change?", answered "ok i trust your judgment"
- The same pattern for follow-up beads: 186ae567 "file them", 182a586e "yeah, and continue", f54f050d and 9cc7dc47 "yeah"

Current owners and why they failed:
- AGENTS.md "Decisions" (local overlay): it separates scope from technical choices, but the agent keeps labelling budgets, thresholds, governance mechanics, and follow-up beads as scope. Ambiguous.
- AP-PLAN-001 (canonical): "Report unapproved findings; create issues only for material out-of-scope or schedulable work, deferred outside authorized batches". Agents read this as needing approval before filing follow-ups (186ae567: "this run owned only fx-pcb, so I haven't created them"). Ambiguous. That fix belongs in the Starcompass source repository and is reported, not filed, here.
- AP-SCOPE-001 "stop when a missing scope choice would materially change the result" pulls toward asking. Nothing local says which way an unclear case should go.
- User memory `no-technical-questions`: wording only, and it lives only on this machine.

## Scope

In scope:
- `.claude/settings.json` (permissions)
- the Decisions section in `.agent-protocols.local.md`, with a re-render of `AGENTS.md`

Out of scope:
- canonical protocol text (AP-PLAN-001, AP-SCOPE-001)
- the owner's real scope calls: new features, priorities, publishing, repository moves

## Acceptance

- The AskUserQuestion tool is unavailable in this project.
- In a behavior trial with no expected answer given, a fresh agent faces the three recorded cases (the 25k→30k budget, adding a governance change to a pending commit, filing two follow-up beads). It decides each one, records it, and reports it without asking.
- A control case (whether to publish the repository to a collaborator) is still asked, because it is a scope call.

## Implementation Notes

Recommended enforcement, highest that works:
1. Structure: deny `AskUserQuestion` in the project's `.claude/settings.json` permissions. That removes the menu path entirely. The owner's earlier correction answered such a menu.
2. Behavior-trialled wording: add one line to Decisions that classifies the recurring cases. Budgets, thresholds, review mechanics, and filing follow-up beads are the agent's. When a case is unclear, the agent decides, records it, and reports it. Then run the trial in Acceptance (AP-TEST-001).

Rejected:
- A Stop hook that flags messages ending in "?": it blocks real scope questions and conversational answers.
- Wording without a trial: that is the state today, and it failed twice.

## Verification

- `claude -p` in this repository cannot call AskUserQuestion (it is denied by settings).
- The behavior trial above, run by a fresh subagent, with its transcript summarized on this bead.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the owner wants to keep AskUserQuestion for scope questions. Then do only step 2.
- Stop if the trial still asks on the recorded cases after two wordings that use different mechanisms.

## Maintenance Notes

- To report to Starcompass if the owner asks: AP-PLAN-001 should say whether a run may file follow-up issues for material findings without per-issue approval.

title: Decide File::close(self) under cancellation (TASK-3 consuming checkpoint)
description:
## Why

`File::close(self) -> io::Result<()>` consumes the `File`, and every `File` operation suspends and
so is a cancellation checkpoint (03 §1.1). TASK-3 requires an operation that consumes a value to
return it inside its cancellation error, and an `io::Error` cannot hold a `File`. TASK-6 says
cleanup I/O is "an explicit `close(self)` called under `shield`", but nothing says what an
unshielded `close` in a cancelled scope does. fx-obr fixed the same conflict for
`Child::wait_with_output` by taking `&mut self` (round 70 B1); `close` needs its own decision.

## Evidence

comments.text:
Decision (03 §0, §1.1 File row and Receivers note, TASK-3, TASK-5, TASK-6; core 7.2): File::close(self) is shielded: it may suspend but is not a checkpoint, always closes the descriptor and returns the close's own result even in a cancelled scope. title: Define the transition from ordinary Ferox to optional contracts, ghost code, and deeper verification
description: Ferox has a promising long-term verification direction, but the transition point is still vague. This task is to define how Ferox should move from the safe core to optional verification layers: what the first contract/spec features should be, how ghost/spec code should remain narrow, how verification should interact with ownership and tooling, and how to prevent the language from drifting into proof-first everyday programming.
design:
Primary question: How should Ferox grow from a safe core into optional verification without turning everyday programming into proof engineering?

Define the transition as a staged gradient:
1. First verification layer: contracts, invariants, pure spec functions, ghost code.
2. Interaction with ownership, checked IR, diagnostics, and tooling.
3. Erasure and runtime model boundaries.
4. Non-goals: what deeper proof features stay out of the core language.

The result should explain where verification begins, what it can prove, and how it stays optional.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- What is the first verification layer Ferox should adopt?
- How does that layer interact with ownership and the safe-change tooling contract?
- What stays optional, narrow, and erasable rather than becoming ordinary source-language complexity?
- What verification ambitions are explicitly deferred beyond this layer?

Include:
- one phased roadmap and at least two small examples of the intended contract/spec style;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for contract/spec semantics, pass/fail corpus tests for verified and rejected cases, and end-to-end scripts that exercise mixed ordinary-code plus optional-verification workflows;
- detailed logging/tracing requirements for contract checking, spec/ghost handling, erasure boundaries, and verification-related diagnostics.
notes: Decision: Ferox should grow verification in a staged gradient. V1 remains ordinary code only. The first optional layer is a narrow V2 contract/spec/ghost layer built around requires, ensures, invariants, pure spec functions, and erased ghost code. Stronger proof-oriented constructs remain V3-or-later and should not shape everyday programming unless the narrower layer proves insufficient.

title: Specify resource-handle API surface: Command authority, Child fields under ROOT-4, Stdio
description:
## Why

03 §0 now defines resource handles (fx-zm4), but their API surface is underspecified: the
reference never says a `Command` carries authority, never names `Child`, `Signals`, or `ReadDir`,
and its "every capability method takes `&self`" rule does not fit handles. ROOT-4 says handle
types have no public fields, yet Rust's `Child` exposes `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr` as public
fields, and how a `Stdio` built from a `File` is classified is unstated. Found by round 32 (N1,
N2) and round 33 (N3) while reviewing fx-zm4.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §0 (resource-handle list), §1.1 `Proc` row (`Command`,
  `Child::wait`, `Signals::recv`), ROOT-4 (no public fields, cannot be made from data).
- `design/reference.md` 6.1: `Proc` row says only "`command(prog) -> Command` (Rust's builder)",
  the same words 6.3 uses for the inert `OpenOptions`; 6.1's `&self` bullet; 12.3 paths table.
- Rust std: `Child { pub stdin: Option<ChildStdin>, pub stdout: .., pub stderr: .. }`;
  `Stdio: From<File>`.
- `reviews/round32-consistency.md` N1, N2; `reviews/round33-consistency.md` N3.

## Scope

In scope: in 03, decide how `Child`'s pipes are reached under ROOT-4 (keep Rust's public fields
and narrow ROOT-4, or methods), classify `ChildStdin`/`ChildStdout`/`ChildStderr` and `Stdio`,
and say which receivers handles take; then state in the reference pair that `Command` carries
`Proc`'s authority (unlike `OpenOptions`) and where `Child`, `Signals`, and `ReadDir` live.

Out of scope: process semantics under simulation beyond naming.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides each point with reasoning; the reference or companion states it.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`; detail goes to the
  companion).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction among 02, 03, and the reference pair.

## Notes

Prefer Rust's API (D18). The core reference is at 24,997 of 25,000 tokens. Docs-only: review
rounds, not converge.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decisions (recorded in 03 §1.1 and ROOT-4; reference pair updated):
- Child keeps Rust's public pipe fields (stdin/stdout/stderr: Option of a pipe end), so child.stdout.take() ports unchanged (D18). ROOT-4 narrowed from 'no public fields' (already false of Root) to: each capability/handle type has a private field (no struct literal or Shape construction), and a public field holds a capability or handle, an Option of one, sink config (Root::log), or test-only sim controls. Rejected: accessor methods (break the universal Rust idiom; ROOT-4's purpose is construction, not field visibility).
- ChildStdin/ChildStdout/ChildStderr are resource handles with Proc's authority (kind proc); reads/writes suspend.
- Stdio: piped/inherit/null take no capability; From only for File and the three pipe ends; From<io::Stdout>/<io::Stderr> dropped (sink handles, not fds), and From<OwnedFd>/PipeReader/PipeWriter dropped. Stdio can hold a handle, so not Pure.
- Command is a resource handle carrying Proc's authority, unlike Pure OpenOptions; ambient Command::new stays FX0501.
- Receivers: capability types take &self; handles keep Rust's receivers, except Child::wait_with_output takes &mut self (round 70 B1: a consuming checkpoint must return its value inside the cancellation error per TASK-3, which io::Error cannot hold). Tide-only methods: File::sync, read_owned, write_owned, Signals::recv take &self; File::close takes self.
- Paths: std::process for Command, Child, pipe ends, Stdio, Signal, Signals; std::fs for ReadDir, DirEntry (companion 20; core 12.3 unchanged for budget, Rust's paths).

title: Decide origin syntax: from clauses vs Rust lifetime syntax by a held-out trial
description:
Decide how Ferox spells origins (borrow sources) by a held-out learnability trial.

Context: design/01-design.md D2 replaces Rust's named lifetimes with origins. The semantics are fixed in design/02-memory.md; only the spelling is open. The current spelling uses `from` clauses (`fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&str from self.src>`, struct reference fields without `<'a>`), and accepts named lifetimes that map exactly onto origins as a legacy spelling the formatter rewrites. reviews/round2-simplicity.md argues that because the meanings match, D1's rule (keep Rust's spelling wherever the meaning is the same) favors Rust lifetime syntax. D0 keeps D1/D2 syntax provisional until E1 decides it.

Method:
- Write a held-out task set of about ten tasks that design/reference.md does not mirror, heavy on borrowing: parsers and lexers over &str, iterators over borrowed data, structs holding references from one or several sources, functions returning borrows from several inputs, closures capturing borrows.
- Make two reference variants that differ only in origin spelling: (A) `from` clauses as today; (B) Rust lifetime syntax under Ferox's rules (per-field origins and elision still apply).
- Run a fresh agent per arm that reads only its variant, then grade both arms with one independent grader using the rubric in trials/e1/grading.md.

Acceptance:
- trials/e1-origins/ holds both arms' programs, notes, and a grading with first-check pass rate, borrow-related error counts, and iterations to green per arm.
- design/01-design.md D2 records the chosen spelling with that evidence, and design/reference.md and design/02-memory.md use it.

title: Respell v1 proof forms and field-borrow declarations as valid Rust under D18
description:
## Why

D18 makes every Tide program a valid Rust 2024 crate, but the v1 proof forms
and field-borrow declarations are still written in draft 3.5's grammar,
which rustc cannot parse. 01 D10's last bullet and D2 record this as
pending: the spelling is decided before v1, and E1 does not cover it.
Until it is decided, 04 describes a v1 that cannot exist under D18.

## Evidence

- `design/01-design.md` D10, last bullet: v1's proof forms (`spec fn`,
  `proof fn`, `law fn`, `ghost let`, proof blocks, views, spec integer
  types) must become attributes, toolchain `!` forms, or library types.
- `design/01-design.md` D2: field borrows (`fn advance(&mut self.{pos})`)
  are not Rust; their spelling (a source transform or Rust's view types) is
  open until v1.
- `design/04-contracts.md` §0 "Spelling" and §1.2 grammar: the v1 forms are
  labeled as draft 3.5 grammar pending respelling; `tide` fences mark the
  blocks that use them.
- `design/02-memory.md` §7: field-borrow syntax labeled as not Rust.
- `research/15-rust-dialect.md`, v1 table: `prove`, `spec fn`, `decreases`,
  laws are "Lib: attributes, as Prusti, Creusot, and Verus show";
  field-borrow declarations are "Open".
- Already decided in fx-pcb (keep): `#[requires]`, `#[ensures]`,
  `#[decreases]`, `#[diverges]`, `decreases!`, `#[invariant(..)]` on types,
  `requires!`/`ensures!` in closures, `hole!(goal)`. The `!` clause forms
  are rewritten by the enclosing function attribute and not exported,
  because an attribute and a `!` macro cannot share a name (E0252).

## Scope

In scope:
- A spelling for each v1 form: `spec fn`, `proof fn`, `closed spec fn`,
  `law fn` (trait items and impl discharges), `ghost let`, `proof { }`
  blocks, `assert ... by(..)`, `assume`, `reveal`, `x@` views, `int`/`nat`

title: Decide whether a spawn under Tasks::limit suspends and how it meets cancellation
description:
## Why

Under `Tasks::limit(n)`, `spawn` waits for a free slot (`design/reference.md` 7.1), but 03 §1.2
lists `Scope`'s waits as "none", and the Tasks row in §1.1 does not list `spawn` among the
operations that suspend. So the chapter never says whether a limited `spawn` suspends, whether it is
a checkpoint, or what it returns when its scope is cancelled while it waits. Found by round 73 while
reviewing fx-nyy; predates it.

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §1.1 Tasks row, §1.2 `Scope` row, §6.1, TASK-3.
- `design/reference.md` 7.1 (`limit` and `spawn`).
- `reviews/round73-consistency.md` (out-of-scope findings).

## Scope

In scope: decide whether a `spawn` under `limit` suspends, whether it is a checkpoint, and its
behavior in a cancelled scope (`spawn` takes `self` and returns `Task`, so it has no error to
carry cancellation); align §1.1, §1.2, and the reference.

## Acceptance

- 03 decides it with reasoning; §1.1, §1.2, and the reference agree.
- The core stays under D14's budget (recount with `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds, not converge.
close_reason: Decided in 03 §6.1/TASK-3, core 7.1, companion 15.2: a limited spawn is a checkpoint; in a cancelled calling scope it starts nothing. Reviews: rounds 80-83, 85 (Opus), 84, 86 (Codex, approve). Follow-ups: fx-0ai.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Decision (03 §0 Checkpoint, §1.1 Tasks row, §1.2 Scope row, §6.1 new paragraph, TASK-5; core 7.1 Bounded concurrency):
Under Tasks::limit(n), Scope::spawn waits for a free slot. The wait suspends but is shielded like a join: not a checkpoint, never interrupted by cancellation. In a cancelled scope spawn still waits, the child still starts and observes cancellation at its first checkpoint, so TASK-2/TASK-4 decide outcomes exactly as for an unlimited scope. The core's provisional rule becomes firm.
Reasons: spawn returns Task, not Result, so it has no error to carry a cancellation; every spawned child runs, so a child that turns cancellation into a value (companion 15.2 fetch_one) still reports one.
Rejected: (a) skipping the child in a cancelled scope (pre-cancelled Task): its join fails with no child error behind it and per-item outcomes are lost; (b) starting it immediately over the limit: breaks the attenuation; (c) making spawn a checkpoint returning Result: changes the std::thread::scope shape at every call site for a wait only limited scopes have.
Cost: a body in a cancelled limited scope drains its remaining spawns at width n; it can stop early by checking tasks.checkpoint() in its loop. The wait is as soft as deadlines (TASK-5).
Core at 24,993 of 25,000 tokens.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Addendum after round 80 (B1): the limit is one count shared by all scopes from that Tasks (matches the Semaphore mapping, companion 14.3). A task that holds a slot and waits for one (spawning into its own scope, or a nested scope from the same Tasks) can deadlock the pool, as with any semaphore; cancellation and deadlines do not break it, and the simulator reports it (§9.3). Skipping children in a cancelled scope (rejected option a) would break that deadlock only when something cancels the scope, so it stays rejected; 03 §6.1 says so and advises nested work use its own Tasks or no limit. Rejected: slot lending (a slot holder releases its slot while it waits) — more state and a new notion of 'live' for a pattern a separate Tasks avoids. N1/N3/N4/N5 fixed in text; N2 not applied (core at 24,993 of 25,000; 7.1 already states it).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Reversal after round 81 (B1). Final decision: the slot wait of a limited spawn IS a checkpoint. In a cancelled scope a limited spawn returns at once and starts nothing, even with a free slot (level-triggered, so the outcome does not depend on slot timing). The child counts as one whose first checkpoint returned the cancellation and which returned E::from(TaskError::Cancelled): TASK-2/TASK-4 apply unchanged (echo when body Err/sibling failure caused it; DeadlineExceeded when the scope's own deadline did; join returns Err(Cancelled)). TASK-3 notes it.
Reason: the count is shared across scopes from one Tasks, so slots can be held by other scopes' children that this scope's cancellation never reaches; an uninterruptible wait could outlast the scope's deadline without bound and go unreported (round 81). A checkpoint also lets a deadline or cancel() break hold-and-wait deadlocks (child spawning into its own scope or a nested scope from the same Tasks); otherwise the simulator reports a global deadlock.
Cost: an unstarted child cannot turn cancellation into a value. Companion 15.2 therefore drops its scope deadline and relies on the operation deadline it already passes to net.get (a late-starting child gets Timeout at once). 03's 12.2 example uses an unlimited scope and is unaffected.
Superseded: the earlier shielded-wait decision and its addendum. Still rejected: starting over the limit (breaks attenuation); spawn returning Result (a ? on every spawn).
Core 7.1 states it plus a one-line deadlock warning (round 81 N3); core at 24,995 of 25,000.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Refinement after round 82 (B1, N1-N4): the limited spawn observes the CALLING task's cancellation (TASK-3). It drops f unrun and, like any checkpoint returning a cancellation, sets the caller's echo bit; the child's join returns Err(Cancelled). If the scope spawned into is itself cancelled, the 'as if cancelled at its first checkpoint and propagated' rule applies (TASK-2/TASK-4 unchanged). If not (a task in a cancelled nested scope spawning into an enclosing scope passed down), the unstarted child is an echo and that scope is unaffected, so one request's deadline cannot cancel a server scope. Not applied: 14.3 timeout row and 03 §6.5 deadlock pointer (nits).

title: State the Pure status of simulator objects (sim.world, faults, nodes, LogConfig)
description:
## Why

The `Pure` status of the simulator's own objects is never stated: `sim.world`, `sim.faults`,
`SimNode`, `NodeTask`, and `Root`'s `log: LogConfig` field. A test helper that takes one of these
cannot tell whether a `Pure` bound or a `par_map` capture accepts it. The risk is low because
they exist only in test code, but 02 §9 claims to own the full table. Found by round 32 (N4).

## Evidence

- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §9.2 (`sim.world`, `sim.faults`, `sim.node`), §9.5
  (nodes, `NodeRoot`); `design/reference.md` 6.2 (`Root`'s `log` field), 6.8; companion 17
  (`SimNode`, `NodeTask`, provisional).
- `design/02-memory.md` §9: none of these appear.
- `reviews/round32-consistency.md` N4.

## Scope

In scope: classify each object (most act on the simulated world without a capability argument,
so they are resource handles of the simulated capabilities and not `Pure`; `LogConfig` may be
plain configuration), and state it in 02 §9 or 03 §9.2, with a companion line if agents need it.

Out of scope: changing simulator APIs.

## Acceptance

- Each named object's `Pure` status is stated once, in its owner, and the other documents agree.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds. Avoid core reference changes (24,997 of 25,000 tokens).
close_reason: 02 §9 states the Pure status of SimRoot, NodeRoot, sim.world's type, Faults, SimNode, NodeTask, and LogConfig; companion §17 points to it. Reviews fx-t99-r1 (Opus, Codex), r2 (Opus), r3 (Codex) approve.

title: Decide OnceLock and Sync-mutation types in the Pure table (owner decision)
description:
## Why

02 §9 owns the `Pure` table, but reference 6.6 and 03 §3.1 call more types not-`Pure` than 02
does, and nothing says whether a local (non-static) `OnceLock` is admitted at all. If one were
admitted and `Pure`, a `par_map` closure calling `get_or_init` on a shared `&OnceLock` would
observe which branch ran first, breaking 02's determinism guarantee for parallel regions. Found
by round 32 (N3) and round 33 (N4) while reviewing fx-zm4.

## Evidence

- `design/reference.md` 6.6: synchronization handles include "`OnceLock`, and any `Sync` type
  whose `&self` API can observe or cause mutation".
- `design/03-authority-concurrency.md` §3.1: not-`Pure` includes "everything in
  `std::sync::raw`"; §1.2: `Mutex`, `RwLock`, and weak atomics live in `std::sync::raw`.
- `design/02-memory.md` §9 "`Pure`: no authority reachable": lists neither `OnceLock`, the
  general `Sync`-mutation rule, nor `std::sync::raw`.
- 03 GLOBAL table and companion 14.1 forbid `static` `OnceLock`/`LazyLock` (`FX0502`), but say
  nothing about a local one.
- `reviews/round32-consistency.md` N3, `reviews/round33-consistency.md` N4.

## Decision needed (owner)

Is a local `OnceLock` (and `LazyLock`, `OnceCell`) admitted? Options: (a) admitted, created
with `&Tasks` like other synchronization handles, and not `Pure`; (b) rejected by ADMIT-1
(`FX0520`), with a pattern to use instead; (c) admitted and `Pure` only when `!Sync`
(`OnceCell`). Recommend before writing; this changes which programs check.

## Scope

In scope: the decision above; make 02 §9 the single statement of the not-`Pure` set (add
`std::sync::raw`, the `OnceLock` outcome, and decide whether to keep reference 6.6's general
"any `Sync` type whose `&self` API can observe or cause mutation" rule, and if so state it in
02); align 03 §1.2/§3.1 and reference 6.6.

Out of scope: other `Pure` questions (resource handles were settled by fx-zm4).

## Acceptance

- 02 §9, 03 §3.1, and reference 6.6 name the same not-`Pure` set.
- A review round in `reviews/` finds no contradiction.

## Notes

Docs-only: review rounds. The core reference is at 24,997 of 25,000 tokens (companion "Core
count" line); any core change must be paid for by a cut. Stop and ask before changing 01 D7 or
D9.
close_reason: OnceLock/LazyLock rejected (FX0520); OnceCell/LazyCell Pure; 02 §9, 03 §3.1/§3.3/ADMIT-1, reference 6.4/6.6/6.9, companion 14.1 aligned; rounds 34-35 (approve with notes, resolutions applied); core 24,969 tokens.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision (2026-10-20): (b) OnceLock and LazyLock are rejected by ADMIT-1 (FX0520); fix: build the value before spawning, or Shared<Option<T>> with `with`. OnceCell and LazyCell stay admitted and Pure (not Sync, task-local like Cell). Reference 6.6's general 'any Sync type whose &self API can observe or cause mutation' rule is replaced by a structural rule in 02 §9: a type with a user-written `unsafe impl Sync` is a synchronization handle, so not Pure unless #[trusted_pure]. Fits D7's existing 'synchronization handle' term; no D7/D9 change. Reason: OnceLock/LazyLock shared by & in par_map make the winning branch observable (init value, sink output, panic); their remaining Tide use (cross-task lazy init) is covered by Shared::with; the general rule was not structurally decidable.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Owner decision revised (2026-10-20), after round 34 B2: drop the 'user-written unsafe impl Sync => not Pure' clause. Reason: it conflicts with D7's Pure definition unless D7 is edited, changes no verdict for sound code (a sound Sync type mutating through &self synchronizes via atomics, locks, raw pointers, or FFI, all already not Pure), and falsely flags &mut-only UnsafeCell wrappers. 03 §3.3 instead states the structural argument: std's Sync interior-mutable types are listed or rejected; outside std, Sync needs unsafe impl Sync, a trust hole under the unsafe grant whose soundness obligation covers this, as for unsafe impl Send. No D7 change. The OnceLock/LazyLock decision (b) stands.

title: Enforce every FX rule the reference names in tide-admit
description:
## Why

E1's gate run (fx-ic2) compares Tide writers against Rust writers. If the driver does not reject
code that breaks a rule the reference teaches (for example a lossy `as`, FX0301), a Tide writer can
pass with code that is not Tide, and the comparison flatters Tide. No bead owns enforcing the FX
rules beyond fx-kw8's allowlist, `Pure`, and authority checks: `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md`
§10.1 lists this as E1-P14.

## Evidence

- `trials/e1-checked/protocol.md (§10.1 row E1-P14, §10.2 item 3)`
- `design/reference.md (every FX code it names)`
- `conformance/README.md (AWAITS CHECKER cases)`
- `reviews/fx-gfq-r1-codex.md (finding 2)`

## Scope

Make tide-admit report, with the stated code and at the reference's severity, every violation
of a rule whose FX code design/reference.md names: reject the error-level ones, including FX0301 (lossy `as`), the macro and derive codes, globals,
`Root` misuse, async, thread::spawn, Mutex/select habits, catch_unwind, ignored `Result` (FX0702),
unused imports (FX0913), and the contract-placement codes, and report the lint-level ones
(FX0508, FX0607, FX0608) as lints without rejecting the crate. Conformance case marks record
only errors today, so the runner needs a lint mark for these cases. Split into child slices if one session
cannot finish it. No new language semantics.

## Acceptance

For every FX code that design/reference.md names, a conformance case violating it gets that code
from the driver at the reference's severity (rejected for an error, reported without rejection for
a lint), and `conformance/run.sh` reports no AWAITS CHECKER line for those codes.
