comments.author: lucca

Revisit only if it proves heavy; narrowing it would loosen protocol §10.2's readiness item 3, which is the owner's call.

description:
## Why

## Evidence

title: Port conformance/run.sh to a Rust test target
description:
## Why

`conformance/run.sh` (149 lines of bash and awk) has become the corpus's verdict engine: it parses
`//~` marks with awk, scrapes rustc's and the driver's short-format diagnostics with awk, and
decides binary versus library with `grep '^fn main'`, a heuristic that forced a dummy `fn main`
into `root_no_main.rs` (fx-kw8.8) and bit fx-nkv.1's `root_main_nested.rs`.

Decision (2026-11-01, agent, after a web research pass at the owner's request to pick among Rust,
xtask, mise tasks, Python, and Nushell): port it to Rust as a `harness = false` integration test
target in the root workspace. Reasons: compiler UI-test runners in the Rust ecosystem are Rust
(rustc's compiletest; `ui_test`, used through `harness = false`), and the corpus already follows
their `//~`/`//@` conventions; a test target runs under `cargo test` with no new tool; the stable
oracle can use `--error-format=json` instead of text scraping; mark parsing gets types and unit
tests. Rejected: xtask (a workspace-automation convention, not a test mechanism); `ui_test` as a
dependency (its `//~ LEVEL: msg` grammar differs from Tide's per-line code lists, two compilers,
two modes, and the AWAITS CHECKER verdict; adopting it means rewriting every case's marks; revisit
if the formats converge); mise tasks (adds a tool and still leaves the logic in shell); Python (a
second runtime and no types for the verdict logic); Nushell (still working toward 1.0 stability,
and niche for agent authors). `scripts/autorun.sh`, `scripts/handoff-guard.sh`, and the
spike and trial scripts stay shell.

## Scope

Replace `conformance/run.sh` with a Rust test target (for example `cargo test --test conformance`)
that keeps the case format, verdicts (PASS, AWAITS CHECKER, FAIL), the `--trace` listing, and the
stable-rustc oracle plus pinned-driver checks. Decide crate type from the case explicitly (a `//@`
directive or rustc's own entry detection), not by grep. Update README.md, conformance/README.md,
AGENTS.md's Verification section (through `.agent-protocols.local.md`, then re-render), and every
open bead whose Acceptance names `conformance/run.sh`.

## Acceptance

The Rust runner gives the same verdict per case as `conformance/run.sh` on the full corpus
(compare both outputs once before deleting the script), runs with stdin closed and exits non-zero
on any FAIL, and `cargo test --workspace` passes.

title: Define Ferox line span semantics with and without trailing line breaks
description: Formatter and diagnostics work is cleaner if Ferox explicitly distinguishes a line span excluding the trailing line break from a span including it. This task should define those concepts, where each is used, and how they map onto the authoritative span model.
design: Primary question: should Ferox explicitly model both the logical span of a line excluding its terminator and the physical span including the trailing line break? Define where each form is used, how they compose with byte-authoritative spans, and how formatter and diagnostics code should request the right one.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task defines both line-span concepts, names their intended uses, clarifies newline-edge cases such as final lines without terminators and CRLF, and explains how diagnostics and formatting avoid ambiguity by using the right span flavor.
notes: Decision: keep this idea. Ferox should explicitly model both line spans excluding the trailing line break and line spans including it. The excluding-break span should be the default logical line-content view for diagnostics text snippets, parser-facing line reasoning, and most user-facing source displays. The including-break span should be an explicit secondary view for formatter/layout logic, faithful source slicing, and operations that must preserve or reason about physical line terminators. CRLF counts as a single logical line break whose full byte extent belongs only to the including-break span. Final lines without terminators have identical excluding/including spans. Rationale: Roslyn's TextLine model shows this split removes ambiguity around line boundaries and keeps formatting and diagnostics from overloading one span concept. Apply in v1 immediately as part of the bootstrap source contract, before formatter and richer diagnostics behavior harden further. This is a small foundational distinction, not a later optimization feature.

title: Settle D18 review notes before the checker's test corpus
description:
## Why

Review rounds 12–15 on the D18 application (fx-pcb) approved v0 with no
blocking contradiction, but left notes the reviewers said must be settled
before the checker's conformance test corpus is written. Each is an
under-specified rule or a small inconsistency a test would have to guess.

## Evidence

Each note's full text, with file:line evidence and a proposed fix, is in
the review file named:

- `reviews/round12-consistency.md`:
  - N4: float functions do not cover `from_bits`, `f32`, `mul_add`, `sqrt`.
  - N6: whether a plain `fn main()` without `#[tide::main]` is allowed;
    the habit row for it cites rustc's E0580 instead of an FX code.
  - N7: property tests need Tide's std to replace Rust's `#[test]`; no
    design text states it. `#[error]`/`#[from]`/`#[source]`/`#[codec]` are
    derive helper attributes, not proc macros.
  - N8: the Bend example's `#[ensures(.., by = ..)]` puts a top-level
    comma in a clause, against 04's one-expression rule.
  - N9: "stack overflow fails the seed" has no mechanism when the
    simulator runs in one process.
  - N11 (part): the spike's `tide-admit` reports the `Pure` check as
    `FX0510`, which the design uses for the least-authority lint.
  - N12: `design/reference.md` (about 87.7k characters, estimated 22–24k
    tokens) has never been counted against its 25,000-token budget; no
    counting script exists.
- `reviews/round13-consistency.md` N3: 04 §1.2's `trait_fn`/`impl_fn`
  grammar rules lack a tier mark; the reference does not say v0 rejects
  clauses on trait methods, or with which FX code. Also: D18 and D12 give
  different reasons for building an interpreter; RUST-6 has no tier.
- `reviews/round14-consistency.md` N3: reassigning a `&mut` parameter
  (`cur = &mut n.next`) is rejected by the spike's closure lowering
  (E0521, E0597) in any function with `#[ensures]`, and "value at return"
  is ambiguous for it, which affects `tide fix`'s rewrite to `final(*x)`.
  N4: the README's "no package code runs at build time" needs a qualifier

title: Define a sharper ownership-aware concurrency model that makes Ferox safer to evolve without capability-lattice complexity
description: Ferox currently has a prudent but still underpowered concurrency story. This task is to define a more compelling ownership-aware concurrency direction: make ownership transfer, immutable sharing, and synchronized sharing visually and semantically distinct; identify what should remain explicit and restricted; and find a model that is safer to change than ad hoc concurrency without importing Pony/Verona-scale capability machinery.
design:
Primary question: What concurrency model makes Ferox safer to evolve while staying ownership-centered and mechanically simple?

Define the model around:
1. Concurrency modes: ownership transfer, immutable sharing, and synchronized shared mutation.
2. Surface syntax and APIs: what should be visually explicit in code.
3. Structured execution: task spawning, lifetimes, cancellation/join boundaries, and what remains out of scope.
4. Safety and change story: which race-prone or maintenance-hostile patterns are prevented by construction.

Do not import a full capability lattice. The goal is a small, explicit model that composes with Ferox ownership rules.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- What are the core Ferox concurrency primitives?
- How do ownership transfer, immutable sharing, and synchronized sharing differ in syntax and semantics?
- Which concurrency patterns are intentionally disallowed to keep reasoning simple?
- Why is this model safer to change than ad hoc concurrency in comparable languages?

Include:
- a few canonical examples and one explicit list of non-goals;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for concurrency typing/checking rules, scenario tests for allowed and forbidden sharing patterns, and end-to-end scripts that exercise task spawn/join/error flows;
- detailed logging requirements for task lifecycle, ownership transfer, synchronization boundaries, and concurrency-related diagnostics.
close_reason: Defined the ownership-aware concurrency model in spec/LANGUAGE.md, V1_DIRECTION.md, and spec/IMPLEMENTATION.md, including access modes, task capture rules, non-goals, and validation expectations.

design: Primary question: how should Ferox plan for multiple text metrics later without introducing multiple authoritative position systems now? Define the later-performance stance for fast conversions across bytes, human-facing columns, and editor encodings, while keeping one canonical internal metric.
acceptance_criteria: Done means this task records the canonical-metric rule, describes later conversion/indexing layers Ferox may add for performance, explains why v1 should not expose multiple authoritative coordinate systems, and notes expected validation/benchmark implications.

title: Define the concrete Ferox source-language personality so the language feels readable, regular, and worth using
description: The high-level thesis is now much sharper than the concrete day-to-day source-language feel. This task is to define what writing normal Ferox should actually feel like: expression orientation, control-flow style, patterns, API conventions, common function shapes, and the balance between restriction and pleasantness. The goal is to turn the current FP-shaped readability direction into a more concrete source-language identity without widening the semantic core.
design:
Primary question: What should everyday Ferox code look and feel like when the language is working well?

Define the source-language personality through concrete examples:
1. Function and module shape.
2. Expression orientation versus statement-heavy style.
3. Pattern matching and destructuring norms.
4. Mutation boundaries and transformation style without relying on pipeline syntax.
5. API conventions that support readable left-to-right data flow through named steps, nested calls, or expression blocks without widening the semantic core.

This task should make Ferox feel tangible, not just principled.
acceptance_criteria:
Done means this task answers all of the following clearly:
- What does idiomatic Ferox code look like?
- Which syntax and style choices are central to the language's identity?
- How do transformation-heavy helpers, mutation boundaries, matching, and helper functions fit together in normal code?
- What source-language moves are intentionally discouraged because they raise entropy?

Include:
- 3-5 canonical code snippets that illustrate the recommended Ferox style;
- a downstream implementation validation plan with unit tests for the relevant syntax/forms, formatter and parser golden tests for the canonical snippets, and end-to-end scripts that exercise normal authoring/refactoring flows;
- detailed logging requirements for parser, formatter, and diagnostic output so source-language ergonomics issues are easy to debug.
notes: Decision: Ferox source personality should be explicit, expression-oriented, ADT-heavy, and regular. Idiomatic code uses match for typed state, named intermediates across representation or failure boundaries, small helper functions where they clarify transformations, tight local mutation, and honest public APIs built from enums, Option, and Result. Discouraged styles include flag-driven APIs, operator-driven composition, broad mutation chains, and grab-bag modules.

title: Task limits, deadlines, checkpoints, and isolation
description:
## Why

Tasks::limit, Scope::set_deadline, Scope::cancel (unless fx-nkv.3 ships it), Tasks::checkpoint, Tasks::shield, Tasks::spawn_isolated and Panicked, TaskError::DeadlineExceeded, on the thread runtime and under the seeded scheduler. title: Settle seal mechanism gaps: phase, stable IDs, erased clauses, writer, manifest owner
description:
## Why

fx-koo planned the implementation of SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 (`design/04-contracts.md` §11.1),
the v0 seal check that fx-gcs waits on. Five points the code needs are unstated or
loose in the design, and each implementation slice would otherwise decide them alone,
giving several owners for one invariant (AP-OWNERSHIP-001). Settle them in their
owning documents first. These are technical choices; decide them (AGENTS.md, Decisions).

## Evidence

1. Where the check runs. `design/04-contracts.md:1319-1320` (SEAL-3) and
   `design/01-design.md:743` say the driver checks the seal "before rustc runs", but
   SEAL-2 (`04:1265-1274`) hashes what paths, method calls, operators, and
   projections resolve to, and counts an impl as applying "where the driver's trait
   selection cannot rule an impl out", which needs rustc's resolution and type
   analysis. D18 (`01:978-992`) already reads "before rustc runs" as before the crate
   is admitted, with checks before and after rustc's analysis. State which phase
   computes seal hashes and that nothing is emitted or run before FX0920 is decided.
2. Stable IDs. D14 (`01:894`) says "symbols have stable IDs"; SEAL-1 lists entries
   "by stable ID", and §11 (`04:1207`) and SEAL-2 resolve names "to stable IDs and
   content hashes" so a rename leaves a hash unchanged. Nothing defines a v0 stable
   ID, how hashed text abstracts the names it references, or how cycles (mutually
   recursive functions, recursive types) hash. The identity must extend, not
   duplicate, the public-item identity fx-kw8.10 and fx-kw8.11 introduce.
3. Erased clauses. Release builds erase clauses (`04:634-637`), but SEAL-2 computes a
   seal hash per configuration "after cfg evaluation", release included, and an
   interface entry fixes the contract. Say what a release-configuration hash covers.
4. The writer. SEAL-1 (`04:1247-1264`) has `tide seal` write `tide.seal`, but v0's
   toolchain is the `tide-admit` driver called by a trusted build caller, with no
   `tide` CLI yet (README "Status"). Name v0's writer and the provisional file format,
   so the corpus and the check share one.
5. The manifest. The manifest entry fixes grants, dependency grants, authority
   policies (D17, v0), and the `[contracts]` table. `tide.toml` is provisional
   (`design/reference.md:1022`), and grants reach the driver only as operator flags
   (`crates/tide-admit/src/invocation.rs:96-102`). Name the one owner that reads the
   manifest and passes its content to the check.

## Scope

In scope: `design/04-contracts.md` §11.1 (and §11 if stable IDs land there),
`design/01-design.md` D11, D14, or D18 where a point belongs there,
`conformance/rules.md` SEAL rows if they change, and `design/reference.md` only if the
core states something that changes (within 25,000 tokens, `scripts/count-tokens.sh`).

Out of scope: code; new seal semantics beyond what SEAL-1..6 state; SEAL-4 and SEAL-5
(`tide review`, FX0921).

## Acceptance

- Each of the five points is decided with reasons in its owning document, with no
  change to what a seal fixes (SEAL-2's covered parts stay as written).
- The decisions name one owner each for stable identity, clause normalization, seal
  file format, and manifest reading, matching fx-kw8.15 (identity), fx-kw8.16 (clauses), fx-kw8.17 (seal file), and fx-kw8.20 (manifest).

## Verification

- Review rounds under `GOVERNANCE.md` (docs-only design work: Opus review plus the
  Codex pass).
- `scripts/count-tokens.sh` if `design/reference.md` changes.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if a point cannot be settled without changing what a seal fixes; that is a
  scope call for the owner.
